19890-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary was the journal of the American Missionary Association. Volume 50, number 6, is the June 1896 issue. Its notices direct letters about the work to corresponding secretaries in New York. Financial letters go to the treasurer. Woman's work has its own secretary at the Woman's Bureau. The Association ran missions among freedpeople, Native Americans, and immigrants.

Missionary monthlies mixed reports, appeals, and obituaries. Field letters showed donors what their money built: schools and churches. The AMA had abolitionist roots and a long Southern school network. A single issue preserves that machinery in motion. Historians of education and race use such runs heavily. June 1896 sits deep in the Jim Crow era.
20093-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary for April 1896 is volume fifty, number four, of a monthly journal. Various hands wrote its reports on mission work at home and abroad. Letters on funds went to the treasurer in New York. Letters on women's work went to the Woman's Bureau secretary.

Inside are field reports, news, and appeals from the association's work. Such journals linked far-off missions with churches that gave the funds. Readers can see how missions were run, staffed, and sold to supporters. The issue is a plain window on American mission life in 1896.
21595-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary for February 1896, volume fifty, number two, comes from the American Missionary Association in New York. The monthly sold for fifty cents a year from Bible House, on Fourth Avenue. Merrill E. Gates of Massachusetts led the association, with M. E. Strieby as editor.

Contents promise an outlook editorial, a Lincoln Memorial Day piece, and a tale called Pat's Miss'n Box. An essay treats the problem of illiteracy, a core concern of the group's schools. Lists name field workers and teachers' homes across the South and beyond. Receipts close the number, accounting for gifts to the cause.
21952-the-american-missionary-volume-50-:
The American Missionary Association reports its work in this March 1896 number of The American Missionary, the fiftieth volume's third issue. Editorials ask what now, remember Bishop Haygood, and plead the present need of the Indians. Memorials honor a college president and a teacher lately dead. Reports from the South bring word of Wilmington, North Carolina, a mountain family feud, and funny answers from mission schools.

Other pages cover Thanksgiving among the Indians, the Watsonville and Santa Cruz missions to the Chinese, and women's state organizations. The Association, born of the abolition movement, ran schools for freed people, Native Americans, and immigrants. This monthly is its bulletin board: receipts, needs, and small victories, printed for the churches that paid the bills.
23057-how-the-redoubt-was-taken-1896:
Campfires line the heights in How the Redoubt Was Taken, a war tale dated 1896. The narrator, always superstitious, was troubled by a piece of augury at that moment. He sought his couch but could not sleep. He got up and paced for a while, eyes on the enemy's long line of campfires along the heights past Cheverino village.

A redoubt, an earthwork fort, must be stormed before the story ends, and the sleepless night loads the assault with dread. The tale descends from Tolstoy's Sevastopol world, where a young officer's fear and vanity share the same tent. Battle here is confusion, smoke, and sudden clarity. Readers get a compact, honest piece of nineteenth-century war writing, more interested in what a soldier feels than in what his generals planned.
a-brief-history-of-the-united-states-pg6: John Bach McMaster, one of the great tellers of the nation's past, sums up the story of the United States for students in this clear, trusted textbook. From early days through the modern age he keeps the tale moving while covering the ground. A classroom classic that taught young readers how their country came to be.
aristophanes-lysistrata-1896: Lysistrata, Aristophanes's great anti-war comedy, 1896 edition. The women's sex strike. This book preserves that classic. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
arxiv-2511-20096:
Ahmed, Armaghan, Naweed, and colleagues build an early warning system for forest fires. Their 2025 paper compares top detection models on new data. Catching fires at the smoke-plume stage saves forests. Existing datasets mostly show fires already raging widely. Models trained on them miss faint early signs.

The team generated early-fire images inside a game engine. Red Dead Redemption 2 supplied synthetic smoke and flame scenes. Published real images were merged into the dataset. Four detectors were benchmarked on the combined set. YOLOv7 and its tiny variant faced detection transformers. Transformers entered forest fire prediction here for the first time. YOLOv7 posted the highest accuracy and fastest inference. Its memory footprint suits small embedded devices. YOLOv7-tiny was judged best overall for early warning. Deformable DETR produced fewer false alarms instead. But it missed more fires and ran slower. Watchtower cameras could run the tiny model continuously.
arxiv-2511-20296:
Shi, Jiang, Lian, Yu, and Fu rebuild CT scans from few views with one provable model. Their 2025 paper presents PromptCT for sparse-view reconstruction. Sparse scans cut patient radiation dose substantially. Missing angles leave heavy streak artifacts though. Clinics need one model per view setting today.

Separate models for each setting cost too much storage. Worse, prior networks rarely prove their stability properties. LipNet, their prior network, is Lipschitz by construction. That bound is proved explicitly, not just hoped. A prompt module tells the network the sampling setting. One model then serves many view counts. The unfolding framework embeds LipNet as its prior. Convergence of the iteration is analyzed formally. Simulated and real data both tested the system. Image quality beat benchmark reconstruction methods. Storage costs dropped versus per-setting rivals. Data and code are publicly shared. Hospital deployment gets simpler and safer.
arxiv-2511-20696:
Dan Li, Hye-Bin Shin, and Yeon-Woo Choi tackle in 2025 a headache for brain-computer interfaces: decoding that forgets earlier users. Brainwave signals differ so much between people that a decoder trained on new users overwrites what it learned from old ones. The usual cure stores old recordings and replays them, but privacy rules and memory limits make that unattractive. Their framework, ProNECL, keeps the knowledge while storing no original signals.

Instead of recordings, ProNECL stores one prototype per class: an average feature pattern for each imagined movement. When a new subject's brainwave data arrives, feature alignment pulls its patterns toward the stored prototypes. Knowledge distillation, training the new model to mimic the old one's behaviour, guards earlier learning. On the BCI Competition IV benchmarks, datasets 2a and 2b, the framework balanced remembering old subjects against adapting to new ones better than rival continual-learning methods did.
arxiv-2511-20996:
Jingxi Chen and colleagues teach in 2025 an image model a new trick by recycling one. Editors love layered images, foreground objects separated from background so each can be edited, but splitting a photo into layers is hard and training data is scarce. The team noticed layer decomposition is inpainting and outpainting in disguise: remove the object and fill the background, or extract the object and complete its covered parts.

So they fine-tuned a diffusion-based inpainting model for the job, adding a fusion module mixing text and image context with linear-cost attention to preserve detail. Training used a synthetic dataset built from open-source assets. On background object removal the adapted model gained 1.71 decibels of PSNR, a fidelity score, and cut the FID gap by 9.99 points over baselines. It recovered occluded object parts better than rivals on the MULAN dataset, and a user study backed the gains.
arxiv-2511-21196:
Economists Zhang Xu and Wei Zhao tackle a design problem in 2025: which signals, meaning structured releases of information, can be shared without breaking privacy limits? Their framework ranks signals by the Blackwell order, a standard way to say one signal teaches strictly more than another. The authors describe the full frontier of allowed signals, the best achievable trade-offs between usefulness and privacy.

Xu and Zhao show that this frontier splits into two building blocks. One block is the minimum informative signals, the leanest signals that still reach the privacy frontier for the guarded variables. The other block keeps privacy intact once some information is already out. They characterize the first block completely, then apply the framework to ex-post privacy notions such as differential and inferential privacy, and to limits on average beliefs after release.
arxiv-2511-21296:
Milan Rosko builds in 2025 a toy radar model inside Minkowski spacetime to show a sharp limit on what measurement can ever certify. An observer bounces pulses off a stationary reflector and infers its distance from the round-trip time. Rosko chooses a computable family of distances, each between 1 and 1.5 units, encoding whether a given computer program halts: a hair above 1 gives the halting step, while exactly 1 means it never halts.

Any fixed-precision radar protocol terminates, returning an interval whose error shrinks as precision grows. Yet deciding from finite data whether the reflector sits at exactly distance 1 would solve the halting problem, which is impossible. Rosko proves the consequence: every effective theory sound about such absence claims, statements that no reflector exists beyond a bound, leaves infinitely many true ones undecided. These statements have the logical form called Pi-1 sentences, universal claims no finite evidence can settle.
arxiv-2511-21396:
Rafał Gruszczyński, Paula Menchón, and William Zuluaga give a logical algebra for spatial contact in a 2025 paper bridging geometry and logic. Standard contact algebras describe when two regions touch, using a two-place relation. The extended contact relation, introduced by Ivanova in 2020, uses three places, capturing richer claims like one region connecting two others, and Boolean algebras carrying it are called extended contact algebras.

Gruszczyński and his coauthors recast the ternary relation as entailment, one region's contact forcing a conclusion. They define pseudo-inference algebras, PSI-algebras for short, where a monotone ternary operator replaces the relation outright. The relational members of this class match extended contact algebras exactly, and the strict ones form a discriminator variety. Extending Stone duality, they build descriptive frames and establish three related dualities, giving the structures a unified spatial and logical meaning.
arxiv-2511-21696:
Wei Liu, Muhammad Aamir Ali, and Yanrong An rebuild the calculus of interval-valued functions from new arithmetic, in 2025. Intervals represent quantities known only within bounds, but the classical rules for them have a defective structure where some problems cannot be solved. The space of intervals ends up only semilinear, frustrating rigorous work.

Under the authors' new operations, the interval space turns into a strict linear space, indeed a Hilbert space with distance, norm, and inner product. Derivatives and integrals built on these operations keep every key property of classical calculus while borrowing tricks from multiplicative calculus. The hybrid framework removes the case-by-case switching-point checks that the older gH-derivative demands. The paper proves an existence theorem for such equations and tests the method on examples. Unlike the gH approach, the count of possible solutions does not explode as switching points multiply.
arxiv-2511-21896:
Dabash and colleagues compare two methods for finding symmetries and conserved quantities in f(R) gravity, where Einstein's curvature term becomes a general function. They work with the Reissner-Nordström spacetime, the geometry around a charged, non-rotating black hole, building a canonical Lagrangian for its radial metric functions and the curvature scalar.

The standard Noether approach ties symmetries of the action to conservation laws, and the authors classify its symmetries and write down explicit generators. The Mei approach instead demands that the equations of motion themselves stay unchanged, which suits higher-order theories. For the quadratic model where f(R) equals R squared, the Mei analysis produced eight independent symmetry generators and new conserved currents, some with no Noether counterpart at all in their results. Mei symmetries thus extend the older framework for black hole dynamics.
arxiv-2512-00396:
Detecting gait from a wearable sensor could help track Parkinson's disease outside the clinic. Andrea Procopio and co-authors study tiny separable convolutional networks for wearable gait detection in 2025. They work with short windows of triaxial acceleration on resource-constrained devices.

The team compares magnitude thresholding with three one-dimensional convolutional networks, including an ultra-light purely separable model and one with residual connections. They also study optimal sensor placement. Small, efficient models matter because a wearable must run all day on a tiny battery while still catching the gait changes clinicians care about. Short acceleration windows keep the data rate low enough for cheap wearables. Sensor placement decides signal quality before any model runs, so optimizing it matters.
arxiv-2512-00596:
Recommender systems increasingly receive rich multimodal features from language models, but those features are high-dimensional and noisy. Jiahao Tian and Zhenkai Wang present DLRREC in 2025, a framework that denoises latent representations through multimodal knowledge fusion. Treating the features as static inputs decouples them from the recommendation task.

The framework is built on deeply fusing multimodal and collaborative knowledge for representation denoising. Collaborative signals record what users actually chose, grounding the language model's descriptive features. Cleaner representations should sharpen recommendations in media and shopping systems that now lean heavily on model-generated descriptions. Denoising inside the model beats cleaning features once, because the task itself guides the cleaning. For folks who shop or watch on their phones, the gain is picks that feel less random. The noise is wrung out, and the true likes shine through more clearly.
arxiv-2512-00696:
Hasi Hays, Yue Yu, and William Richardson introduce Hierarchical Molecular Language Models in a 2025 paper on cell biology. Artificial intelligence is changing how biologists decode the networks cells use to signal each other. Their idea treats cell signaling as a specialized language with its own parts and rules.

In that picture, signaling molecules act as tokens, the words of the language. Protein interactions supply the syntax, or grammar, that joins them. The effects that follow supply the semantics, or meaning. Framing signals this way lets language model tools work on cell communication. That could help researchers predict how cells respond when signals change.
arxiv-2512-00896:
Jiang Zhou and Changjiang Bu study the spectra of graphs and hypergraphs in a 2025 math paper. A graph's spectrum is a set of numbers from its connection matrix that summarize its structure. The largest of them, the spectral radius, is especially telling.

The authors link the spectral radius to local structures, the small patterns sitting inside a graph. They show that when a certain ratio of spectral values is large, particular local subgraphs or subhypergraphs must appear. They also bound the local vector chromatic number using tensor eigenvalues. Such results let one number reveal what small shapes a network must contain.
arxiv-2512-00996:
Raymond Hinton, Pepa Ramírez Cobo, and Brani Vidakovic present a new view on measuring signal roughness in a 2025 paper. Self-similar signals look alike at many scales, and the Hurst exponent sums up their long-memory roughness. Wavelet methods estimate it by watching how detail energy decays across decomposition levels.

The authors define dual wavelet spectra, an alternative starting point for that estimate. They apply the idea to mammogram classification, where texture differences can separate healthy tissue from signs of disease. A better roughness measure could sharpen such texture-based tools, giving radiologists one more signal in a hard screening task.
arxiv-2512-01396:
Zhiqing Zhong, Jiaming Huang, and Pinjia He build a test for patch backporting. Software grows fast, with new traits and safety fixes. Many users stay on old versions since upgrades can break their code. Backporting moves a fix from a new version to an old one by hand.

That hand work is slow and prone to error. The team made BackportBench to score tools that do it on their own. The test spans more than one language. Good scores would show which tools can keep old code safe with less human toil and less risk of a bad port.
arxiv-2512-01996:
Teaching a humanoid robot to walk inside a simulation is fast now, thanks to massively parallel computing that cut training from days to minutes. Younggyo Seo and co-authors present a 2025 recipe that makes the transfer to a real robot both quick and reliable, despite the jump from virtual to physical.

The transfer is hard because humanoid control is high-dimensional, and randomizing the simulation to cover reality adds further strain. Their recipe builds on off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms, which reuse past experience efficiently. The title's promise is training in about a quarter of an hour. Fast, dependable transfer would let robot skills be developed at software speed.
arxiv-2512-02096:
The James Webb Space Telescope found a puzzling new class of distant objects: compact, red points of light with a distinctive V-shaped spectrum. Shuqi Fu and ten co-authors report in 2025 on two of these little red dots that appear to be turning into quasars.

The dots' broad hydrogen emission lines suggest active galactic nuclei, black holes feeding at their centers, hidden inside. Catching two in transition offers a rare before-and-after view of how these objects evolve. The discovery helps astronomers decide what little red dots are and how they connect to the growth of early black holes and galaxies.
arxiv-2512-02196:
Lead titanate is a crystal with a built-in electric slant: its charges sit slightly off center, and they can be flipped. It is also a semiconductor with useful traits for light-based work. Pietro Pacchioni, Lorenzo Varrassi, and Cesare Franchini compute in 2025 how its bent shape changes its excitons. Excitons are bound pairs of an electron and a hole, and they shape how the crystal takes in light.

A sound first-principles account of the light spectrum was still missing. So was a clear view of what the bent shape does to it. That gap counts, since the crystal is a prospect for splitting water with light and for light-based devices. If bending the lattice steers the excitons, strain becomes a knob for tuning the response.
arxiv-2512-02696:
Omid Reza Heidari, Yang Wang, and Xinxin Zuo adapt object detection for security X-ray scans across different machines. A detector trained on one scanner often fails on another, since devices and settings shift the images. Such domain gaps degrade performance in real screening work.

Their ALDI-ray method adapts the ALDI framework to X-ray object detection. The goal is steady detection of threats despite scanner changes, without full retraining each time. Reliable adaptation matters at airports and borders, where new machines should not mean missed bags or long retraining delays. Scans change when bags move to a new hall, so a tool that adapts on the fly saves real time.
arxiv-2512-02796:
Menhaz Ahammed, Matthew Campbell, and Han-Bom Moon hunt for the simplest curves that fill a surface in algebraic geometry. Their surface is the product of two projective lines, a basic four dimensional stage. A space filling curve there must be smooth and reach every part of the surface.

The authors prove that plenty of minimal degree examples exist, in an explicit sense. The result extends an earlier existence theorem by Homma and Kim. Explicit families matter because geometers can compute with them, testing broader ideas about curves on surfaces over any base field. Plain forms that peers can write down beat vague claims that some curve must exist out there in the dark.
arxiv-2512-02896:
Akankshya Majhi and four co-authors study how ridged walls stir a thick fluid that only flows above a stress threshold. Yield stress fluids, like gels and pastes, resist motion until pushed hard enough. The standard Herschel-Bulkley model treats that threshold as a fixed material constant.

In Couette systems, where fluid is sheared between surfaces, ridges change the flow pattern. The title reports that ridged geometries induce axial flow vortices. Side flows of this kind affect mixing and transport in processing equipment that handles pastes, foods, and slurries every day. Ridges are cheap to make and hard to fake, so flow marks they leave are a fair test of how pastes move in plant gear.
arxiv-2512-02996:
Asim Sharma and Avah Banerjee coax quantum chaos from circuits built by rule, not by lottery. Quantum chaos shows in entanglement spectra that follow Wigner-Dyson statistics and in decaying out of time order correlators. Random circuits reach that behavior, but hardware builders prefer deterministic constructions that repeat across platforms.

The pair studies derandomized Clifford plus T circuits with causal cover architectures. Candidate designs include bitonic sorting networks and permutation based routing circuits. Structured routes to chaos could give benchmarks and random unitary designs that any quantum lab can reproduce exactly. Rule built chaos can be set, set, and set once more with the same end state. Prize tests and shared marks both need that trait to work.
arxiv-2512-03396:
Decisions under deep uncertainty can be framed in two orders. Zachary Van Oosten and Ruodu Wang compare those orders in this 2025 work. A decision maker has a statistic for pure-risk preferences, like expected utility, and faces an ambiguous act.

One framework evaluates the act under each plausible model, then aggregates. The other aggregates first, then evaluates. The order can change the final choice, so the difference matters. Clarifying it helps in finance and insurance, where ambiguity about models is unavoidable. Order effects warn analysts that two sound steps can still yield different decisions.
arxiv-2512-03596:
Health cost studies hinge on whose costs count. Dylan Mordaunt presents a Python tool for that choice in this 2025 work. Studies differ under a health system view versus a wider social view, and guides often urge one of them.

The cost of that choice is rarely measured, though it can flip a funding call. The tool supports fair cost studies across groups and a value-of-view check. It shows how often the two views lead to unlike choices. Clearer counts help leaders fund care that is fair and works well.
arxiv-2512-04096:
Meta's advertising systems must copy messages to thousands of consumers across data centres worldwide, in order and without loss, within seconds. Sushant Kumar Gupta and colleagues describe the system built for that job, Fast ACS, in a 2025 preprint. The design is file-based and leans on two communication styles for its two scales of problem.

Between clusters, the system uses remote procedure calls. Inside a cluster, it uses one-sided remote memory access. Consumers pull messages at their own pace instead of being flooded. Ordering and at-least-once delivery are guaranteed by design. The deployment record is substantial: dozens of production clusters, several thousand consumers per cluster, and terabit-scale internal traffic at peak. Delivery worldwide lands within a few seconds, often under one second at the ninety-ninth percentile.
arxiv-2512-04296:
Fine-tuning a transformer normally means retraining billions of weights; parameter-efficient methods update only a sliver instead. Malyaban Bal and Abhronil Sengupta introduce GRASP in a 2025 machine learning preprint, a fine-tuning scheme built on grouped activation sharing. It also targets a deployment problem: models that must survive noisy, energy-stingy edge hardware.

GRASP partitions token representations in layers into a small number of groups, learning one shared scaling and shifting vector per group. That slashes trainable parameters while keeping task-specific learning. A stochastic variant, StochGRASP, learns Gaussian perturbations to the pretrained weights and trains with a noise-aware loss, modelling hardware variability. On GLUE benchmarks with RoBERTa models and on an E2E generation task with GPT-2, the method matches or beats established approaches. It uses an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than LoRA. Under noise, the stochastic variant consistently wins.
arxiv-2512-04796:
Pedro Caro and Alberto Ruiz extend a uniqueness result for the initial-to-final-state inverse problem in quantum mechanics to Hamiltonians with unbounded potentials. The problem asks whether knowing a system's state at one fixed time, for every possible starting state, determines the Hamiltonian that drove it. The authors framed the question to explain why data-driven prediction can work in quantum settings at all. Their earlier work settled the bounded case, where potentials decay fast at infinity. Their 2025 arXiv paper removes that comfort.

The key step proves a family of Strichartz estimates, including the sharp endpoint case of Keel and Tao. A counterexample in the paper shows that Bourgain spaces, a rival tool, cannot capture the needed mixed norms here. That limit result justifies the harder route. Uniqueness for rougher potentials widens the class of quantum systems whose rules can, in principle, be read off from observed behavior.
arxiv-2512-04996:
Qiong Chang, Weimin Wang, Junpei Zhong, and Jun Miyazaki work on making a fast three-dimensional scanning method fit on small hardware. The method, called VANICP, matches up point clouds — the clouds of measured points that describe a surface — by spreading neighbor information outward instead of searching the whole cloud each time. It is quick, but it eats memory, which shuts it out of the modest graphics chips in embedded devices.

The team adds a memory plan that hands out and reuses space for the spreading step only as needed. Built into a new version of the framework, the plan cuts memory use by more than ninety-seven percent while keeping the original speed. The code is released openly, so builders of robots and compact scanners can run accurate point cloud matching on hardware that could not hold the method before.
arxiv-2512-05196:
Davis Welakuh, Vasil Rokaj, Michael Ruggenthaler, and Angel Rubio detail cheaper ways to handle light with many modes when it couples to matter. In cavity quantum electrodynamics, atoms and molecules sit inside structured light fields, and tracking every mode of the field is ruinously expensive. For equilibrium properties, though, the authors show much of that complexity can be cut away without losing the physics.

They lay out a family of approximations: keeping only the electric field's polarization part in one formulation, or replacing the many modes with a few effective ones. The methods are designed to stay accurate from weak to strong coupling and across complicated photonic environments. The team demonstrates them on atomic and molecular models and on a two-dimensional quantum ring, showing the shortcuts are versatile. The work lays groundwork for first-principles simulations of real materials inside optical cavities.
arxiv-2512-05696:
Paula Mellado, Francisco Muñoz, and Javiera Cabezas-Escares study a striped state of charge in a toy system built from two chain-like legs. In a charge density wave, electrons settle into a regular pattern of higher and lower density that need not match the crystal lattice. The team uses a half filled, four band ladder model. A slight shift between the legs creates a moiré pattern that flattens energy bands near the Fermi level.

Once short range repulsion between electrons is switched on, the pattern that forms is excitonic, driven by bound pairs of electrons and holes. The wave's shaking splits into two collective modes: a gapped amplitude mode, and a gapless sliding mode carried by long lived neutral phasons. The results warn that even tiny mismatches between layers can reshape charge order in layered materials. They also suggest the puzzling charge wave in hafnium tritelluride is excitonic.
arxiv-2512-05896:
János Engländer turns a classic puzzle about lonely passengers into a moving process. The original problem, due to Tóth, seats passengers at random in empty buses and counts the lonely ones. More buses tend not to reduce the lonely count. Engländer's step is to treat the number of buses as time itself. At each moment the state is Tóth's seating with that many buses, and all passenger counts couple into one object: the detachment process.

Detachment is the event where every passenger sits alone. The paper studies when detachment happens and how clumping behaves. Four critical time scales govern the story, tied to the passenger count, its square, and logarithmic corrections. Modeling passengers with a Poisson distribution simplifies the analysis, aided by a comparison theorem with a new proof. The process is a clean lens on random occupancy.
arxiv-2512-05996:
Yi Liu, Jingyu Song, Vedanth Kallakuri, and Katherine Skinner teach one model to find, outline, and count fish underwater, using only sparse hints for training. Underwater imagery is murky, and dense labeling is expensive. FishDetector-R1 is a unified multimodal framework working under weak supervision. On the standard DeepFish benchmark it beats baselines clearly: detection accuracy up twenty percent, segmentation quality up ten, counting errors down by roughly a third.

Two ingredients drive the gains. A detect-to-count prompt forces the model's detections and its count to agree spatially, so the fish it lists are the fish it numbers. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards tunes it further. The improvements transfer to other underwater datasets. Surveys could run on a model trained from points and prompts. Automated counting would change how widely ocean health gets measured.
arxiv-2512-06196:
Charlie Masters, Marta Grzeskiewicz, and Stefano Albrecht present ARCANE, a way to steer long running AI agents while keeping their goals open to view. When an agent works for hours, its owners need to see what it is being scored on. They also need to change that scoring without training the system again.

ARCANE turns user wishes into short written rubrics: weighted lists of checks that anyone can read. A team of model based agents drafts and refines these rubrics from the task at hand. The rubrics are learned with a tuned training method that balances clear wording, faith to the user's wishes, and low cost. In tests on hard tasks that need many steps and tools, the rubrics gave compact scores and let users swap goals, such as favoring right answers over short ones, at run time.
arxiv-2512-06296:
Sooho Moon and Yunyong Ko argue that the usual scores for fact guessing systems grade them with a blind spot. These systems fill gaps in webs of facts, such as who directed a film or where a person was born. Standard scores can be too lax or too strict about near misses, and they favor facts about famous things over rare ones.

Their framework, PROBE, adds two lenses to grading. One step rescales each guess by how strict the grader wants to be. The next adds the scores up in a way that gives rare items their fair weight. On real fact webs, the authors show that old scores can puff up or shrink a model's true skill, while PROBE gives a steadier picture. Better grading matters because labs pick which models to build on based on these very scores.
arxiv-2512-06396:
Shovan Roy presents AgenticCyber, a team of AI agents built to watch for cyber threats across many kinds of data at once. Enterprise networks and smart device fleets face attacks that no single tool sees whole, because logs, camera feeds, and sound each sit in their own silo. AgenticCyber assigns specialist agents to cloud logs, surveillance video, and room audio, and has them reason together through large multimodal models.

The system was tested on public data sets for each stream: cloud activity logs, crime video frames, and city sound clips. Roy reports it caught threats with high scores, answered in well under a second, and cut the average time to respond by a large share compared with standard intrusion systems. Its modular design aims to scale across company networks and device fleets, shifting defense from fixed tools that wait for alarms toward agents that act early.
arxiv-2512-06596:
The XRISM Collaboration reports the first direct measure of gas motion in the hot heart of the Virgo galaxy cluster, around the giant galaxy M87. Clusters hold gas in a vast hot atmosphere, and the central black hole stirs it through feedback. The Resolve instrument on the XRISM satellite reads gas speeds from the shifts of X ray lines, and Virgo is the closest case where this can be done in detail.

Near the center the gas churns with a wide spread of speeds, falling off steeply within a short span. Bulk motion stays close to M87 itself. If the central spread were pure turbulence, it would run near the speed of sound, with much of the pressure from motion, not heat. Models mixing shocks, sound waves, and turbulence fit. Among clusters XRISM has seen, M87's core is the most disturbed.
arxiv-2512-07296:
Qidi Peng and William Wu take on the practical problem of simulating self-similar processes, random curves whose statistics look the same at every zoom. Such processes model everything from river flows to financial volatility, yet simulation recipes tend to be one-off crafts, each built for a single process with its own constraints and flaws. A general, efficient simulator has been missing.

The authors first review the leading recipes for specific processes and improve several of them. Then they propose a method meant for the whole class: a modified inverse Lamperti transformation converts self-similarity into stationarity. A tamer property that standard machinery can handle, and converting back yields the desired process. The method is demonstrated on the two workhorses of the field, fractional Brownian motion and its sub-fractional cousin.
arxiv-2512-07696:
C. Ganot and twenty-nine co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on Type Ia supernovae. These explosions serve as standard candles for measuring cosmic distances. Their brightness must be standardized with care.

The team builds a large, uniform sample from the Zwicky Transient Facility. Thousands of spectra from its second data release feed the work. Flux calibration is tightened using photometry that is accurate to the percent level. On a subset of explosions near peak light, they replay a special method. The Twins Embedding method once achieved remarkably low scatter in brightness. Its three steps are applied here. The phase correction proves precise. A color standardization step, called Read Between The Lines, also performs well. It beats the standard SALT approach while using one fewer parameter. The full method stalls, limited by the survey's modest spectral quality.
arxiv-2512-07796:
Sridhar Mahadevan wrote this 2025 paper on building large causal models from language models. Traditional causal inference builds small models from experiments and numeric data. Mahadevan wants causal maps that span whole fields of knowledge instead.

His system, DEMOCRITUS, mines a strong language model for causal claims. It proposes topics, poses causal questions, and extracts plausible statements. Those fragments arrive scattered, ambiguous, and sometimes in conflict. The hard problem is weaving them into one coherent structure. Claims become relational triples inside a large causal model. New categorical machine learning methods were invented for that weaving. The paper focuses on the system side of the construction. A six-module pipeline carries text in and organized models out. Cost profiling shows where scaling the system currently bottlenecks. Trials span archaeology, biology, climate, economics, medicine, and technology. Limits of the current system are discussed frankly at the end.
arxiv-2512-07896:
Alexander Chipps, Daniel Forgette, and Kerri Cahoy wrote this 2025 space engineering paper. Small satellites now travel beyond Earth orbit on interplanetary missions. Their designers need thermal predictions, yet pro tools are costly and demand deep training.

Their answer is SATMO, an open-source thermal model for CubeSats. The MATLAB program uses six nodes to represent the satellite's heat balance. It targets low-altitude circular orbits around Earth and other solar system bodies. Mission planners in the early, sketchy stages are its audience. A Mars-orbiting CubeSat serves as the worked example in the paper. Outputs show what temperatures each configuration of the craft will face. Validation runs against the industry standard, Thermal Desktop, come out close. Temperatures agree within a narrow margin across Earth, Venus, and Mars cases. Quick trade studies become possible without a specialist's toolbox. Interplanetary small-satellite planning gains an accessible first pass at thermal design.
arxiv-2512-08096:
Georgios Chionas, Olga Gorelkina, Piotr Krysta, and Rida Laraki, researchers in economics and computer science, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is privacy in blockchain transactions, where users may want to sell the right to execute a transaction without exposing their economic preferences. They model users whose welfare falls as more of their private information leaks.

First, they study an order flow auction in which a user auctions execution rights to specialist agents called searchers. They characterize the optimal auction, a sealed bid design, and show how the level of privacy affects revenue and user welfare. Next, they analyze a Dutch auction variant where price and privacy both fall over rounds. Finally, they build a two sided privacy marketplace with many users and searchers. Their posted price mechanism keeps both sides honest, balances the budget, and still guarantees a constant share of the best possible social welfare.
arxiv-2512-08396:
Barbara Baldoni, Mickael Delcey, Yoann Cheny, and colleagues, engineers and physicists in France, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They use physics informed neural networks to measure how granular materials flow. Sand, grain, and powders have rheological parameters that normally demand complex, costly experiments to pin down, yet those numbers decide how silos empty and how piles collapse.

Their test case is simple: a column of granular material collapsing under gravity. The network learns the flow fields from synthetic data while recovering the rheological parameters at the same time. As a bonus, it reconstructs the pressure field inside the material, something experiments can barely reach. The proof of concept worked on synthetic data. The authors present the method as data driven rheometry for granular matter, ready to be tried on real experiments. Such tools could make designing with powders and grains far less trial and error.
arxiv-2512-08696:
Nathan Dalaklis and Yan Mary He study multifractal analysis for equilibrium states of holomorphic maps on complex projective space. The map has degree at least two, and the work focuses on a uniformly expanding set where the dynamics are non conformal. Equilibrium states come from Holder continuous potentials, a standard class in dynamics.

Instead of Hausdorff dimension, the authors use a newer volume dimension theory to define local dimension spectra. They show each spectrum forms a Legendre transform pair with the temperature function, matching the pattern known in the conformal case. As a use of the main results, they also prove a conditional variational principle for those spectra. The work extends multifractal formalism to a broader non conformal setting, giving tools to describe how local scaling varies across the expanding set.
arxiv-2512-08896:
Gang Liu and coauthors report the results of the Open Polymer Challenge, a community competition for predicting polymer traits with machine learning. Progress toward sustainable polymers has been slowed by a lack of large, high quality, open data sets. The challenge releases a new benchmark with ten thousand polymers and five traits, including thermal conductivity, density, and glass transition temperature.

Participants had to work under realistic limits: small data, uneven labels, and mixed study sources. Winning methods used feature augmentation, transfer learning, self supervised pretraining, and targeted ensembles. The report draws lessons on data preparation, distribution shifts, and consistency across study groups. Those lessons can guide future large polymer data efforts. The models, study, and released data, including a data generation pipeline covering many more properties, form a new base for molecular machine learning in polymer science.
arxiv-2512-09496:
Anissa Alloula and colleagues challenge a standard assumption in machine learning fairness: that training data should always be balanced across demographic groups. Unequal representation can hurt a model's performance on underrepresented groups, yet recent results show imbalanced data sometimes helps a subgroup. Sometimes a subgroup's performance is unaffected even if it is missing from training entirely.

The authors propose the latent separation hypothesis. A fine-tuned model's dependence on subgroup representation, they argue, is set by how far apart the subgroups sit in the pretrained model's internal representation space. They formalize the hypothesis, back it with theory, and validate it across four vision and language datasets. Regularization experiments add early evidence that the effect is causal. Their practical message is that measuring latent subgroup separation can guide real decisions about data collection and balancing when fine-tuning foundation models, instead of balancing by default.
arxiv-2512-09596:
Arkadiusz Ryś and colleagues present a framework for managing the artifacts produced by systems engineering work, as the field shifts from documents to models. For cyber-physical systems, experts from many domains run workflows and use models in many formalisms, each with its own tools. Knowledge about those workflows and their outputs is valuable for repeating work and for reasoning over results, but it is scattered.

Their framework defines the workflow concepts, formalisms, and artifacts in an ontology, written in an ontology modeling language. From that ontology they build a knowledge graph holding the engineering data, over which reasoning can run. Tools help engineers design workflows, execute them, and store artifacts with versioning, querying, and reasoning, while hiding the graph's complexity. Applied to a drivetrain smart sensor project, the framework eased storage and versioning problems and cut the time needed to find information and inferences.
arxiv-2512-09696:
Asher Sabbagh and colleagues demonstrate that some objects are impossible to push, pull, or trap with light, even using the best shaped light beams. Optical manipulation is a powerful tool across biophysics and nanotechnology, and wavefront shaping with spatial light modulators had seemed able to move arbitrary objects. The authors show this assumption fails for a variety of shapes.

Working in two dimensions, they use inverse design, starting from the desired behavior and computing the shape that produces it. That finds objects resistant to manipulation under even the optimal wavefront shaping protocol. For their counterintuitive shapes, the maximum pulling force drops by up to four orders of magnitude and the maximum trapping stiffness by nearly two. The authors note the designs provide a foundation for extension to three dimensions. Such resistant objects could serve micromachines that need a predictable mechanical response no matter what light falls on them.
arxiv-2512-09896:
Anuj Apte and five coauthors improve the best efficient approximation algorithm for the EPR Hamiltonian problem. Problems of this kind ask for a quantum state that nearly maximizes an energy-like quantity, and approximation algorithms guarantee a fixed fraction of the optimum. Their new algorithm guarantees a stronger fraction than before. The gain comes from two ingredients. One is a new nonlinear bound on monogamy of entanglement for star shaped interaction graphs. The other is a refined parameterization of a shallow quantum circuit used in earlier work.

The team also proves limits on what current methods can deliver. Their barriers show that today's techniques cannot push the approximation ratio substantially higher. That tells researchers the next improvement needs fundamentally new ideas. The paper is a theoretical contribution to quantum algorithms and entanglement theory.
arxiv-2512-09996:
Giacomo Venturi leads a large team reporting powerful gas outflows from active galaxies in the early universe. The targets lie at redshifts three to six, before cosmic noon, an era poorly explored for this kind of feedback. Using the James Webb Space Telescope's integral field spectrograph, the team mapped ionized gas around mostly X-ray selected active nuclei in the GOODS-S field. Combined with a twin sample in COSMOS, theirs is the largest spatially resolved outflow sample at these redshifts, with outflows in most of the galaxies observed.

The outflows are fast and compact, and in some cases they expel ionized gas faster than the host forms stars. Even so, the analysis hints that mass outflow rates were higher long ago, especially beyond redshift three. Stronger early outflows would have been better able to reshape their hosts.
arxiv-2512-10596:
J Xiao and co-authors search satellite images with words, and skip training altogether. Finding the right remote sensing image for a text query is hampered by the semantic gap between raw visual features and human concepts. Vision-language models can bridge it, but domain training is costly, and nobody had properly benchmarked how far model-written captions alone can go.

The team built the Remote Sensing Rich Text dataset, with several structured captions per image. And a reference method called TRSLLaVA that never trains. It turns cross-modal search into text-to-text matching: the query is compared against a database of model-generated captions inside one shared text embedding space. On the RSITMD and RSICD benchmarks the training-free method nearly doubled the recall of a standard zero-shot CLIP baseline and passed several supervised models.
arxiv-2512-10796:
Ross Dempsey and co-authors corner the energy-energy correlator of the most symmetric gauge theory, N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills. This observable records how energy arrives at two detectors set at an angle, a clean probe of how the theory's excitations share energy. The team attacks it with every tool available: perturbation theory, holography, supersymmetric localisation, integrability, and numerical conformal bootstrap.

For finite numbers of colours they derive lower bounds on the correlator's second and fourth angular multipoles at several couplings, plus a smeared angular profile. And find evidence the theory nearly saturates those bounds. In the planar limit, dispersive functionals give tight two-sided bounds on the first three multipoles and the full angular shape. As the coupling grows, dominance in the collinear limit passes from single-trace to double-trace operators, mirroring the parton-to-hadron transition seen when detectors close in during QCD collisions.
arxiv-2512-10996:
Seonok Kim introduces MedBioRAG, a system that helps large language models answer medical and biological questions by first finding relevant documents. Retrieval augmented generation grounds answers in sources rather than memory alone. MedBioRAG combines meaning based search with word based search, ranking, and supervised fine tuning of the model.

The system was tested on document retrieval, short answer questions, and long form answers using well known sets such as MedQA, PubMedQA, BioASQ, and COVID related collections. It beat earlier best models and a strong general model on every task measured. Retrieval scores and answer accuracy both improved. The findings support pairing careful semantic search with fine tuning for biomedical question answering.
arxiv-2512-11096:
Ben Wang and Jiqun Liu study how people use ChatGPT to plan long term life tasks, from health goals to career learning and big events. Such planning is complex and uncertain, and little was known about how AI chatbots support it in practice. The authors interviewed fourteen participants about their planning sessions and examined the prompts they wrote.

ChatGPT helped people break large goals into manageable steps, generate ideas, and stay motivated, acting as a reflective partner. Its plans were often generic or idealised, though, lacking personal detail, realism, and flexibility when life changed. Users had to adapt and check the output themselves. Participants wanted systems that admit uncertainty and plan for failure, not just success. The findings frame long term planning as an evolving human AI collaboration.
arxiv-2512-11196:
O. Ramirez and Y. Bonder derive the first law of black hole thermodynamics for a wide range of gravity theories using the language of differential forms. Black hole thermodynamics, linking mass, entropy, and surface gravity, hints at the microscopic structure of spacetime. A general derivation has existed since the nineteen nineties, but in the traditional metric formalism.

Differential forms are a natural language for gravity theories, especially those that go beyond general relativity. The authors build a unified prescription in that language, covering theories with torsion, a twisting of spacetime geometry, and generic matter fields. Their framework produces concrete expressions for the first law in each case. The result should make thermodynamic checks easier to apply when testing proposed extensions of Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2512-11296:
Yasaman Hashem Pour, Nazanin Mahjourian, and Vinh Nguyen use vision language models to check student written machining code jointly with the machine's own display. Learning to program CNC lathes by hand matters. Earlier checking tools based on text only models could read the code, but not the human machine interface, which shows live status and errors.

Their few shot approach feeds the model paired cases of code and interface screenshots from a training lathe, covering both correct and faulty cases. A structured output schema built from expert heuristics guides the model's judgements. Compared with a zero shot version, the guided model caught more interface errors and more mismatches between code and machine state. The setup suits the manually written code typical of CNC training programmes.
arxiv-2512-11496:
Jelena Losic argues that finding communities in a network should blend two rival toolkits, because no single strategy wins everywhere. Popular graph methods such as Louvain optimise a modularity score, yet they can miss communities defined by geometry. Topological data analysis methods like ToMATo find density based clusters in embedded data powerfully, but depend on how the data were projected.

Losic's framework first embeds the network spectrally, exposing a geometric skeleton where communities appear as basins in a density landscape. ToMATo then extracts the persistent clusters from that landscape in a parameter aware way. Across synthetic benchmarks the hybrid proved highly robust, performing on par with Louvain on networks with clear modular structure. The results support a new class of hybrid algorithms that choose or combine strategies according to a network's geometry, rather than forcing one method onto every problem.
arxiv-2601-06996:
Yue Ban and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers quantum state engineering of spin-orbit coupled ultracold atoms in a morse potential. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Achieving full control of a Bose-Einstein condensate can have valuable applications in metrology, quantum information processing, and quantum condensed matter physics.

The authors propose protocols to simultaneously control the internal (related to its pseudospin-1/2) and motional (position-related) states of. A spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate confined in a Morse potential. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07196:
Zhe Luo, Shoulong Li, and Hongwei Yu wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on neutron stars in a new kind of gravity. The kind is called Einstein-bumblebee gravity. It pairs a vector field with the pull of mass in a close way. Such a frame lets teams test if a deep rule of physics, Lorentz symmetry, can break, by what we see in the sky.

For black holes, the frame gives exact forms that stand still and round. Those forms rest on a key guess. The guess says the field's potential drops to zero once the field gains a value that points out from the core. The authors show that the guess, if held at all points, blocks sound forms for dense stars. They then build forms for neutron stars that hold up as a whole, and show how the guess must be eased.
arxiv-2601-07696:
Nick Ferguson, Alan Bundy, and Kwabena Nuamah separate two levels of reasoning in language models and test the higher one. Meta-level reasoning means thinking about the steps a task needs. Object-level reasoning means carrying those steps out. Their 2026 preprint uses a tool-based task with multi-hop questions over tables. Multi-hop questions need several linked facts before an answer is possible.

Focusing on the meta level clarifies what models actually plan versus execute. A model might pick the right steps but fail a calculation, or compute well with a poor plan. Their task design separates those failure modes. Tool use adds another layer, since the model must decide when to call a tool. The paper speaks to scholars evaluating reasoning claims for large language models. It offers a cleaner test than end-answer accuracy alone.
arxiv-2601-07896:
D. Ramos and colleagues describe a new neutron beam monitor installed at a French nuclear facility. The setup sits in the time-of-flight area of the Neutrons For Science facility at GANIL-SPIRAL2. It uses position-sensitive parallel-plate avalanche counters. These detectors catch both fission fragments, in coincidence, from neutron-induced fission in uranium-238 targets. Their 2026 preprint appears in a nuclear instruments journal.

Beam monitors tell experimenters the intensity and shape of the neutron beam during a run. Without them, cross-section measurements lose their reference. Detecting fission fragments from a known reaction gives a reliable count. Position sensitivity adds the beam's profile, not just its total rate. The paper serves nuclear physicists who run neutron experiments. It documents hardware that other facilities may copy.
arxiv-2601-08296:
Vedad Dzanic, Sumesh Thampi, and Julia Yeomans connect two kinds of turbulence that arise without inertia. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers elastic turbulence in polymer solutions and active turbulence from self-driven particles. Both produce chaotic flow fields even when inertia is negligible.

The authors show a close link between the two classes that had gone unrecognized. Polymer microstructure can drive elastic chaos, while swimmers and motors drive active chaos. A shared frame could let results from one field inform the other. Soft matter researchers may gain new tools for flows in biology, printing, and microfluidic devices.
arxiv-2601-08396: Jeremie Bigot and Luis Fredes study the Kantorovich distance through spanning trees. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats optimal transport between probability measures on a shared finite metric space. The ground cost comes from distance in a weighted connected graph. Recent work recast this distance as a minimization over spanning trees of the graph. The authors study what that reformulation implies for building optimal transport plans and dual potentials. Tree-based forms could make transport cheaper to compute for data on networks.
arxiv-2601-08896:
Sahaj Raj Malla and four co-authors build a forecast tool for the Nepal stock index. The index tracks the joint worth of firms on that trade floor. To call its next day move is hard, since news and mood shift fast. The team aims for a one step call on the log growth of the index, a form that tames wild swings.

They use a boost tree tool called XGBoost. Inputs span a month of past moves, plus known chart signs such as past spread and a strength gauge. Each test runs in walk steps, so no future facts leak in. A reader in finance gets a strict test plan for a small market. It shows how to grade a call tool with no cheat by hindsight.
arxiv-2601-09296:
Ivan Burenev, Michael Kearney, and Satya Majumdar give one joint take on a classic first cross task. A count grows by steps at random times, as calls come to a desk. A line moves at a set pace next to it, with a head start. When does the count first cross the line. Old results on that time lie in more than one place, in unlike forms.

The team shows two paths to the answer are the same. One path works in time, by a split of paths. The next works by a change of scale, with a known sum rule. A clear joint take helps a reader see why both must agree. Such cross times set waits, risks, and stock sale rules.
arxiv-2601-09396:
Paul Leask, Calum Ross, and Egor Babaev study bound pairs of two swirling defects inside ferromagnetic superconductors. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins magnetic skyrmions, tiny whirls of magnetization, with superconducting vortices. The pairs form inside materials that are both magnetic and superconducting at once.

Using a Ginzburg–Landau framework with Zeeman coupling between magnetization and field, the authors show the pairs form stable bound states. Such composite excitations mix two fields that usually fight each other. Stable pairs could shape how these materials carry current and respond to fields. The work adds a concrete case to the study of topological matter.
arxiv-2601-09696:
Shan Randhawa, Agha Ali Raza, Kentaro Toyama, Julie Hui, and Mustafa Naseem ask when a health answer needs empathy, before it is written. Their 2026 arXiv paper models empathy applicability for general health queries. Language models are entering clinical work, but they often lack clinical empathy.

Older frameworks label empathy in doctors' replies after the fact. Far fewer tools predict, in advance, how much empathy a given question calls for. The authors build toward that anticipatory modeling for general queries. A system that senses the need early could answer a scared patient differently from a routine one.
arxiv-2601-09796:
Renjing Xie and a large team read the chemistry of two puzzling groups of halo stars. Their 2026 arXiv paper, HR-GO II, gives chemical abundances for 35 stars in the retrograde groups Rg8 and Rg9. Dynamically tagged groups in the Milky Way halo may be debris of swallowed galaxies, or home-grown stars in disguise.

In-situ contamination makes the origin of such groups uncertain. Chemistry offers a sharper test than motion alone. The authors find that one structure, Thamnos, stands out as very metal-poor. Such fingerprints help rebuild the Milky Way's merger history star by star.
arxiv-2601-09896:
Jordan Taylor, William Agnew, Maarten Sap, Sarah E. Fox, and Haiyi Zhu audit the taste machine inside image AI. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines the LAION-Aesthetics predictor, which scores images for beauty. Generative models are trained on a single, one-size-fits-all measure of aesthetic appeal.

What counts as aesthetic is tied to personal taste and culture. The authors ask whose taste the predictor encodes. Their audit mixes measurement with ethnography of the model's use. The answer matters a lot because beauty scores quietly decide which images teach the next generation of models.
arxiv-2601-10296:
Andrew Granville and Francesco Pappalardi use cover sets in two dims to force prime facts. A cover set hits each count pair with one of a set of rules. The team build pairs of bases a and b with a strong trait. For all power pairs, a to one power minus b to the next has a prime factor from a fixed set.

That is, the value is never free of those primes. Two dim cover sets give the tool to force this. Such results tie prime gaps to cover tricks. They show how a finite prime set can rule a vast grid of values.
arxiv-2601-10496:
Ali Al-Kaswan leads a team with Claudio Spiess, Prem Devanbu, Arie van Deursen, and Maliheh Izadi. They ask if code models pick a bug they have seen over a fix they have not. Models now write and debug code each day. Their code can hold bugs that came from train text. A fix may be right but new to the model.

The team test that pull. They show a model pairs of code: a known bug and its fix. They track which one the model rates high. They also track how oft the model saw each in train. The work shows if fame can beat truth in code picks.
arxiv-2601-10596:
Xueyuan Ren, Frank Li, and Yang Wang look for speed gains in database transaction processing. Most tuning work happens inside the database engine. They ask what the application side can do instead. Their idea is to merge statements or whole transactions that have a similar shape before the database ever sees them.

The method rewrites transactions in three ways. It merges like statements using SQL rules, cuts reads that repeat work, and joins transactions that clash by pre-computing their joint effect. Each step trims the load the engine must handle. The paper offers database builders a fresh lever for speed that sits outside the engine itself.
arxiv-2601-11196:
Luisa Carpinelli, Filippo Natoli, and Marco Taboga ask how AI shows up in the books. Their 2026 preprint looks at the United States economy. AI now sits at the core of talks on policy and markets. Yet its true size in the economy is still not well known.

The authors give a survey of how the new AI wave is logged. They check how it is counted in the national accounts of the United States. For this they join two tools in one frame. One is a plain accounting frame at the macro scale. The other is a simple sketch of how AI goods are made, step by step.
arxiv-2601-11296:
The XENONnT team report a blinded hunt for light dark matter in this preprint. Their 2026 work uses ionization-only signals from the detector. XENONnT holds tonnes of liquid xenon deep underground. A dark matter hit would leave a small burst of charge.

The data cover 579 days across three science runs. Total exposure comes to 7.83 tonne-years of xenon watched. The team reads only the S2 signal, the ionization part. That choice gives reach to very low-energy recoils. New methods cut background noise in that faint range. They also built the first full S2-only background model for the detector. The hunt was blinded, so no one peeked before the cuts were set.
arxiv-2601-11496:
Eilam Shapira, Moshe Tennenholtz, and Roi Reichart name a poisoned apple effect in markets. Their 2026 preprint studies AI agents in mediated markets. Adding AI agents to markets changes strategic play at its root. The team asks what new technologies do to outcomes.

They expand the set of tools agents can pick from. Three classic game settings carry the test of that change. Bargaining over resource division is the first setting. Negotiation with asymmetric information is the second. Persuasion, or strategic information flow, is the third. In such markets, a tempting new tool can hurt its users. The poisoned apple name captures that trap for agents.
arxiv-2601-12396:
J. Kamulali and nine co authors return to a known gap in the census of exoplanets. The gap is called the radius valley. It is a dip in the count of planets with radii near twice that of Earth. NASA Kepler data first showed this dip for small planets on short orbits.

The shape of the valley can hint at how planets form and lose their air. To read it well, one needs good data on the host stars, not just the planets. The team draw host star data from the SWEET-Cat catalog for this fresh look. Careful star data sharpens planet radii, since those radii are tied to star size. Their revisit tests whether the valley holds up with this cleaner base.
arxiv-2601-12696:
Tassallah Abdullahi and six co authors build a safety benchmark for AI in African languages. Guardian models check AI outputs for harm, but most are Western centric. They are tuned for high resource languages and set safety categories. Low resource African languages are left open to cross lingual safety failures and cultural misalignment.

Rigid, predefined categories also fail to generalize across sociocultural contexts. What counts as harm, and how it is phrased, varies by culture and tongue. Their benchmark, UbuntuGuard, is culturally grounded for this reason. It tests whether safety systems judge African language content fairly and well. Equitable safety is a precondition for fair global AI deployment.
arxiv-2601-12896:
Eric Vansteenberghe presents a course text on quantitative methods in finance. The course is designed for Master 2 research students. It gives a comprehensive introduction to advanced econometric and statistical methods. Those methods come with direct applications in finance throughout.

The text opens with a literary touch, quoting Balzac on the stock exchange. That framing suits a course that joins hard statistics with market life. Students meet tools for time series, risk, and asset data in a research oriented form. A course text of this kind trains the next cohort of quantitative researchers. It also serves practitioners who need the theory behind their models.
arxiv-2601-12996:
Shiyuan Li and five co authors design collaboration topologies for multi agent systems with a generative model. Multi agent systems offer a powerful paradigm for solving complex problems. Their performance depends critically on the design of the underlying collaboration topology. As such systems spread into web services like search engines, adaptive design becomes essential.

Diverse cross domain user queries need different agent layouts, not one fixed chart. Their system, OFA-MAS, uses mixture of experts graph generative models for one for all design. It aims to propose a fitting topology per task family. Their paper was set for the ACM Web Conference in 2026. Adaptive topologies could make agent teams cheaper and sharper at once.
arxiv-2601-13096:
Muhayy Ud Din, Waseem Akram, Ahsan B. Bakht, and Irfan Hussain study how to inspect ports with robots. Port checks keep trade safe and help sites meet rules. Old ways lean on hand work and plain image tools. Those ways scale poorly and miss the sense of a scene.

The team pairs two kinds of craft, a flying drone and a surface boat craft. They join a large language model with a vision language model to guide the pair. The joint brain can read scenes with more context than plain image tools. Their frame aims for checks that cover more ground with less hand work. Port teams may use it to spot risks and faults with more care.
arxiv-2601-13196:
Jacob Swindell, Marija Popovic, and Riccardo Polvara plan drone flights that map weeds where it counts most. True weed maps help farms spray less and yield more. Old ways fly a fixed path and crunch all data back at base. That wastes flight on clear ground.

Smart path plans fly where data is most needed. The team pairs such plans with a Gaussian process map, a smooth field that also states its own doubt. They use a discrete form of that field to steer the drone. As doubt falls in one spot, the drone moves to the next most in doubt spot. Farm teams gain maps built with less flight and less waste.
arxiv-2601-13296:
Andreas Rusu, Gabriela Ileana Sebe, and Dan Lascu prove core limit laws for a class of continued fraction like growths. Such growths, called theta expansions, write a number as a chain of digits by a fixed rule. The sum of digits is a key stat to read.

The team first proves a weak law of large numbers in Khinchin's form for that sum. They next prove a strong law in Diamond and Vaaler's form. That law treats the sum with its top digit struck out. The pair of laws part in a key way, and the team marks where the strong law fails. Such edge cases shape how digit stats can be used.
arxiv-2601-13496:
Anna Karanika and co-authors rethink how smart spaces are run, past plain remote calls. Remote calls are the base of most system stacks. A home, store, or work hall full of smart gear is user facing in a way a back end stack is not. The team says such fleets need a more rich base form.

Their frame is called RASC. Past work made IoT links more sound. This work aims at two next traits. One is sight, to see what the fleet did. The next is program reach, to state joint acts with ease. For smart space teams, sight and reach beat raw link trust as the fleet grows.
arxiv-2601-13996:
Rui Abreu and a large team survey how to test software written for quantum computers in 2026. Quantum computing offers significant speedups for simulating physical, chemical, and biological systems. It also helps optimization and machine learning tasks. As quantum software grows in complexity, old quality methods fail.

Classical simulation of quantum computers has long served quality assurance. That simulation becomes infeasible as machines grow past a set size. New methods must operate directly on real quantum computers. The survey maps this shift for testers and builders of quantum software. The field needs test tools built for quantum rigs from the start. This map of the shift can help course and lab leads plan that move.
arxiv-2601-14096:
Benedikt Hartl, Léo Pio-Lopez, Chris Fields, and Michael Levin seek a shared principle of cognition in 2026. The emerging field of diverse intelligence studies problem-solving across very unlike agents. Agents range from subcellular chemical networks to swarms of organisms. Evolved, engineered, and chimeric systems all fall in scope.

The team hypothesizes scale-invariant principles of decision-making across them. Their focus is remapping and navigation of an embedding space via error minimization. In plain terms, agents may think by moving through a mental map toward lower error. A shared principle could unite biology and AI research.
arxiv-2601-14496:
Shi Feng and Nandini Trivedi study spin liquids under magnetic fields in this 2026 paper. Quantum spin liquids host a variety of fractionalized particles, excitations that carry fractions of the usual quantum numbers. The key example is Kitaev's honeycomb model. In it, a spin one-half fractionalizes into two kinds of particles.

One kind is a Z2 flux, tied to an emergent Z2 gauge field. The other is matter Majorana fermions. The authors study phenomena that a magnetic field induces in Kitaev spin liquids. Readers get a map of how these exotic states respond when a field pushes on their fractional parts.
arxiv-2601-14696:
Zhaiyu Fang and Ruipeng Sun study tool use by language models in this 2026 paper. Tool-Integrated Reasoning has significantly enhanced the capabilities of large language models. Current agents, though, tend toward cognitive offloading. They redundantly invoke external tools even for simple tasks. Each call costs time and money, and can add errors.

The authors argue that true agentic intelligence requires adaptive wisdom: knowing when to use a tool and when to answer directly. Their method, AdaTIR, uses difficulty-aware policy optimization. The agent learns to match tool use to task difficulty. Readers get a training scheme for agents that reach for tools only when the problem earns it.
arxiv-2601-15296:
Longxuan Wei, Yubo Zhang, and co-authors guide a language model's search with its own doubt. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with decoding, the step where a model picks its next words. Current methods either sample at random or repeat the same sampling many times.

The team proposes Entropy-Tree, a tree-based decoding method. Entropy measures how unsure the model is at each step. The search tree branches only where that doubt is genuine. Wasted branches are skipped, and the model's effort goes to the points where the answer is truly in play.
arxiv-2601-15396:
Andreas Bauer and Seth Lloyd seek a common frame for several quantum models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some families of quantum systems can be solved fast on a normal computer. The list includes Clifford circuits for qubits and qudits, and stabilizer codes. It also includes free-boson and free-fermion models. Certain rotor and GKP codes belong on the list too.

The authors show that one structure sits behind all of these cases. Each family can be written with quadratic functions over abelian groups. More broadly, the same holds over Hopf algebras and their super versions. A single language for these models is useful. Tools built for one family may then carry over to the rest.
arxiv-2601-15696:
Kyongwon Kim and Bing Li learn graph structure from functional data in a 2026 arXiv paper. In functional data, each observation is a curve, not a single number. A functional graph shows how those curves relate to each other. Many model families already exist for this task. The list runs from Gaussian and copula versions to Bayesian and additive ones. Each makes its own trade-offs.

The authors add nonlinear sufficient dimension reduction to the toolkit. Dimension reduction compresses data while keeping the structure that matters. Nonlinear versions can capture bends that linear maps miss. Their title promises learning functional graphs with that tool. For fields like neuroscience and climate science, curve data are common. A graph of how curves drive each other is often the real prize.
arxiv-2601-16096:
Hyunsoo Kim and five coauthors build cells that move as free grains, not fixed dots. Their 2026 preprint sets out Neural Particle Automata. Past cell nets pin each cell to a grid dot. Here each cell is a grain with a place that can shift. Each grain also holds a state that shifts in time. One shared learned rule drives all grains.

The shared rule reads near grains and updates place and state. From plain rules, rich group acts can grow on their own. The team frames the tool for acts like swarms and flows. Free grains fit such acts far more than fixed grids. The work opens a new path for learned group dynamics.
arxiv-2601-16196:
Wanting Jin, Guorong Wu and Quefeng Li build tests for the worth of one input type in joint models. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that join types like pics and text. It is not clear how to test if one type truly counts. That gap is wide in high size joint linear models. Past tools lack strict tests for that case.

The team gives a strict test for one type at a time. The test holds in high size joint models of broad form. Firm tests stop teams from trust in a type that adds nil. They also show which types earn their cost. The work aids sound use of joint health models.
arxiv-2601-16296:
Dohun Lee and coauthors add a past store to video to video spread models. Their 2026 preprint deals with tools that edit a clip by text cues. Top tools now edit look, move or cam path with skill. Real edit work is oft done in rounds, not in one pass. Each round builds on the last round and its flaws.

Round by round work needs the tool to recall past rounds. A past store gives the model that recall as it edits. Recall should keep edits in line through rounds. It should also stop drift of look and scene facts. The work, named Memory-V2V, targets true edit flows.
arxiv-2601-16796:
Szymon Wąsowicz speeds a hard sum task for a niche class of curves. Some curves bend the same way at each small span. His class bends in a fifth-order way, both up and down. Plain sum rules can drift on such curves. His 2026 preprint builds a smart rule that adapts as it goes.

The rule leans on a refined gap bound. That bound ties two famed sum rules, Gauss and Lobatto. Their point sets frame the gap with care. A smart rule can hit tight marks with fewer steps. Such sums feed codes in flight, drugs, and finance math.
arxiv-2601-17596:
Yunxiang Zhang and seven co-authors present MLE-Ideator for machine learning engineering agents. Such agents build and tune ML systems on their own. They often fail to improve their own work in loops. The authors split the job in two. An implementation agent writes the code. A dedicated Ideator gives strategic help on request.

Separation lets each agent do what it does best. The Ideator can step back and see the big picture. The builder stays close to code detail. The team shows the approach works in two ways. Better ideas in the loop mean better final models. The design mirrors human teams with a planner and a builder.
arxiv-2601-17996:
Aude Amari, Lorenzo Costigliola, and Jeppe C. Dyre simulate how a glassy liquid ages after a sudden heat jump. Their 2026 preprint studies a binary Lennard-Jones system of the Kob-Andersen type. The liquid starts in deep, well-settled states with very long relaxation times. Then the heat jumps up by a large step. The team watches how the material ages after that shock.

They test the material-time idea of Tool and Narayanaswamy on this extreme case. The idea says a clock tied to the material itself can tame aging curves. First, they study a triangular relation for the potential energy. The results check whether a trusted tool survives far outside its usual range.
arxiv-2601-18096:
Yuting Zhang and co-authors give language model recommenders a better sense of what users like. Their 2026 preprint starts from a known gap. Language models are weak at the complex preference patterns that classic recommenders capture well. Past fixes fed classic recommendation embeddings into the model. But a gap persists between smooth embedding space and the model's discrete word space. The team's method mines preference hints from a knowledge graph to bridge that gap.

Hints drawn from a graph carry facts about items and their links. Those facts can be stated in words the model handles well. Better preference sense means picks that fit the user more closely. The work joins graph knowledge with language skill.
arxiv-2601-18696:
Paul Whitten, Francis Wolff, and Chris Papachristou weigh ways to tell why a tool flags a chip as rigged. A rigged chip holds a hid extra part that can leak facts or break the chip on cue. Smart tools can flag such chips with good grades. But a flag is of small use if the staff who guard chips cannot tell what drove it.

The team set the main tell-why tools side by side on this task. Tools built for shots may give tales that chip staff cannot act on. The test checks which tales point to real parts of the flaw.
