Clear tales could cut the time from flag to fix. They could also help staff trust a flag or drop it with cause. Chip guards need both: sharp flags and tales they can use.
arxiv-2601-18796:
Brian Ondov and four colleagues teach text models to read, walk, and turn back the codes that stand for trial texts in health work. Such codes crush a long trial text into a short string of counts. The crush is one-way in most tools: staff can make the code but can't read what it holds or write a new trial from it. That blind spot cuts trust and blocks fresh uses, such as to draft a trial like past ones.

The team pair a text model with the codes of health trials. The pair learns to turn a code back to words and to bend a code by a text ask. A two-way code could let staff search trials by feel, not just by key words. It could also let them draft new trials from the form of old ones.
arxiv-2601-18996:
Pankaj Munbodh tests how future electron colliders could catch a rare rule breaking event. Lepton flavor violation, where one kind of lepton turns into another, would be a clear sign of physics past the Standard Model. The study looks at a process where electrons collide and produce a tau and a muon.

The work uses the broad frame that adds small extra terms to the Standard Model. It checks the reach of two planned machines, the ILC and CLIC. A catch of this kind would prove the lepton families mix in ways the old model forbids, and would point to new forces or particles.
arxiv-2601-19096:
Sohhyung Park and three co-authors build a counseling chatbot that asks, not just answers. Mental health chat tools have grown with language models, but most only react to what the user says. Real counseling has an exploration phase, where a good counselor probes gently to learn the client's state.

Their system, PsyProbe, tracks the user's mental state as the talk unfolds, using a structured frame. That tracking lets it steer the talk with apt questions, and its steps stay readable to a human reviewer. A proactive, legible style could make early stage support talks safer and more useful.
arxiv-2601-19196:
Egor Morozov studies the shapes of tori that make a drum like tone as large as it can be. On a torus, the first Laplace eigenvalue sets the lowest tone for its size. Inside a fixed conformal class, shapes that share angles but not lengths, some shapes push that tone to an extreme.

Morozov looks at the rotationally symmetric critical shapes among them. Known results tie such extreme shapes to harmonic maps into spheres. The work adds concrete forms to that tie, helping geometers see what the best shapes actually look like rather than just knowing they exist.
arxiv-2601-19396:
Marc Cheneau and François Goudail detect single atoms in sharp photos of microtrap arrays with a playful strategy. The arrays hold atoms in a grid of tiny traps, and the task is to say which traps are filled. Their Mikado strategy alternates estimation and detection steps, round after round.

The trick drops the need for an explicit model of the posterior odds for each site. Each round feeds its best guess into the next detection pass. Atom arrays are testbeds for quantum simulation, and a reliable census of filled traps is the first step of every run.
arxiv-2601-19696:
David Touzeau, Alexandre Barthelemy, and Francis Bernardeau study how gravity bends light from distant galaxies. This weak lensing effect distorts the shapes of galaxies in a way that maps dark matter. But lensing also washes out fine features in how matter clusters. One lost feature is the baryon acoustic oscillation pattern, a set of ripples with a known size.

Those ripples are a standard ruler for measuring the universe's expansion. In lensing maps they normally vanish because lensing projects everything along the line of sight. The authors look for ways to probe the ripples and other scale-dependent features without that mixing. Recovering them would give lensing surveys a powerful extra measurement. The work matters for the big cosmology missions now collecting data.
arxiv-2601-19996:
Suhani Surana and colleagues characterise three binary stars whose members are low-mass M dwarfs. Models of low-mass stars still disagree with observations of their masses and radii. That mismatch limits our understanding of the most common stars in the galaxy. Binaries help because their orbits let astronomers measure masses dynamically.

The team uses the Habitable-zone Planet Finder spectrograph to monitor the binaries over time. High-resolution spectra track each star's motion, yielding dynamical measurements. Characterising both the stars and their orbits tightens the mass-radius relation. Better low-mass models matter beyond stellar physics: they set the sizes of planets found around such stars. The work adds precise benchmarks where theory needs them.
arxiv-2601-20596:
Mohsen Asgharzadeh investigates the annihilator of an Ext module in commutative algebra. For an ideal of a given grade, he studies a divisorial ideal built from the annihilator of the top Ext group of the quotient ring. The main focus is a containment problem: whether this ideal sits inside the integral closure of the original ideal.

Containments of this kind link homological data to the geometry of ideal closures. Ext groups measure how far a module is from being free, so their annihilators carry fine structural information. The paper tests how much of that information the integral closure captures.
arxiv-2601-20696:
Samira Yazdanpourmoghadam, Mahan Balal Pour, and Vahid Partovi Nia study planning software for a metal plant. Their 2026 paper deals with enterprise resource planning in the ferro-titanium trade. Such planning must solve hard puzzle-like tasks. Two classic ones are the job-shop problem and the knapsack problem. Both ask how to fit many jobs or goods into tight limits.

Older ways to solve these tasks rely on rules of thumb and search tricks. The authors turn instead to transformer models, the design behind much of modern AI. They use more than one type of transformer for the planning task. The paper sits where deep learning meets plant logistics. It asks if learned models can find near-best plans fast enough to use in daily work.
arxiv-2601-20796:
Yiran Huang and three co-authors take apart how multimodal models learn from examples in context. Their 2026 paper studies transformer-based multimodal large language models. Such models often show in-context learning: they pick up a new task from examples in the prompt. The team asks how this ability works when inputs mix images and text.

Their focus is on two things: asymmetries between modalities and the circuit dynamics inside the model. An asymmetry would mean image and text examples do not play equal roles. Circuit dynamics means the internal pathways that carry the task. By dissecting both, the study shows where the learning actually happens. The work helps explain a skill that users rely on daily but rarely see inside.
arxiv-2601-20896:
Ryan Whetten and three co-authors ask which training data a speech model truly needs. Their 2026 paper studies data selection for self-supervised speech models. Self-supervised learning has transformed speech processing. Its success, though, rests on massive pretraining datasets. Robustness is often credited to scale and diversity alone. The role of the data distribution is less understood.

The team systematically examines curated subsets of pretraining data. They measure how each subset shapes automatic speech recognition performance. A smaller, well-chosen set might beat a huge random one. That would cut cost and speed up training. The study helps builders choose data with intent, not just volume. It is part of a wider push to make model training leaner and greener.
arxiv-2601-20996:
Shreshth Malik and six co-authors build proving grounds for machines that discover materials. Their 2026 paper introduces MADE, short for Materials Discovery Environments. Current benchmarks test static prediction or lone sub-tasks. Real discovery is a loop: try, learn, and try again. Static tests miss that loop in full. MADE benchmarks end-to-end autonomous discovery pipelines.

In these settings, an agent must close the loop. It proposes candidates, runs tests, and updates its plan. Scores then reflect discovery skill, not just prediction skill. The frame lets labs compare full pipelines fairly. That matters as autonomous labs move from demos to daily use. MADE gives the field a shared track for that race.
arxiv-2601-21096:
Hongzheng Chen and a large team of co-authors present an agent that discovers compiler tricks on its own. Their 2026 paper introduces Magellan. Modern compilers rely on hand-crafted heuristics to guide optimization passes. Human-designed rules struggle with the complexity of modern software and hardware. They also carry a high maintenance burden. Magellan is an agentic framework that evolves the compiler pass itself. It synthesizes executable C++ decision logic.

Instead of tuning knobs, the system rewrites the rules. Evolution tests each variant and keeps the winners. The name nods to exploration: the agent charts unknown heuristic space. AlphaEvolve supplies the evolutionary engine named in the title. Success would cut the human cost of keeping compilers sharp. The work joins Google and Cornell researchers in one team. It points toward self-improving toolchains.
arxiv-2601-21296:
Shaobo Wang and co-authors revisit how to shrink a large dataset into a small synthetic one that still teaches models well. Good distilled data can cut training cost a lot. Many current methods rely on rules of thumb to balance speed and quality.

The link between the real data and the synthetic set is still poorly understood. The authors reframe the task inside knowledge distillation with a firmer theory. They focus on making the small set both informative and useful for training. A clearer theory should help builders know what to keep when they compress data.
arxiv-2601-21596:
Felix Rott, Zhe-Feng Xu, and Matteo Zanardini carry a classic geometry rule into the world of relativity. The Ptolemy rule is an old statement about distances among four points. The authors define its analogue for spacetime. In spacetime, distances run along time-like paths.

In spacetimes that behave well on the large scale, they prove the rule matches a curvature bound. The bound says a certain time-like curvature is no greater than zero. They also link the rule to hyperbolic inversion. And they draw out rigidity results. Such work gives relativists a distance-only way to detect curvature bounds. No direct measure of the curvature is needed.
arxiv-2601-21696:
Alexandre Chaussard, Anna Bonnet, and Sylvain Le Corff find independent components inside streams of count data. Modern collection yields growing piles of counts over time, from gene reads to event logs. Standard component methods were built for smooth continuous data, not counts.

Their generative model pairs regime-switching dynamics with a Poisson log-normal emission law. It finds disentangled components whose weight shifts with the regime. Clean components make the data easier to interpret and to perturb in analysis. The method suits fields where the raw signal is a count and the hidden drivers change their mix over time.
arxiv-2601-21996:
Jianhui Chen, Yuzhang Luo, and Liangming Pan trace interpretable parts of language models back to the data that created them. Mechanistic interpretability has found circuits inside models that humans can understand. But where those circuits came from during training has remained elusive.

The team's 2026 preprint introduces Mechanistic Data Attribution, a framework that uses influence functions to link interpretable units to specific training samples. It is built to scale to real models and datasets. Knowing which data formed a circuit could help teams remove the sources of bad behavior, audit models for regulators. And understand training itself as a process that builds structure, not just statistics.
arxiv-2601-22096:
Qian Zhang, Feng Zhao, Tongxin Zheng, and Le Xie revisit how energy storage gets credited in capacity markets. Many United States electricity markets are adopting marginal accreditation reforms, judging each resource by the reliability it adds at the margin. Storage complicates that judgment, since a battery's value depends on when it discharges.

The authors reformulate the storage accreditation problem using Marginal Reliability Impact, a measure of how a resource changes the risk of shortfalls. Their 2026 preprint draws new insights from that framing. As grids add storage at scale, accreditation rules gain weight. They decide what gets built and paid for. Getting the storage math right shapes the future grid's reliability and cost.
arxiv-2601-22196:
Piotr Przymus and co-authors dissect how Linux kernel vulnerabilities get patched. In 2024 the Linux kernel became its own CVE Numbering Authority, formalizing how its security flaws are identified and tracked. That change created a rich new record of vulnerability handling in the world's most deployed kernel.

The authors analyze kernel CVEs through their metadata, associated commits, and patch latency, the time from report to fix. Their title previews the findings: how recent the kernel version is matters, the severity score does not, and history fades. Their 2026 preprint gives maintainers and security teams evidence about what actually speeds fixes, instead of what the process assumes drives them.
arxiv-2601-22496:
Jinu Hyeon, Woobin Park, Hongjoon Ahn, and Taesup Moon design goal codes that hold just what an agent needs to act. Their 2026 preprint works in offline goal-based learning, where a high level picks subgoals and a low level carries them out. The goal code is the bridge between the two levels.

A code that keeps action-relevant facts, and drops the rest, should plan and act better. The team call such codes action-sufficient. Their work tests how to learn them from past data alone. Better bridges could help robots chain long tasks. It is a design claim with wide reach.
arxiv-2601-22596:
Abdelrrahman Moubane built FOTBCD, a large bench for spotting new and gone buildings in aerial photos. Their 2026 preprint draws on French orthophotos and official map data from IGN France. Past benches hug one city or a small zone; this one spans twenty-eight departments.

Twenty-five departments train the models; three held-out ones test them. Wide ground truth makes scores mean more for real map-keeping. Planners and map firms need fresh building maps at national scale. The data set gives that task a fair, hard test. It is a resource paper, built to be used. Anyone can use it to grade a new method on the same ground.
arxiv-2601-22996:
Yiding Feng, Zonghan Yang, and Yuhao Zhang schedule the memory that language models use while answering. That memory, the KV cache, grows with every token a model writes. A scheduler must cut waiting time under a hard memory cap, yet reply lengths are unknown in advance.

That non-clairvoyant setting is the core difficulty: choices must be made without knowing job sizes. The authors study competitive scheduling rules for this setting. Better cache scheduling means cheaper, faster service for chatbots and coding tools. The hard memory budget is non-negotiable at serving time, so schedules must stay feasible even when lengths surprise.
arxiv-2603-01496:
Hiroyuki Kasahara and Weina Zhou ask what being in the womb during the Great Chinese Famine did to later schooling. Their 2026 study faces a hard bias: boys exposed before birth died at higher rates, so survivors are not a fair sample. That bias can hide or distort the true long-term harm.

To cut the bias, they compare exposed children with their own same-sex siblings who were not exposed. Famine strength is scored from county and year records of excess deaths. On average, exposure raised illiteracy by a similar amount for boys and girls. It also cut years of schooling by a similar amount for both sexes. The matched pattern helps separate famine harm from survival bias in fetal-origins research.
arxiv-2603-01596:
Switching a Python project from one code library to a twin library takes care and a lot of hand edits. Matthias Kebede, May Mahmoud, Mohayeminul Islam, and Sarah Nadi bring that switch into the editor in this 2026 work. Their earlier command-line tool used a language model to do the full switch on its own.

The new plug-in, MigMate, runs inside the VS Code editor that many coders use daily. It shows each planned change and lets the coder confirm edits before they apply. That review step keeps a human in charge of a change that can break a project. In an early user study, the plug-in cut the time for a switch task each time it was used. Users also rated it highly on a standard ease-of-use scale.
arxiv-2603-01696:
Haonan Jia, Shichao Dong, Xin Dong, and colleagues stop image captions from dropping key visual facts. Their 2026 work starts from a flaw: large vision-language models often omit or distort what an image shows. Loss is hard to measure, since text and image live in different forms.

Their insight is that a good caption should let a search find the same image again. Their frame, CIM, scores captions by how well retrieved images match the source in two ways. Reinforcement learning then trains the model to cut that measured loss, with no extra hand labels needed. Results beat even supervised fine-tuning on caption quality in their tests. On one hard benchmark, relation reasoning improves by a fifth for a mid-size open model.
arxiv-2603-02096:
Yiweng Xie, Bo He, Junke Wang, and colleagues compress streaming video memory so models can watch live feeds cheaply. Their 2026 framework, FluxMem, needs no training and adapts its compression to each scene. Streaming understanding piles up visual tokens fast, which inflates latency and memory for multimodal models.

A temporal module first removes redundant tokens across adjacent frames of the stream. A spatial module then merges repetitive regions within each frame into compact representations. Self-adaptive rules set the compression rate from scene statistics, not from manual tuning. Online benchmarks reach new top results under real-time settings in their tests. Latency and peak memory drop sharply on one benchmark, while offline performance stays strong with far fewer visual tokens.
arxiv-2603-02296:
Rajeev Singh and Alexander Soloviev study spinning fluids on a curved expanding backdrop in this 2026 paper. Relativistic fluids from heavy-ion collisions can carry spin as they expand. A recently found backdrop expands sideways with finite reach inside ordinary spacetime. It differs from the classic Gubser flow, which spreads without bound and has rounder symmetry.

Within perfect-fluid spin theory, the authors derive exact equations for every spin part. Faster early expansion and a causal edge keep spin effects more tightly localized here. One spin part, around the flow axis, wobbles as it fades, unlike the Gubser case. That contrast marks this backdrop as a distinct test bed. It suits spin studies in expanding fluids of finite size.
arxiv-2603-02396:
Dennis Gross verifies an AI policy for blood platelet stocks in this 2026 paper. Platelets expire within five days, so blood banks walk a tight line. Too much stock wastes a scarce resource, while too little risks lives. Reinforcement learning can learn good ordering policies, but its neural choices are opaque.

His tool, COOL-MC, pairs learning with formal checking and explanation methods. It builds a Markov chain from only the states a trained policy can reach. Checks confirm a low stockout risk and a low overflow risk over a long horizon. Explanations show the policy watches inventory age most, not weekday or pending orders. Swapping mid-large orders for smaller ones barely changed safety. The study is a first formal audit of such a policy.
arxiv-2603-02596:
Wenzhe Tong, Yicheng Jiang, Chi Zhang, and colleagues estimate ground contact for tensegrity robots in this 2026 paper. Tensegrity robots are light and resilient, built from rods and cables under tension. Their soft, spread-out ground contacts make state estimation hard. Dedicated contact sensors are one fix, but add weight and wiring.

Their graph network reads only built-in sensing: motion units and cable-length histories. The robot's threefold symmetry is baked into how the network passes messages. That symmetry boosts sample efficiency and generalization across poses. Predicted contacts feed a leading Kalman filter for pose estimation. Simulations show higher accuracy and better scores than baselines while using a fifth of the training data. Pose estimates stayed low-drift and physically consistent.
arxiv-2603-02696:
Shenghua Feng, Jie An, Naijun Zhan, and Fanjiang Xu ask when the averages of a random system can be computed exactly. Their 2026 paper studies stochastic differential equations, which describe motion driven by both steady drift and random noise. Moments, meaning averages of powers of the state, underpin formal checks of such systems but rarely have closed forms.

The authors define moment-solvable equations and give a symbolic procedure that tries to build a small linear system governing any chosen moment. They then name a broad class, marked by a block-triangular shape, where this always works for polynomial moments. That class strictly extends linear equations and covers many nonlinear models. Experiments confirm the procedure performs well in practice.
arxiv-2603-03196:
Paolo Angella, Vito Paolo Pastore, and Matteo Santacesaria extend a sensing method to signals that live in endless dimensions. Deep learning models now serve as priors to rebuild signals from few readings, beating older sparsity tricks. But the math behind them assumed finite lists of numbers, while real signals are often curves.

Their frame works in Hilbert spaces, where curves are points in an endless space. They extend two key tools, local coherence and a recovery guarantee, to that setting. The headline result: the needed reading count tracks the prior's true size, not the display grid. Tests on a flow equation confirm the math. With very few readings, a lower-grade model even steadied the rebuild.
arxiv-2603-03296:
Ke Yang and eight colleagues give language model agents a memory that plugs into any task. Long-term memory helps agents in complex settings, but existing designs are either built for one task or generic yet weak, drowning the model in raw retrieved history. Their 2026 module, PlugMem, draws on cognitive science: what matters for decisions is abstract knowledge, not raw experience.

PlugMem compresses episodes into a compact knowledge graph holding two kinds of knowledge: facts about the world and prescriptions for action. Retrieval then reasons over that knowledge instead of verbose traces. Tested unchanged on three different benchmarks, covering long conversations, multi-hop retrieval, and web tasks, PlugMem beat other generic memory designs and even task-specific ones. It also packed the most information per unit of memory under a shared analysis.
arxiv-2603-03596:
Marcel Torne and seventeen colleagues give robot policies a memory with two timescales. A robot cooking dinner must remember which recipe stages are done, a long-horizon fact, and also where the object in its grip went when its own arm hides it, a short-horizon one. Feeding raw past observations to the policy handles neither well. Their 2026 approach, Multi-Scale Embodied Memory, splits memory by kind.

Short-horizon memory is video, compressed by a video encoder into recent visual context. Long-horizon memory is text, holding abstracted semantic facts about progress. Mixed together, the two let vision-language-action policies complete tasks lasting up to fifteen minutes, like cleaning a kitchen or making a grilled cheese sandwich. Policies also adapted their manipulation strategies in context, using memory to change approach mid-task.
arxiv-2603-03696:
Weitao Zhang, Han He, and Jun Zhang chart how a star's outer atmosphere brightens as the star spins faster, and where that brightening stops. The data come from China's LAMOST survey, whose calcium emission lines measure chromospheric activity for solar-like stars. This 2026 paper, the third in its series, cross-matches the activity catalog with rotation periods from the Kepler and TESS space telescopes, assembling more than eleven thousand stars.

Activity climbs with rotation rate until it saturates, then flattens no matter how fast the spin. The saturation point shifts systematically with surface temperature, arriving at longer periods for cooler stars. Saturation shows most clearly in stars with thick convective zones and fades for hotter stars. Recalibrated basal flux indices, which strip out the quiet floor of emission, sharpen the rotation connection throughout.
arxiv-2603-03896:
Tiantong Cheng and Hongbo Cheng ask whether a quantum-corrected anti-de Sitter black hole carrying global monopoles can split into two. The black hole may host regular or phantom monopoles. The authors test the possibility of fragmentation against the second law of thermodynamics: a split is allowed only if the total entropy does not decrease. They derive the entropies of the original black hole and of its would-be fragments, with the difference depending on quantum-gravity oscillations, the monopole factors, and the anti-de Sitter environment.

Both kinds of monopole keep the black hole intact, because the entropy difference is negative. Strong quantum fluctuation can reverse the sign when one fragment is tiny and the other huge, and a large enough AdS radius can also make fragmentation favorable near equal masses. The work clarifies how quantum corrections and environment decide black hole stability.

Marked for the Truth Commission, the file concerns the priests' killing. Readers should note the dating caution in the heading itself, which the catalog record preserves openly.
cia-0000096496: Progress report on Recommendation number two of the Report to the President by the President's Board is declassified CIA document 0000096496, dated October 4, 1957. The heading is cut short in the catalog. The brief file revisits the same recommendation tracked months earlier, giving readers a later checkpoint in the board's long follow-up sequence.
cia-0000113196: Dated January 1, 1945, with that date marked as an estimate, declassified CIA document 0000113196 concerns names and a description of a person. Its untitled heading notes pages as received, then breaks off at As R. No person is named in the surviving heading text itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000119696:
Also from January 1954, this CIA paper surveys Soviet bloc strength in economic warfare and the courses of action open to it. Trade bans, credit pressure, and control of key goods were weapons in the Cold War alongside armies. The paper maps that quieter battlefield as Washington saw it.

Knowing what economic harm the other side could do, and how, shaped Western trade rules for years. The study sets out the bloc's tools and the moves analysts thought it might make. For readers, it explains a contest fought through ports, contracts, and embargo lists, where the damage was measured in stalled factories rather than lost battles.
cia-0000124296: A December 1957 CIA report covers the Soviet rocket program and its earth satellite. Two months after Sputnik, the questions had sharpened: how many rockets, how large, and how soon the next launch. The paper gives the agency's accounting at the end of that startling year. Year-end accountings forced analysts to commit numbers to paper, and those committed figures drove the budget fights over American rockets in the season that followed.
cia-0000132296: Situation Report 605 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 1, 1991, covers military developments, but part of its own headline was deleted before release. Military reporting was the core of the series as the deadline for Iraq to quit Kuwait approached. The deleted section may have held the most sensitive material. What remains still shows the shape of the daily military watch.
cia-0000132496:
World reaction to possible American moves against Cuba is forecast in a CIA document dated January 4, 1961. Its headline breaks off at the word again, short for against. The agency was gaming out Washington's options and their likely costs abroad that winter.

The document sets out how other governments and publics might answer each course of action. Such forecasts helped shape the choices that led toward the Bay of Pigs. For readers, it shows planning at its most careful and most uncertain. The real reactions, when the invasion came that April, would test every line of the forecast. Some held up well, and others did not.
cia-0000132596: Possible Cuban work to stir trouble inside Venezuela fills a CIA paper dated August 2, 1960. Havana's hand in the unrest in Caracas was suspected then but not proven. Cuban aid to rebels there would grow much larger in the years ahead. The short paper weighs the proof in hand that summer. It takes each claim in turn and tests it.
cia-0000135696: This Spanish-language item from the 2506 Brigade files is dated 2 January 1961. The brigade of anti-Castro exiles was then in its final months of CIA-run training. The catalog record names no subject for the document, and it shares its date with other items in the release. It stands as a dated piece of primary evidence in Spanish, part of the paper trail of an operation that would fail publicly within four months.
cia-0000135796:
Plans to kill leaders in Guatemala, weighed by the agency from 1952 to 1954, fill a CIA paper carrying an estimated date of May 4, 1995. The paper came out decades after the events it covers. It shows what officers once put on paper at the darkest edge of the Guatemala campaign.

The record gathers the proposals in one place for the first time. Names, lists, and memos from the coup years stand behind its dry title. For readers, it is among the most sobering papers in the whole file. It also shows why the Guatemala operation stayed a byword for covert action long after the Cold War ended.
cia-0000135896: A meeting record of 1 February 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with a report on the OAS conference. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136096: Filed on 6 March 1954, this CIA cable concerns the King Program, one more coded project whose work the file itself has to explain. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136196: The record dated 2 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about SECANT, vehicles, a Quetzaltenango contact, and a further item the heading cuts off as pil. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136296: The record dated 3 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about the need to visit STORAX, a coded place drawing a trip in the operation's travel orders. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136396: A reported conversation with Major Jaime Rosenberg, head of Guatemala's Guardia Judicial, is forwarded to LINCOLN in this January 1954 cable. The talk touched on activities against the Guatemalan government being carried on in El Salvador and the need for vigilance over them, plus continued contact with a source given a phonetic name. Headquarters traces records, suggests the local station chief have no contact until the matter is resolved, and advises checks. The cable shows the agency watching Guatemala's security chief.
cia-0000136996: PBSUCCESS Situation Report No. 3, from the post-coup period in 1954, describes Guatemala's security services being purged. Investigations are being hampered by destroying documents or denying access to the preceding government's records. The Guardia Civil, roughly penetrated by communists under Presidents Arevalo and Arbenz, is described as alert to subversives and cleaning out communists remaining in government offices. An unknown number of communists who took asylum in embassies have been leaving secretly, with no strict border controls yet evident.
cia-03023196: This March 11, 1959 bulletin carried the day's intelligence summary. Policymakers got the analysts' take on world developments. The Cold War's daily brief. Those who study the era will use it. This file preserves that declassified paper.
cia-06785496: USSR SITUATION REPORT, a CIA assessment. The Soviet report. This file preserves that declassified paper. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06827996: OHB MAIN CAFE 11/28/16, a CIA document. The dated cafe file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06974496: REPORT OF INVESTIGATION ALLEGATIONS OF CONNECTIONS BETWEEN CIA AND THE CONTRAS, a CIA document. The Contra probe. This file preserves that declassified paper. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
collectanea-chymica-leidensia-oder-auser: Collectanea chymica Leidensia, 1696. The Leiden chemical collection. This book preserves that alchemy. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
conrad-outcast-islands-1896:
An Outcast of the Islands, Conrad's second novel, appeared in 1896 and returns to the Malay world of his first book. Peter Willems, a clerk who has disgraced himself by theft in Makassar, is hidden away by Captain Lingard on a remote river.

There Willems betrays his protector, falls for Aissa, a Malay chief's daughter, and helps rival traders break Lingard's monopoly. Almayer, from the earlier novel, watches his own hopes rot alongside. Conrad builds the tale from treachery, desire, and the rot of the colonial fringe. It is apprentice work beside the later novels, but the atmosphere is already unmistakable.
constitution-ghana-1996: Ghana's 1992 Constitution, amended through 1996, anchors its democracy. It guards rights. The Tower library holds the full text. It led Africa's wave. Soldiers left. Voters came. Gold stayed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cope-primary-factors-organic-evolution-1:
Edward Drinker Cope was a famed American fossil hunter, quick with a pick and a pen. His Primary Factors of Organic Evolution, from 1896, states his rival theory to Darwin's. Cope had dug up hundreds of extinct species across the West.

Cope argues that use, habit, and inner growth drive change more than chance selection. Traits gained in life, he thought, can pass to offspring. This neo-Lamarckian view lost ground as genetics rose in the next century. The book still shows the real fight over how evolution works in Darwin's own era. Cope backs his case with examples drawn from his own fossil finds.
corneille-cid-mongan-1896:
Pierre Corneille's The Cid was first staged in Paris in 1637 and made its young author famous at once. Roscoe Mongan translated the play into English verse in 1896. Its hero, Rodrigue, loves Chimène, but honor forces him to fight her father, who has insulted his own aged father.

Rodrigue kills his beloved's father in a duel, and Chimène must demand his death. Duty pulls both lovers apart even as Spain needs Rodrigue's sword against the Moors. The play's success sparked a famous quarrel over the rules of drama. The Cid fixed the pattern of French classical tragedy and gave French its byword for a hero.
cumont-textes-monuments-mithra-tome2-189:
Cumont's second tome of Textes et monuments, published at Brussels in 1896, holds the monuments of the Mithraic mysteries. The text is in French, and the volume came out before tome one. It catalogues and describes the cult's surviving art: 493 figures and nine heliotype plates fill its pages.

Bull-slaying reliefs, cave temples, altars, and statues from across the Roman world stand in ordered ranks. Cumont reads each image for what it proves about rite and belief. Paired with tome one's texts, the volume completes his monumental corpus of Mithraic sources. Archaeologists still begin Mithraic work with Cumont's catalogue in hand. Few nineteenth-century corpora have served so long without replacement.
demachy-les-rothschild-1896:
Edouard Demachy wrote this French book on the Rothschilds in Paris in 1896. Its title calls them a family of Jewish financiers of the 19th century. Demachy wrote from the records of French finance, where the Paris house stood at the core.

He sets out the work of the Paris bank through the wars, loans, and rail lines of the age. The book is a grave French record of the house, free of the wild tales of the pamphlet press. It holds its place as the chief French view of the bank in its own time.
dickinson-poems-three-series-complete-18:
Emily Dickinson wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems in her quiet Amherst life and published almost none of them. After her death in 1886, her sister found the poems tied in small bundles. Her friend Mabel Loomis Todd and Thomas Wentworth Higginson edited three small volumes in the 1890s. This 1896 book gathers all three series in one volume.

The editors smoothed Dickinson's dashes and capitals to suit the taste of the day, but the voice survives: startling, compressed, and funny even about death. Poems on bees, storms, faith, and immortality crowd the pages. This volume is the complete public-domain record of how the nineteenth century first met Dickinson. Modern readers can watch a major poet arriving in disguise.
dubois-pithecanthropus-erectus-english-1:
Eugene Dubois presented his Java ape-man to English readers in 1896. The paper appeared in the Journal of the Anthropological Institute. He called Pithecanthropus erectus a transitional form between apes and humans.

Dubois lays out the skullcap, thigh bone, and teeth from Trinil in Java. He argues the thigh proves upright walking while the skull stayed ape-like. British experts debated him sharply at the meeting and after. The fossils are now placed within Homo erectus. Dubois's English paper marks the moment the missing link became an international argument. Dubois had carried the bones back from Java at great personal cost.
europmc-pmc10188596:
Zhang and co-workers chart the global burden of blood cancers and how it changed over thirty years, in a 2023 study. Blood cancers, called hematologic malignancies, include leukemias, lymphomas, and myelomas. Knowing where cases and deaths rise or fall helps health leaders aim prevention work and research funds where they matter most.

The team gathered detailed data on rates and deaths across countries and years. They describe clear shifts in the pattern of these cancers over three decades. The paper gives a current map of a major slice of the world cancer burden.
europmc-pmc10300796:
Balasubramaniam and co-authors review how plants respond to salinity stress in a 2023 paper. Salt buildup in soil is a severe and growing threat to farming worldwide. It stunts plant growth, disrupts their water and nutrient balance, and in the end endangers the global food supply.

The review explains how plants sense salt and defend themselves. Defenses include pumping salt out of cells, storing it safely, and making protective compounds. The authors also cover breeding and gene approaches for salt-tolerant crops. The paper links plant science to food security. It also points to traits breeders can select for.
europmc-pmc10349496:
Chen and Yu reviewed in 2023 how tau protein and brain inflammation feed each other in Alzheimer's disease. Tau builds tangles inside brain cells, a hallmark of the illness. Tau harm tracks loss of memory and thought more closely than amyloid clumps do. Inflammation runs alongside both and adds to the decline.

Chen shows that immune cells in the brain, once switched on, can worsen tau harm. Worse tau harm then stirs yet more inflammation, in a loop. Changes to tau after it is made, and its spread from cell to cell, both tie into this loop. The review sums up trials that aim at tau or at inflammation. It backs plans that hit more than one target at once.
europmc-pmc10460796:
Sun and co-authors reviewed immune checkpoint therapy for solid tumours in 2023. Such drugs lift brakes on immune cells so they can attack cancer. The known brakes go by names such as CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1. A newer brake, LAG-3, has joined the drug list. Gains have been stark in skin and lung cancers.

Four blocks still limit wide use, Sun reports. Effects and side effects are hard to split, and true growth can be hard to tell from swelling. Tumours also build complex webs of resistance. Fresh hope comes from drug pairs, gene-edited viruses, mRNA vaccines, and nano carriers. Marks that predict who will respond now guide patient choice.
europmc-pmc1135296:
Nordborg and a large team resequence gene fragments across a model plant's range in this 2005 study. Arabidopsis thaliana is a small self-pollinating weed used as a model organism. The team resequenced 876 short DNA fragments in 96 plants, mixing stock centre lines with a structured sample from natural populations. They asked how genetic variation is patterned in a selfing species.

Despite selfing, variation broadly matched a widely distributed sexual species, they found. Linkage disequilibrium, the correlation between nearby variants, decayed within 50 kilobases. Variation was shared worldwide, though population structure and isolation by distance showed. The data broke standard neutral models in several ways. There was a genome-wide excess of rare alleles, partly due to selection. Local variation fell as gene density rose and rose near duplicated segments. Genome-wide surveys are needed to spot selection, they conclude.
europmc-pmc12375796:
Xu and co-authors reviewed tumor-associated macrophages in 2025. These immune cells gather inside and around tumors. They arrive from blood cells drawn by chemical signals. Once there, they settle into distinct states with opposite effects.

One state attacks tumors and boosts immune defense. The other state helps tumors grow blood vessels and spread. It also dampens immune attack and reshapes nearby tissue. Signals, pathways, and fuel use steer which state dominates. Xu surveys drugs that kill, block, or reprogram these cells. Their dual role makes them a rich but tricky target.
europmc-pmc1257596:
Richard and co-authors tested glyphosate and Roundup on human placental cells in 2005. Roundup is a weed killer built on glyphosate. Its residues enter food and rivers worldwide. Farm workers using it had reported pregnancy problems.

Glyphosate killed placental cells within 18 hours in dishes. Toxic doses sat below levels used in farming. Roundup proved more toxic than glyphosate alone every time. At lower doses the herbicide disrupted aromatase, the estrogen-making enzyme. It altered both enzyme activity and its gene message. Helper chemicals in Roundup boosted those effects. Aromatase makes estrogen, so its disruption matters for pregnancy.
europmc-pmc1281296:
Israel and co-authors drew lessons from community-based children's health research in 2005. Child health problems have grown in incidence and severity over decades. Their causes mix many factors at once. Low-income communities and communities of color bear the heaviest burden.

Research centers partnered directly with affected communities on studies. Partners included academics, health services, and community groups. Shared control shaped research questions and interventions. The authors distill lessons from the Centers for Children's Environmental Health. Community voice, they argue, improves both science and fairness. The lessons span several national research centers.
europmc-pmc1847696:
Curran and Ruvkun screened in 2007 the genes a worm cannot live without, asking whether any of them also govern aging. Theory says aging mechanisms must have early-life roles to be shaped by evolution. In the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, 2,700 genes are essential for development, yet their effect on lifespan was untested.

The team switched each gene off only after development finished. Sixty-four of them extended lifespan when inactivated, and many matched the strength of the strongest known aging regulators. The hits were conserved from yeast to humans and clustered in insulin and metabolic pathways, plus protein-making, RNA, and chromatin factors. Some larvae arrested by early switch-off outlived normal adults, and that survival needed the factor daf-16. The work ties insulin signaling to aging at every life stage.
europmc-pmc1925096:
Raubeson, Jansen and co-authors added two chloroplast genomes in 2007 from early-branching flowering plants. Chloroplasts are the green compartments that run photosynthesis, and their small genomes are a workhorse for plant family trees. Basal lineages, the earliest splits, were still thinly sampled.

The new sequences came from Ranunculus macranthus, a basal buttercup relative, and from Nuphar advena, a water plant in one of the earliest-branching lineages. Both genomes matched the usual plastid layout in gene content and order, and both were rich in the letters A and T outside their RNA genes. Comparing Nuphar with its cousin Nymphaea showed over two thirds of their genomes at least 95 percent identical. The study also reassessed two disputed genes and cataloged repeat patterns across flowering plants, seed plants, and all photosynthetic lineages.
europmc-pmc2020496:
Vandenbroucke and co-authors, with the STROBE Initiative, wrote the explanation document in 2007 for new reporting guidelines. Observational studies make up much medical research, yet their reporting is often too weak. Weak reports block judgement of quality and of whether results apply elsewhere. This companion piece explains each item in the STROBE checklist so authors and readers use it well.

The checklist has 22 items covering all major sections of a research article. Eighteen items are shared by cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies. Four items differ by design. For each item the authors give its meaning and rationale. They add published examples and references to supporting studies. Example flow diagrams show how participants move through a study.
europmc-pmc2034396:
Brayton and a large team sequenced the full genome of Babesia bovis, a tick-borne parasite of cattle. The parasite belongs to the apicomplexans, a group of single-celled blood parasites. It causes babesiosis, which harms livestock health and farming economies worldwide. The team compared its genome with two relatives, Theileria parva and Plasmodium falciparum, the malaria parasite. One aim was finding targets for vaccines.

At 8.2 million base pairs, the genome matches Theileria in size and layout, with extensive shared gene order. It differs sharply from the malaria parasite in size, chromosome number and gene set. About 150 ves1 genes vary the parasite's surface proteins, likely helping it evade immunity. The genome also lacks many metabolic pathways, and the team identified several new vaccine candidates.
europmc-pmc2041996:
Shen and co-workers profiled DNA methylation across gene promoters in normal human blood in 2007. Methylation is a chemical mark that can silence a gene. Dense clusters called CpG islands sit in many gene promoters, and they are usually unmarked in normal tissue. The team used a combined amplification and microarray method to check 6,177 genes at once.

Among 5,549 genes with dense CpG island promoters, 4.0 percent were nearly fully methylated in normal blood. That breaks the usual rule limiting such marks to X chromosome silencing and imprinted genes. Seven genes studied closely were silenced in most tissues but active in testis and sperm. Several switched on in cancer, and a demethylating drug could restart silenced genes in the lab.
europmc-pmc2098796:
Zahn and a large team launched AGEMAP in 2007, a database of gene activity changes during ageing in mice. A project called the Atlas of Gene Expression in Mouse Aging catalogues how expression changes with age. It covers 8,932 genes across 16 tissues. The team asked which tissues change most, whether tissues age together, and how mouse ageing compares with other species.

Some tissues showed large transcriptional changes in old mice, while others barely changed, suggesting strong upkeep for life. Tissues fell into three ageing patterns: neural, vascular and steroid-responsive. Individual mice aged in a coordinated way, ageing fast or slow across many tissues at once. Genes of the electron transport chain, the cell's energy system, aged similarly in mice, humans, flies and worms. Yet overall mouse and human patterns did not correlate.
europmc-pmc2124996: A medical paper on the duration of induced resistance toward tumor transplantation. The cancer defense. This article preserves that oncology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2126296: A medical paper with an improvement in the method of isolating the bacillus of cattle. The better cattle germ catch. This article preserves that veterinary bacteriology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2128196: A medical paper with studies on X-ray effects of small low-penetration doses. The soft X-rays. This article preserves that radiology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131296: A medical paper on the etiology of Oroya fever, pathological changes in experimental animals. The fever's damage. This article preserves that tropical medicine. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131396: A medical paper on the use of histamine as a standard test for diminished resistance. The histamine test. This article preserves that pharmacology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140896: A biology paper on duration of life of an aseptic drosophila culture inbred in the dark. The dark flies' lifespan. This article preserves that genetics. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2146996:
Sadauskas and co-workers traced gold nanoparticles in mice in 2007 to see where injected particles end up. Gold particles are chemically inert and easy to trace under the microscope, making them a good model. Adult female mice, some pregnant, received particles by vein or into the abdomen. Sizes were 2 and 40 nanometres. Tissues were checked after one, four and twenty-four hours.

Particles appeared only inside macrophages, the immune cells that engulf debris. After vein injection they clustered rapidly in Kupffer cells, the liver's resident macrophages. Abdominal injection gave slower liver uptake, plus some uptake in lymph nodes, spleen and gut. No particles appeared in kidney, brain, lung, placenta or fetal liver. The authors conclude the particles enter cells only by engulfing, and that liver macrophages are central to clearing them.
europmc-pmc2409296:
Du, Kou, and Coghill checked a widely used child behaviour questionnaire in China in 2008. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire asks parents, teachers, and young people themselves about emotions, conduct, attention, friendships, and kindness. It was built in Britain, so the team tested whether the Chinese translation holds up.

They collected full parent and teacher reports for 1,965 children aged 3 to 17 across Shanghai, plus 690 self-reports from older children. Score bands for normal, borderline, and abnormal ranges were set from this urban sample. The five-part structure held only partly, strongest for kindness, hyperactivity, and emotional symptoms. Reliability was the weak point: some scales scored as low as 0.30 on internal consistency, and repeat ratings six weeks later ran lower than expected. Agreement between raters matched earlier countries, at 0.23 to 0.49 in correlation terms.
europmc-pmc2410296:
Dahiya and co-authors profiled small gene regulators in ovarian cancer in 2008. The regulators are microRNAs, tiny RNA pieces that dial down target genes. They guide normal development, and broken levels had been tied to several cancers, so the team measured them in ovarian tumors and cell lines.

One microRNA, miR-221, stood out as highly raised in ovarian cancer. Another, miR-21, was lowered, and several members of the let-7 family were also down. Computer predictions listed targets for the strongest changers. The team then inserted these microRNAs into cancer cells and watched which gene messages actually fell. Surprisingly, the measured targets barely matched the predicted ones, and they differed between cell lines. The authors said target choice is far more context-dependent than databases suggest.
europmc-pmc2483296:
Kosiol and co-authors scanned six mammal genomes for genes shaped by positive selection in 2008. Positive selection means evolution favoured new versions of a gene, usually because they helped survival or breeding. Earlier scans used fewer genomes and missed much. Six high-quality assemblies, from human to dog to rat, gave this scan more power.

Of about 16,500 human genes traceable in other mammals, 400 showed solid signs of selection overall, and 144 more on single branches of the family tree. Immunity, smell and taste, and breeding dominated, as before. New patterns included the complement arm of immunity and whole pathways that work as a set evolving together. Most selected genes had flipped between selection and neutrality many times, so selection comes in episodes. Selected genes were also expressed at lower levels and in fewer tissues than average. Brain-only genes, notably, showed no extra selection.
europmc-pmc2542996:
Bedson and Croft reviewed in 2008 how poorly knee pain and knee X-rays agree in osteoarthritis, the wear-and-tear joint disease. Doctors often assume the two track together, yet studies hinted each is a weak guide to the other. The authors systematically gathered population studies that recorded both X-ray changes and symptoms in the same people.

Among people with knee pain, the share found to have X-ray osteoarthritis ranged widely, from 15 to 76 percent. Among people with X-ray disease, the share reporting pain ranged from 15 to 81 percent. The spread depended on which X-ray views were taken, how pain was defined, how disease was graded, and who was studied. The authors warn that X-ray results should never be used alone when judging a patient with knee pain.
europmc-pmc2577696:
Kasturiratne and colleagues produced in 2008 the first methodical global estimate of the snakebite burden. Snakebite is a major public health problem across the tropics, yet earlier estimates lacked a reproducible method. The team built regional estimates from published studies, United Nations mortality databases, and grey literature gathered through expert informants, grouping countries into 21 regions.

They estimate at least 421,000 cases of envenoming, with 20,000 deaths from snakebite each year worldwide. The true figures could reach 1,841,000 envenomings, with 94,000 deaths, since data are weakest where the problem is worst. Working from the fact that roughly one bite in four injects venom, total snakebites likely number 1.2 million to 5.5 million a year. The heaviest burden falls on sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.
europmc-pmc2642596:
Pyeon and colleagues showed in 2009 that human papillomavirus, a virus tied to several cancers, can only infect a cell that is about to divide. Doctors knew the virus sets up in the bottom layer of skin-like tissue, where cells still divide. Cells higher up have stopped dividing, but the reason for this limit was unclear.

The team used virus particles carrying the full viral genome and human skin cells held at set stages of the cell cycle. Cells kept in the resting stage could not be infected. Drugs that froze cells at early stages blocked infection, while drugs acting late in division did not. Only cells that passed into early division switched on the viral genes. This need to catch dividing cells helps explain where the virus takes hold.
europmc-pmc2690996:
Langmead, Trapnell, Pop, and Salzberg introduced in 2009 Bowtie, a program that aligns short DNA reads to a large genome at record speed. New sequencing machines were pouring out hundreds of millions of short reads per study. Placing each read on the human genome with older tools could take months of computer time, a wall the whole field was hitting.

Bowtie uses a compressed index of the genome, borrowed from data compression tricks, that fits in a sliver of memory. It then streams reads against that index far faster than its rivals. The authors estimate an older tool would need over five CPU-months for one human dataset where Bowtie needs hours. Speed changed what was practical: re-sequencing people, and profiling gene activity and protein binding genome-wide, all ride on this alignment step.
europmc-pmc2718496:
Zhang and co-authors mapped in 2009 where three forms of methylation, adding methyl tags, sit on histone H3 lysine 4 across the genome of Arabidopsis thaliana, a small model plant. Histones are spool proteins that DNA wraps around, and tags on them help set which genes are on or off. A lysine can hold one, two, or three methyl tags, with different effects.

Genome-wide maps in seedlings showed the three forms spread in distinct patterns tied to gene activity. DNA methylation, a separate silencing tag, was scarce where the two- and three-tag forms sat. In sharp contrast, it was enriched where the one-tag form sat, which suggests each form marks a different chromatin state.
europmc-pmc2861696:
Bruns and colleagues showed in 2010 that white blood cells cast DNA nets to fight the lung fungus Aspergillus fumigatus, a mold that can kill people with weak immune systems. The cells, called neutrophils, normally eat small spores, but the fungus grows into threads too large to swallow. The nets, webs of DNA studded with killing proteins, offer another way to attack the threads.

Human neutrophils made nets in dishes when they met the fungus, most strongly against the thread form and less against resting spores. Only some cells joined in, and filming showed the process unfold over hours. In infected mouse lungs the team also found nets forming in living tissue, and a waterproof coating protein on the fungus, called RodA, changed how well the nets worked.
europmc-pmc2909996:
Bellemain and colleagues stress-tested in 2010 the DNA barcode that mycologists use to identify fungi in soil, water, and other mixed samples. The barcode is the ITS region of fungal DNA, copied out by primers, short DNA hooks that start the copying. If a primer matches some fungal groups better than others, surveys silently over-count the favored groups, so the team simulated the copying on public sequence databases.

Several standard primers carried many mismatches against their targets. Some hooks skewed toward basidiomycetes, the group with mushrooms, while others skewed toward ascomycetes, the group with yeasts and molds. A primer sold as basidiomycete-specific caught only a minority of them. Length differences stack the deck further, so mixed-sample surveys need primer-aware interpretation.
europmc-pmc2913796:
Monteiro and Azevedo reviewed in 2010 why obesity and the metabolic syndrome keep the body's defense inflammation switched on at low level. No single trigger explains it, they argue, and several vicious cycles reinforce each other. Swollen fat cells can rupture from sheer physical stress, spilling contents that summon inflammation. Meanwhile, fat that cannot be stored in fat tissue lands in the liver. There it drives insulin resistance.

Every fatty meal also brings a wave of oxidative stress, worse when antioxidant-rich foods are missing. Gut microbes interacting with a rich diet add another proposed route, and disturbed sleep rhythms and psychological stress feed the same state. europmc-pmc3034196:
Linhartová and colleagues reviewed in 2010 a large and varied family of proteins that certain bacteria export in one step. Members share repeating building blocks that bind calcium, and all leave the cell through the same doorway system. Beyond that shared design, their jobs range widely across the bacterial world. Computer searches for this review found more than a thousand family members in sequenced genomes.

Known members include toxins that punch holes in host cells, large multi tool toxins, and proteins that kill rival bacteria. Others help bacteria form nodules on plant roots, coat the cell surface, or chop fats and proteins outside the cell. Some of those chopping enzymes interest industry. For most members, though, the actual job is still unknown. The review sorts what is known by function to guide future work.
europmc-pmc3098796:
Trounson, Thakar, Lomax, and Gibbons surveyed in 2011 the fast widening world of stem cell clinical trials. Bone marrow and cord blood cells remain the workhorses for blood and immune disorders, where some uses are now standard care. Beyond that, trials are pushing connective tissue stem cells into unrelated diseases, from limb ischemia to multiple sclerosis, and neural stem cells into brain and spinal conditions.

Early results outside the blood system have been mixed, often showing small or short lived gains that may come from factors the cells secrete rather than from new tissue. Meanwhile the first three trials using cells grown from pluripotent stem cells, the most versatile but riskiest source, had just begun. The review maps which cell types are being tried for which diseases. It frames a field moving from promise to proof, with safety still the gating question.
europmc-pmc3115896:
Eva Kassi and colleagues reviewed a contested diagnosis in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. The label groups together belly fat, raised blood sugar, blood pressure, and blood fat problems, and people meeting it face higher risk of heart disease and type two diabetes. Several rival definitions exist, each drawing the lines in different places.

The authors ask whether the rival definitions pick out the same people or merely bundle separate risks under one name. Newer factors linked to the pattern, such as inflammation and fat hormones, further blur the borders. They call for one shared set of criteria so studies can be compared. For children, they advise treating each proven risk on its own rather than leaning on the label.
europmc-pmc3125296:
Marieke Rohde and colleagues pulled apart a famous touch illusion in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. When a hidden real hand and a visible fake hand are stroked in sync, people feel the fake hand is theirs, and their sense of hand position drifts toward it. The team asked whether that drift and the ownership feeling are really the same thing.

Robot arms stroked the hands while the researchers paused often to test position sense. Drift appeared even when stroking was out of sync or absent, and never ran stronger with sync stroking than with vision alone. Yet questionnaires showed the ownership feeling needed sync stroking. The two effects thus rest on different brain processes, and drift alone cannot prove the ownership illusion occurred.
europmc-pmc3366996:
Liu and a large team sequenced the microbial community in dental plaque to find what distinguishes periodontal disease at the whole-community level. Periodontitis is driven by pathogenic bacteria and also raises cardiovascular risk, but the system-wide shift from a healthy mouth to a diseased one was poorly understood.

They analysed fifteen samples of plaque from below the gumline, taken from two patients and three healthy volunteers, using both marker-gene and whole-community DNA sequencing. Diseased communities were enriched for virulence factors and shared a common structure absent from healthy samples, as if the disease state occupies a narrow configuration. The team even partially reconstructed an unculturable TM7 organism's genome.
europmc-pmc3368796:
Lipson and co-authors reviewed CTGF in 2012, a protein that cells release and that steers scarring in damaged tissue. When CTGF stays active too long, organs stiffen as extra matrix builds up between cells. The review asks whether blocking the protein could undo that damage.

Animal studies cited here show that silencing CTGF prevented liver scarring and could reverse it after heavy collagen had formed. An antibody drug, FG-3019, eased stiff blood vessels and improved heart function in diabetic rats. In mice with radiation-scarred lungs, the antibody lowered lung density and the gain held after dosing stopped. Together the results make CTGF a serious drug target.
europmc-pmc3383996:
Cremades and co-workers watched single molecules in 2012 to catch the moment a brain protein turns toxic in Parkinson's disease. The protein, alpha-synuclein, clumps into deposits in patients' brains. Using single-molecule methods, the team followed the clumps from their first loose form onward.

The clumps slowly reshaped into a tighter, hardier form, and that reshaped kind is the one that later seeds fibers. In rat nerve cells the converted clumps stirred far more oxidative stress than fresh ones. The conversion is so slow that cells, or future drugs, get a long window to intervene. Left alone, finished fibers can even fall back into the toxic stable form.
europmc-pmc3403996:
Fransson and co-workers engineered immune peacekeeper cells in 2012 that home to the brain and calm the mouse version of multiple sclerosis. The disease, called EAE in mice, mirrors the human attack on the central nervous system. Regulatory T cell therapy helps, but the cells must be stable and reach the brain.

The team fitted ordinary T cells with a sensor for a myelin protein plus the gene FoxP3, which locks in the peacekeeper role. Delivered through the nose, the cells reached many brain regions. Treated mice with advanced disease recovered, with less inflammatory signaling and healthier myelin markers. Even after a second disease trigger, the treated mice stayed well.

freeman-madelon-1896:
Madelon came from Harper in 1896, when its author still signed as Mary Wilkins. A motto up front calls love the crown and the cross of life. Chapter one opens on fresh snow over a village at eight on a winter night.

Burr Gordon picks a short forest road toward the Hautville place through the drifts. Pines bend low with snow, and the whole scene holds a deep stillness. At the story's core stands Madelon herself, a woman of strong will and strong passion. She lives by her own code in a judging town, and love, pride, and scandal drive the tale to a forceful close.
frus-1861-d196:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 May 1861. The dispatch is document 196 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton wrote as Clay drew near to take over the Russian post. His late spring reports kept the file warm through the change of men. The letter shows a handover done with care, in a capital where good will was a real asset. Care in a handover is a small virtue that this file shows more than once. Care of that kind kept the Russian goodwill safe through the change of men.
frus-1861-d296:
24 August 1861 brought Mr. Harvey a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 296 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d96:
Lord Lyons wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 October 1861. The letter is document 96 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Lyons letters in three days point to business that would not wait. The autumn mails carried claims and protests in both directions. His second note shows the British envoy pressing his points while the ink on the first was barely dry. Claims by British merchants, whose goods the blockade had seized, drove much of this pace. Seized goods and halted ships filled the claim books of both governments that fall.
frus-1862-d196:
On 11 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, in a note printed as Document 196 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The two men were the working channel between their governments.

Mid-December 1861 found the Trent crisis at its peak, with Britain demanding the release of the seized Confederate envoys and an apology. Washington had not yet answered. A note exchanged in those days belonged to the most delicate fortnight in Anglo-American dealings during the whole war, when a second conflict seemed possible. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d296:
Filed as Document 296 but dated 11 July 1862, this report from William L. Dayton in Paris went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The printers placed it after a later Seward dispatch in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Dayton wrote while Europe absorbed the news of McClellan's retreat, which made the Union look weaker than it had in spring. His reading of the French response mattered greatly in Washington. The letter's date, not its number, fixes its place: the anxious second week of July 1862. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d396:
Bayard Taylor, at the American legation in St. Petersburg, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 November 1862. It is Document 396 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs. That series is the State Department record laid before Congress with the President's annual message.

Instructions like this one carried Washington's line to its men abroad and told them what to say at foreign courts. In late 1862 the Union still feared that Britain or France might back the Confederacy. A friendly Russia mattered more each month. The dispatch shows Seward working to hold that friendship fast while the war ground on at home.
frus-1862-d496:
The same day Pike's own report was dated at The Hague, 16 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to him. It is Document 496 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Crossed letters like these two show the machinery of the system: Washington sent orders based on month-old reports, while ministers acted on judgment between orders. Seward's April instruction to The Hague dealt with the standing Dutch subjects, from neutrality rules to the war's presentation in the Dutch press. Pike answered in his own blunt fashion in due course. The pair of letters, read together, gives a fair picture of how distant the two ends of the correspondence really were.
frus-1862-d596:
On 28 July 1862 Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 596 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Corwin's late-July report closed the summer's first run of Mexican papers in the volume. The French were in the country to stay, the republic was fighting on, and the United States was reduced to watching with sympathy. His letters from these months gave the State Department its fullest picture of the invasion as Mexicans experienced it. They also fixed the American record for the future. A victorious Union would one day return to the question of a French-backed empire. It would face that question on its border with very different strength.

frus-1862-d96:

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d196:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 9 May 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 196 of the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
