frus-1863p1-d496:
7 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d596:
Dated 25 July 1863, document 596 is a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d96:
On 27 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 96 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, closing the legation's February mail in the file.

A month-end letter often took stock. Adams's February had run from the Queen's speech to a flood of late-month sheets, and this one rounds the set off. His reports gave Washington a clear, cool read on the power it most feared and most needed. The dispatch is a fitting last page for the month in a file that rarely missed a week.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d196:
President Roosevelt sent a short operational-priority telegram to Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on 8 November 1943. It answers Harriman's report of 6 November about attaching the American agreement on Turkey to the protocol signed by Molotov and Eden at the Moscow conference.

Roosevelt grants the permission Harriman asked for, with one change of wording. Where the agreement spoke of the commanders responsible, it must now read the Combined Chiefs of Staff. That small edit, first suggested by Churchill, kept control over how forces were shared among theaters in the hands of the joint chiefs in Washington and London. Commanders in the field did not get it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d296:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a secret telegram from Washington on 23 November 1943 about the Azores. Lisbon reports that an interview with Portuguese leader Salazar about the island facilities has been fixed for five that afternoon.

The American chargé, George Kennan, plans to ask Salazar to confirm two things. Portugal must not object to American forces using the facilities at Horta and Terceira, granted earlier to Britain. Nor must it object to American engineering units improving them. At the same meeting he will sound Salazar out, informally, on the further facilities the American army and navy want. The British ambassador has orders to back the approach.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d396:
A draft declaration on Iran, dated at Tehran on 30 November 1943, is printed here in the shortened form shaped by General Hurley's suggestions. An editorial headnote explains that a longer rough draft by Jernegan, prepared on 29 November, was cut down and altered at Hurley's request, with a reference to the Atlantic Charter inserted.

The draft has the governments of Iran, the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain declare a common policy. Iran's best contribution to victory is speeding supplies across its soil to Russia, and Allied forces stationed there serve only the common war effort and will leave when that need permits. The three powers promise such financial and material help as world shortages allow. They promise joint planning of essential imports. After the war, they promise full consideration of Iran's economic problems, on an equal basis with other United Nations members.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d496:
Britain's chiefs of staff filed a memorandum on December 6, 1943, the last day of the Second Cairo Conference, answering the American paper of the same date. The State Department printed both in its Cairo-Tehran volume. The British chiefs had argued their case through Tehran and Cairo in tandem with Churchill.

Final-day papers reveal what each side still wanted on record when agreement was being sealed. The British memorandum closes London's side of a long strategic debate about the Mediterranean and the cross-Channel attack. Set beside the American text, it lets readers judge how far the two staffs had moved toward each other by the conference's end.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d96: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on November 5, 1943, and the letter is Document 96 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president would sail for the Mediterranean within the week, and the last letters from Washington carried a valedictory weight. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject line. The letter is preserved in the Foreign Relations series, in the volume's final pre-departure run.
frus-1944-quebec-d196: An editors' note records a brief private conversation on September 15, 1944. Morgenthau had a few minutes alone with Roosevelt immediately before the president's meeting with Churchill that day. The subject was the zones of occupation in Germany, then the most sensitive undecided question of the conference. The only trace of the talk is a brief reference in Morgenthau's diary, which the note cites.
frus-1944-quebec-d296: Prime Minister Winston Churchill drafted the text on 17 September 1944, just after the second Quebec Conference closed. Preserved as document 296 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the conference, it records wording from Churchill's own hand rather than a finished agreement. Drafts like this let readers watch Allied language being shaped before it hardened into settled policy.
frus-1944-quebec-d96:
Harry Hopkins prepared a memorandum dated August 18, 1944. Hopkins was President Roosevelt's special assistant and trusted adviser. The State Department printed his paper in the Quebec 1944 volume. It dates from nearly a month before the conference.

Hopkins rarely held formal office, yet he shaped summit work. His memoranda recorded talks, tested ideas, and prepared decisions. August 1944 found Allied armies advancing fast across France. Planning for Quebec had to keep pace with those gains. For readers, the memorandum shows the President's closest aide at work. He organized business that the leaders would settle in Canada.
frus-1945-50-intel-d196:
On 13 June 1946, the General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Group (Houston) sent a memorandum to the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). It is document 196 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d296:
Commander Robert Jay Williams addressed a memorandum to the Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Cassady) on 23 July 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 296 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d396:
J. Prichard Childs, chief of the CIA staff for intelligence planning, wrote to the members of the IAC Standing Committee on 25 August 1949. The memo is document 396 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Intelligence Advisory Committee, or IAC, joined the CIA with the intelligence chiefs of the State Department and the armed services. Its standing committee did the ground work between full meetings. A memo to that group shows how shared views were built, step by step, before they reached the top. The committee's work rarely made news, yet it shaped the joint reports the President saw.
frus-1945-50-intel-d96:
Magruder answered McCloy on 9 October 1945. The SSU chief reported to the assistant secretary who served as his unit's chief defender in the War Department. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Replies in this thread show Magruder accounting for his command: its people, its stations, and its shrinking funds. The SSU still ran secret work abroad that no other American body could yet do, and Magruder's letters pressed that fact politely and often. Readers can follow the exchange month by month as the unit's fate hung between abolition and absorption. Each letter bought time, and time, for the SSU, was the whole game.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d196:
No authority, no eight-division French army: Roosevelt's answer of 18 November 1944 is blunt. These excerpts from his telegram number 649 to Churchill are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The question was equipping France for her postwar part.

Whatever the shipping and the stocks in the United States, the President writes, he has no authority at present to equip an eight-division postwar French army. He sympathizes with the French point of view, all the same. He hopes the allies may together help France meet her postwar duties. But one fact governs his side of the account. Once Germany collapses, he must bring American troops home as fast as transport allows.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d296:
The American chiefs met again at Floriana on 31 January 1945, with Eisenhower's plan under review. These Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, record the second morning of the Malta staff conference. Much of the business waits on word from the front.

The minutes of the combined meeting of the day before are recommended for approval. Then General Marshall turns to strategy in northwest Europe. General Bull reports that General Smith has wired Eisenhower the changes the chiefs recommended in his plan. Eisenhower's reply is expected shortly, and nothing can be added until his views arrive. The third item takes up the planning date for the end of the war with Germany, on the British paper C. C. S. 772.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d396:
Matthews recorded a sharp exchange on Poland at the plenary of February 8, 1945. Eden first read the foreign ministers' report, and a long debate on the world body followed. Then Roosevelt asked whether Molotov had read his proposal on Poland. Stalin said he had received it. Roosevelt read the text aloud to make it clear.

Stalin asked the key question: would this mean withdrawing recognition from the London government? Roosevelt said yes. Churchill explained that recognition would pass to a new interim government. Stalin then asked about the London government's property. The minutes catch the moment one Poland was traded for another.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d496:
Votes in the Assembly worry Roosevelt in this letter to Stalin of February 10, 1945. He has been thinking, he writes, of political difficulties he might meet at home. The Ukrainian and White Russian republics would join the Assembly, and he would certainly carry out the agreement to support their admission.

But Americans might point out that the United States would have only one vote in the Assembly. To insure wholehearted acceptance by Congress and the people, he might need to ask for additional votes for the United States. The letter asks, in effect, for parity of prestige. Stalin's answer, preserved nearby in the volume, granted the request at once.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d96:
Invitations to the founding conference were still contested in January 1945. A briefing book paper titled “Nations To Be Invited to the United Nations Conference” lays out each ally's stand. It was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

At Dumbarton Oaks the question was left open. The United States and China wanted both the United Nations and the nations linked with them invited. The Soviets wanted the conference kept to the signatory nations, though latecomers might join once the Charter was signed. Britain raised no bar. The paper notes that six of the linked nations are American republics, and the other two are Egypt and Iceland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d196:
The British Embassy stated London's position on Turkey in a memorandum extract dated July 7, 1945. The extract is document 196 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears later in the volume.

The surviving passage says the British ambassador in Moscow, Sir Archibald Clark Kerr, has been instructed to set out London's views to the Soviet government. Turkey had consulted Britain about its recent talks with Moscow, in which the Soviets pressed demands touching the Straits and the eastern provinces. London wishes the Soviet government to know its views on these developments, since the whole question will have to be discussed at Terminal. The note marks Turkey as one of the summit's expected friction points.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d296:
Schoenfeld, the American representative in Hungary, questioned a British paper on June 25, 1945, about how peace with Hungary might be reached. Writing from Budapest to the Acting Secretary of State, he doubted the British claim that their listed options were the only choice. Washington, he said, had not yet tested Soviet consent.

Schoenfeld argued that talks with Moscow might still win equal American part in the Allied Control Commission. He also noted that any peace treaty would likely fold in the new Soviet-Hungarian reparations deal. His cable pushed back on British pessimism and kept an American claim to a real voice in Hungary alive.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d396:
American policy on choosing and treating war criminals is stated in an undated memorandum by the Joint Strategic Survey Committee. An International Military Tribunal, it says, should be established for the major war criminals. Their offenses, the committee notes, have no particular national or geographical character, so no single country can try them.

The United States should demand custody of every Axis person triable for a war crime committed mainly against American soldiers or nationals. Punishment should be severe, prompt, and public. On request, and on a reciprocal basis, America should hand over to its allies those charged with crimes against their people, each case judged on its merits.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d496:
The formalities of recognizing Poland's new government are laid before President Truman in a memorandum dated July 2, 1945. Enclosed for his approval are a suggested reply to the Polish Prime Minister, announcing the establishment of diplomatic relations, and a suggested public statement. The statement would be issued at 7:00 p.m., Eastern War Time, on the day chosen for recognition.

For technical and legal reasons, the memorandum explains, an exact hour for establishing relations is essential. The drafts would therefore go ahead to Ambassador Harriman, who would inform the Polish ambassador in Moscow confidentially, in advance, of the action and its exact hour. Truman approved the papers by hand, and the statement issued on July 5.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d596:
Green Hackworth, the State Department's legal adviser, set down a two-sentence memo on July 9, 1945. It is document 596 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The unsigned carbon copy is attached to the draft Allied proclamation on Japan.

Hackworth's lines are a redraft of two sentences in that draft. The first says the present system of military control in Japan must be uprooted. It must not be allowed to assert itself ever again. The second says Japan's people shall be given a chance to control their own destinies along peaceful lines. James Dunn then revised the second line by hand, adding a test. The chance would come once Japan's people had convinced the peace-loving nations that they would follow peaceful lives.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d696:
Under Secretary Grew sent a personal top secret wire to Ambassador Wilson in Ankara on July 3, 1945. It is document 696 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The wire was sent over Secretary Byrnes's signature to clear up a misunderstanding.

A Turkish minister had reported Grew as privately favoring a joint U.S.-British protest in Moscow. The report traced back to Grew's talk with the British minister on June 18. Grew now states exactly what he said on that occasion. He promised the British proposal his immediate attention, nothing more. He could make no commitment, he told London's man, until the whole subject had been carefully studied in Washington. The short wire pins down the record, lest Ankara or London build policy on a sympathy Grew never expressed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d96:
General Bradley demanded faster Soviet decisions in a telegram to General Deane on June 25, 1945. The message is document 96 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. General Parks, in Berlin, had been unable to win local permission to install the radio telephone and teleprinter links tying the conference to headquarters in the west.

Bradley calls it essential that Moscow order the Berlin commander to approve a high-frequency telephone terminal and a relay point near Luckenwalde. No wire circuits yet run west from Berlin into the American or British zones. Handling such small points through Moscow, he warns, is so slow that the target date cannot be met. Air staff and airfield control teams also wait on word about enlarging Parks's party.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1096:
Emilio Collado cabled two Washington officials on July 18, 1945, asking their views on Italian reparations. The Soviets had raised the subject at Potsdam. Collado's own tentative line is that Italy should pay no reparations, and no payments in current goods or productive capital equipment.

He would still require Italy to restore looted articles, such as works of art. Token deliveries to Greece and Ethiopia might also be allowed. Other nations could meet ship-sinking claims by holding Italian assets abroad. Collado asks for background at once: Italy's relief and rebuilding needs, her overseas assets and shipping, and Allied practice on reparations from Finland, Hungary, Bulgaria, and Rumania.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1196:
A third memorandum from the United States Chiefs of Staff is dated 23 July 1945. By the end of the first week, the American military staff had built a running paper record for the team. Each note caught the chiefs' view as the bargaining shifted.

Staff papers of this kind did not decide anything by themselves. They armed the men who did decide, with facts, options, and warnings. This one belongs to the middle of the series. Set among its companions, it shows a staff machine keeping pace with a summit that moved daily, and sometimes hourly.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1296:
On 16 July 1945, the day before Potsdam opened, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The chiefs' eve-of-summit notes formed the base of the brief the team carried to Germany.

Writing before the talks let the staff state its view cleanly, untouched by the day's trades. Later papers would bend with events. This one holds the starting line. It is part of the groundwork stack of 16 July, the day the American machine finished its Potsdam preparations on paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1396:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 31 July 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. It is the second of two Caffery letters to Bidault dated that day.

Two letters in one day suggest either two subjects or one subject that would not wait. Bidault had taken France's foreign policy in hand after liberation. He dealt with Caffery as the voice of the power whose aid France most needed. Readers should read this letter with its twin. Together they show the range of Franco-American business, from the grand settlement in Germany down to the daily needs of a freed but battered country.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-96: This editorial note stands unnumbered after document 710 in the second volume of the Potsdam papers. The historians who edited Foreign Relations of the United States placed such notes where a paper trail runs cold. A note might name the file a text came from or point to a fuller copy elsewhere. Here it keeps a reader oriented inside a long run of conference-week documents.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d796:
The Soviet delegation's proposal kept as document 796 bears the date July 12, 1945. It was written days before the Potsdam Conference opened. Soviet staff prepared their texts in advance, like their rivals. The proposal entered the numbered record of the second Potsdam volume.

A pre-conference text shows a side's aims in their purest form. Nothing has yet been trimmed by contact. Readers can compare this early draft with the final protocol of August 1. The distance between them is the measure of the talks. The document also shows the paper war starting before the leaders even reached Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d896:
Robert Murphy, political adviser in Germany, sent this secret report to the Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. He encloses a memorandum from a German lawyer his staff trusted. The memorandum describes Soviet removal of science and military research institutes from Berlin to Russia.

It tells how V-1 and V-2 research teams were shipped east with their labs, drawings, and patents. It then details the clearing of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society institutes in Dahlem. Professors were told they could have their institutes back in Russia. Some staff went along. Others slipped away to avoid being taken.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d996:
Covey Oliver sent Collado and Rubin a short data telegram from Washington on July 27, 1945. It passes on Fletcher's revised estimates of total German assets in neutral countries. All figures are in millions of dollars. Each new figure is set against the older April 30 estimate in parentheses.

Switzerland leads at 600, doubled from the April figure of 300. That sum counts direct investments only. Portugal stands at 35, up from 27. Sweden stands at 51, down from 57.7. Turkey stands at 51.2, up from 33. Spanish estimates, Oliver notes, are not yet reconciled. The cable is a working paper from the Potsdam weeks.
frus-1961-63v11-d96: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Missile Crisis volume. The aftermath, documented. This entry preserves that memo. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
gao-gaoreports-b-298196: Capps Shoe Company doubled its July 2006 protest — two case numbers, one footwear fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299496: Raymond Associates doubled its May 2007 protest — two case numbers, one contract fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims at once. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim carefully. Paired protests get a single, thorough answer from the referee.
gao-gaoreports-b-309996: A 2007 GAO ruling on two linked contract fights from Earl Industries, LLC, a ship repair firm. The company said the Navy's award missed the mark; the ruling weighs each protest point in turn. For yards bidding on Navy fix-up work, the call shows how GAO judges a tight race — and how repeat filings from one firm get handled.
gao-gaoreports-b-311196: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Marshall Company, Ltd. Decided April 23, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-296: China cloth import rules needed fixing in 2005, and GAO's report says the shield steps should be better. The review writes the fix list. The American mills deserved the fair rules. The rules had to be fair. The fix was written.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-696: Troops' life insurance solicitation needed better controls in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon needed policies on the sales pitches. The findings demand the rules. The report warns that the servicemembers deserved honest pitches. The controls had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-196: Social Security's improper payments needed preventing in 2006, and GAO's report says more actions were required to stop bad benefit payments. The findings demand the safeguards. The report warns that the retirees' money should not leak. The payments had to be proper.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-296: Border security program management needed implementing in 2006, and GAO's report says recommendations to improve management had to be carried out. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the border's shield needed mending. The recommendations had to be implemented.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-396: Tax compliance decisions needed better data in 2006, and GAO's report says opportunities existed to improve decisions and taxpayer service. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the tax machine should serve and collect fairly. The compliance had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-496: Trade adjustment aid data needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says Labor should ensure the performance data were complete and accessible. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the displaced workers' program needed honest metrics. The data had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-596: The Hong Kong trade talks stalled in 2006, and GAO's report says limited progress clouded the Doha agreement's prospects. The findings take the sober measure. The report warns that the world trade round needed momentum. The prospects had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-96: The Chesapeake Bay cleanup needed better strategies in 2005, and GAO's report says improved approaches were required to assess and manage restoration. The findings demand the upgrade. The report warns that the dying bay deserved honest progress. The strategies had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-996: Homeland Security's interagency buying needed discipline in 2006, and GAO's report says better guidance, planning, and oversight were required. The findings demand the controls. The report warns that the young department should not shop like a startup. The buying had to be businesslike.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1096: The one-stop job shops were still finding their feet in 2007 — GAO's report says the workforce system's storefronts kept evolving, but Labor needed to step up. The findings track a well-meant idea — one door for every job hunter — bumping against the realities of funding and follow-through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1196: How many troops sought out as conscientious objectors during an unpopular war? GAO counted in 2007 — and the number was tiny next to the size of the armed forces. The report swaps heat for math on a charged question, tallying formal objector bids to show what the moral-exit lane really looked like.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-296: The New Markets tax credit was drawing investors in 2007, and GAO's report says it appeared to boost investment in poor communities, with caveats. The findings balance hope and doubt. The report asks whether the tax break bought real renewal. The jury was still out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-696: The war commands were fuzzy on flu duty in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon's regional commands needed sharper outbreak roles. The findings map the preparedness gaps. The report's warning: a pandemic would not wait for the chain of command to sort itself out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-96: Space buying needed honest price tags in 2007, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to confront unrealistic cost estimates. The findings target the fantasy numbers. The report warns that the rockets' budgets should not be science fiction. The estimates had to come down to Earth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-996: Four artificial jaw joints won FDA approval — but did the science hold up? GAO's 2007 report puts the agency's green light for TMJ implants under the microscope. The findings probe whether the proof of safety matched the promise, for patients whose jaw pain left them few other options.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-196: GAO published its findings on federal Land Management: Federal Land Transaction Facilitation Act Restrictions and Management Weaknesses Limit Future Sales and Acquisitions in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-296: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at military Personnel: The DOD and Coast Guard Academies Have Taken Steps to Address Incidents of Sexual Harassment and Assault, but Greater Federal Oversight Is N. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-596: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on human Capital: Corps of Engineers Needs to Update Its Workforce Planning Process to More Effectively Address Its Current and Future Workforce Needs. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-896: GAO published its findings on DOD Business Systems Modernization: Important Management Controls Being Implemented on Major Navy Program, but Improvements Needed in Key Areas in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-996: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at US Postal Service: New Delivery Performance Measures Could Enhance Managers' Pay for Performance Program. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gaster-sword-of-moses-1896:
The Sword of Moses is an old Jewish book of magic, printed in London in 1896 by scholar Moses Gaster. Gaster edited and translated it from a manuscript of the 13th or 14th century. His edition gives his intro, the full English text, the Hebrew text, and an index.

The spell book runs through 136 sections of holy and angel names, each tied to a set task. The rites claim power to heal, harm, bind spirits, and win favor. Gaster's edition stayed the main door into this text, a key source for the study of Jewish magic.
gibbon-memoirs-1796:
Edward Gibbon, the historian of Rome's decline, left an account of his own life in Memoirs of My Life and Writings, published in 1796. He died before finishing it, and the memoir appeared two years after his death. It tells how a sickly, bookish boy became the author of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.

Gibbon describes his schooling, his years at Oxford and Lausanne, and the slow birth of his great work. One famous passage recalls the day in Rome when the idea of the book first seized him. The voice is calm, dry, and quietly proud. No better door into a historian's workshop exists from that century.
heads-and-faces-and-how-to-study-them-a-: Heads and Faces, and How to Study Them, 1896. The phrenology manual. This book preserves that book. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
hegel-philosophy-right-dyde-1896:
G. W. F. Hegel published the Philosophy of Right in 1821, his mature work on politics and society. The English text here is S. W. Dyde's translation of 1896. Hegel moves from abstract right to morality and then to ethical life. Family, civil society, and the state form the stages of ethical life.

He treats property, contract, law, work, and corporations in detail. The state, for Hegel, completes freedom rather than crushing it. His views pleased neither radicals nor pure royalists of his day. The book became a root of modern political theory, liberal and Marxist alike. It remains essential for students of the state.
hilton-scale-perfection-1396:
Walter Hilton wrote The Scale of Perfection in the late 1300s. Hilton was an Augustinian canon in the north of England. The book is a full guide to the life of deep prayer. It stands with The Cloud of Unknowing as a peak of English soul lore.

Hilton writes for a woman who has shut her life to God as an anchoress. He maps the steps of reform of the soul, from first stir to full light. Dark and light mark the stages of the soul's slow mend. The book's calm sense has kept it in use for six hundred years.
hobson-problem-of-unemployed-1896:
Hobson published The Problem of the Unemployed in 1896, facing the shame of Victorian joblessness head-on. Mass unemployment was widely blamed on the character of the jobless man himself. Hobson, writing as both economist and reformer, set out to move the blame to the system.

He argues that unemployment arises when saving and spending fall out of balance, so that industry makes more than buyers can take. Remedies follow from the diagnosis: public works, shorter hours, and a fairer spread of income to lift demand. The book is often called the first modern study of unemployment as an economic problem rather than a moral failing. It helped shift British debate toward the policies that later built the welfare state.
housman-shropshire-lad-1896:
A. E. Housman published A Shropshire Lad in 1896 at his own expense, after publishers turned it down. Housman was a London clerk and classical scholar who had barely visited Shropshire. The book holds sixty-three short lyrics, and it slowly became a classic.

The poems speak in the voice of a country lad facing love, parting, soldiering, and early death. Cherry trees, church bells, and gallows recur in spare, singable stanzas. Housman's tone is bleak but never sloppy: every line is cut clean. Young soldiers carried the book through the Boer War and the First World War, and its best poems are still memorized today.
housman-the-were-wolf-1896:
Clemence Housman tells a stark tale of a white wolf in The Were-Wolf, her short novel of 1896. In a far north farm, a fair guest comes out of the snow. One brother greets her with warmth. One holds a dread he can't name. Deaths dog the farm's kin, and a white wolf is seen at dusk on the waste past the fields.

The tale is told in rich, grave prose, with draws by her kin. Faith, love, and the price of a soul turn its end. It is the most fine tale of its kind from its age.
jewett-pointed-firs-1896:
Sarah Orne Jewett, born in South Berwick, Maine, in 1849, wrote The Country of the Pointed Firs in 1896. An opening note says she rode with her doctor father on his rounds as a girl. At nineteen the Atlantic Monthly took her first story, and editor William Dean Howells urged her on.

A summer visitor lodges in Dunnet Landing, a fading Maine fishing village. Her landlady, Mrs. Almira Todd, a tall herbalist who knows every soul on the coast, guides her into village life. Linked sketches honor sea captains' widows, sailors, and country doctors. Henry James praised the book warmly, and it now crowns American local-color writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luther-martinth:
Martin Luther, the German church reformer, is examined in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia only for his ties to Jews and Judaism. Luther was born at Eisleben on November 10, 1483, and died there in 1546. The article, by Gotthard Deutsch, sets his stance inside the Reformation's return to Scripture. That return made Hebrew study central to his movement.

The entry is frank about Luther's limits as a Hebraist. He praised Hebrew as the best and richest language, yet admitted he knew little of its grammar. He read the rabbis mostly through Christian writers like Nicholas de Lyra. Still, he spoke of Jews as God's chosen carriers of Scripture to the world. He called them the children, and Christians the guests and strangers. The article gives readers a documented, Jewish view of a figure whose words about Jews still draw debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mai-joseph-ben-:
Joseph ben Michael Mai, a German printer, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Dyhernfurth on December 29, 1764, he inherited his father's printing house there. He ran it together with his brother. He died at Breslau on December 1, 1810.

The article presents him as more than a tradesman. Mai was a Talmudic scholar in his own right. He wrote prefaces to the works of his father-in-law, Isaiah Berlin, rabbi of Breslau. With his brother he also wrote notes to the four Turim, the great code of Jewish law. Those notes were printed at Dyhernfurth in 1790. The brief entry preserves a printer whose press and pen served the same scholarly world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marcus-brentgen:
Brentgen Marcus, the first Jewish court singer in Germany, is profiled in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. She flourished near the end of the seventeenth century. She lived with her father, Isaac Marcus, at Wesel in Brandenburg. In 1690 Frederick of Brandenburg heard her sing there.

The article follows the prince's response in dated letters. Struck by her voice, Frederick sent father and daughter to Berlin for her musical education. On July 16 he wrote to the Prince of Anhalt about his discovery. He also commended Brentgen to his wife, Princess Sophie Charlotte. Nine days later the Prince of Anhalt replied that he had heard and admired her unusually fine voice. Provision would be made for her as the prince wished. The brief entry preserves a singer known only through a court's correspondence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matzel-ascher-1:
Isidore Singer profiles Ascher Matzel, a Hungarian hospital administrator decorated by two emperors, in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Stampfen in 1763 and died on November 22, 1842. At seventeen he entered the service of the Jewish hospital in Vienna, and he rose to superintendent in 1799. During the war with the Turks, Emperor Joseph II put him in charge of the hospital in the fortress of Leopoldstadt. He then took charge of the hospital at Semlin.

The emperor rewarded him with gifts for that service, including a diamond ring bearing the imperial initials. Back in Vienna after the war, Matzel again ran the Jewish hospital. In 1813 Emperor Francis gave him the gold medal of honor, and the Emperor of Russia gave him an order of merit. He managed the munitions stores of the army from 1814. During the cholera epidemic of 1830 he headed the health board of Rossau, a Vienna suburb.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mekilta-le-sefe:
Mekilta le-Sefer Debarim is a halakic midrash on Deuteronomy from the school of Rabbi Ishmael. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give it a Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. It is a ghost of a book. No Talmud names it, and no medieval author cites it. Even Maimonides, who reports that Ishmael expounded the whole Torah, never quotes it on Deuteronomy, suggesting he knew it only by tradition.

Talmudic passages on Deuteronomy open with “It was taught in the school of R. Ishmael.” One is credited to the same collection that holds the Exodus midrash of Ishmael. The Deuteronomy commentary vanished early, but the compiler of the Midrash ha-Gadol had it and folded passages into his collection. From that collection D. Hoffmann gathered and printed them in 1897. The entry preserves the evidence for a lost classic and the trail by which scholars recovered its fragments.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meribah-strife-:
Meribah, meaning "strife," names two wilderness places. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn treat them in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first is at Rephidim. It is called Massah and Meribah "because of the chiding of the children of Israel." The text adds, "and because they tempted the Lord." It is the Meribah of the Ninety-fifth Psalm. The second is at Kadesh, the "waters of Meribah." Ezekiel makes it the southern border of the land of Canaan. The Septuagint renders the word throughout as "reviling." The Targums treat it as a common noun, not a name.

The critical point closes the entry. In Exodus Moses is ordered to strike the rock. In Numbers he is ordered to speak to it. He is barred from the promised land for disobedience. Otherwise the stories match so closely, the writers note, that some critics take one narrative for a duplicate of the other.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michmash-10796:
Michmash, a town of Benjamin east of Beth-aven, gets a four-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 from Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn. The name also appears as Michmas in Ezra and Nehemiah, and the article says it may mean hidden. Short as it is, the entry ties the place to both war and wheat.

Michmash is best known, the entry notes, as the scene of the war between the Philistines and Saul and Jonathan, told in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters of First Samuel. It also points readers to the fuller article on Jonathan for that story. Against the battles stands a quieter fame: the Mishnah praised Michmash for its excellent wheat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-je:
Mordecai ben Jehiel Michael ha-Levi was a Russian grammarian. He headed the rabbinical court at Slawatyetz on the Bug in the early eighteenth century. Herman Rosenthal and Max Schloessinger entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His one book took on the most-read commentary in Judaism, Rashi's. It used grammar as its weapon.

Mera Dakya was printed at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder in 1734 and often reprinted. It comments on Rashi's notes to the Pentateuch, the Five Rolls, and many Talmudic passages. It corrects the explanations it finds improbable, on grammatical grounds. Its introduction packs in a short Hebrew grammar of its own. It is a specialist's book, kept alive by frequent reprinting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-israel-11:
Moses Israel was an Oriental rabbi born at Jerusalem in the later seventeenth century. Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Sent out about 1710 to collect alms for the poor of Safed, he stopped at Rhodes. The congregation there elected him rabbi in 1715 and made him vow never to leave.

After twelve years, troubles grew so serious that the rabbinate of Constantinople released him from his vow. He traveled through Italy and Holland raising funds for Palestine, and at Alexandria he was elected rabbi again. There he stayed for the rest of his life. His responsa, the Mas'at Mosheh, were printed at Constantinople in his lifetime and after it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mudawwar-abu-al:
Abu al-Bayan ibn al-Mudawwar, surnamed al-Sadid, was a Karaite court physician in Egypt, born in 1101. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He served the last Fatimid caliphs and then Saladin. At sixty-three Saladin pensioned him, and he retired to Cairo.

In twenty years of retirement his house stayed crowded with pupils. He refused to visit patients at home unless they were his friends, and once declined an emir's summons until Saladin's secretary asked him. He died at Cairo in 1184. Works on medicine are ascribed to him, but none of them survive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-menahem-o:
Menahem Nahum of Chernobyl was a Hasidic leader of the later eighteenth century, treated in the Jewish Encyclopedia by Gotthard Deutsch and S. J. Levinson. A pupil of Baer of Meseritz, he was sent to Galicia to spread Hasidism. When Baer died in 1772 and Elijah of Wilna attacked the movement, Nahum helped steady it.

With other leaders he set up the dynasties of the zaddikim, founding one in Little Russia himself. His son Mordecai succeeded him there. His book Me'or Enayim, cabalistic homilies on the Pentateuch, was printed in 1798 and often reprinted. A second work expounds the Talmud's legends in the same cabalistic vein.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nazir-nazarite-:
Nazir is the Mishnah treatise on the Nazarite vow. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The treatise appears in the Tosefta and both Talmuds. It chiefly works through Numbers chapter six, verses one to twenty-one. In the Mishnah it stands fourth in the order Nashim. It has nine chapters and fifty-eight paragraphs.

Chapter one sorts vows, from short terms to life terms. Later chapters treat mistaken vows and wives' vows. One chapter lists all things drawn from the vine. Others cover sacrifices, hair cutting, and corpse uncleanness. Queen Helena's seven-year vow gets its own hard case. The Tosefta adds Simon the Just and a handsome youth. He vowed to escape the pull of his own beauty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-orleans-114:
New Orleans was Louisiana's largest city and an early Jewish home. Cyrus Adler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The city passed to the United States in 1803. Jacob and Judah Touro were among its first Jews. Judah fought under Jackson in the city's defense in 1815.

Touro's gifts built institutions across the United States. A burying ground was the community's first institution there. Its first burial took place on June 28, 1828. From that society sprang the first congregation. Settlers came from Germany, Holland, England, and Jamaica. Gates of Prayer began in 1849, Temple Sinai in 1870. Rabbi Gutheim won a national name in its pulpits. The Touro Infirmary opened its doors in 1854.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-norwich-11596:
Norwich is the capital town of Norfolk, England. Joseph Jacobs wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Only London, Oxford, and Cambridge name Jews earlier. The death of William of Norwich darkened it in 1144. That was Europe's first blood accusation case.

Jurnet was the town's great Jew of that age. A fine of 6,000 marks fell on him in 1186. The riots of 1190 slew those found at home. Others of the community survived in the castle. Isaac of Norwich financed on a national scale. A king's fine of 10,000 marks struck him in 1218. His account book for three years still survives. Four Jews were hanged in 1238 after a charge. Arson twice hit Jewish houses the year before. Records fix the Jewry's streets with rare precision.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ostrog-11796:
Ostrog is a Russian city in the province of Volhynia. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group most likely rose there in the late thirteen hundreds. Lutsk, a near town, had a strong Jewish group by then. The first print word of Ostrog Jews dates to 1532.

That word deals with a tax on horned beasts from Wallachia. One Ostrog Jew bought 1,500 oxen in that trade. In 1536 Ostrog Jews stood charged before the king. They were said to have dodged the due tax on herds. They said they paid the due tax in Poland in full. In 1550 Solomon Luria became rabbi of Ostrog. His fame drew pupils from far and wide to the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappos-b-judah-:
Pappos ben Judah was a sage of tales in old Israel. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first half of the second century. He was a fellow captive of Akiba, the great sage. That was in the hard days under Emperor Hadrian.

In those days it was barred to study the Torah in public. Akiba put his life at risk to teach his pupils still. The mild Pappos warned him to stop that brave work. Spies were all round them, Pappos told him in fear. Akiba told him the tale of the fox and the fish. The Torah was life itself to the Jewish folk, he said. The two men met once more by chance in a jail. Pappos praised Akiba, who was jailed for the Torah's sake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philip-iv-12096:
Philip the Fourth was king of Spain in the 1600s. He was born at Valladolid in 1605 and died in 1665. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Men called him the poet king for his love of art.

Philip left state affairs to his favorite, Olivares. Spain lacked men and money after the expulsions. Olivares invited Spanish-speaking Jews back to Madrid. He promised them a synagogue and free worship. The grand inquisitor fought the plan as a danger. Intolerance won, and Philip pledged expulsion instead. Olivares fell from power in 1643.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pizmon-12196:
A pizmon is a hymn built around a refrain. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It usually crowns the selihot, the penitential prayers. Cantor and congregation sing it in turns. Its stanzas are measured and set in meter.

The word most likely comes from Greek psalmos. Sephardim use the term more widely, though. Any major hymn in stanzas can bear it. Such hymns carry their own old melodies. Ashkenazim keep famous pizmonim for the Days of Awe. Their refrains let the whole room answer together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porto-riche-geo:
George de Porto-Riche was a French poet and playwright born at Bordeaux in 1849. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His parents were Italian. He first worked in a bank as a young man. The bank let him go for his love of verse.

Porto-Riche then read law, but soon gave it up. Verse was his true work, he found. His first book of poems came out in 1872. More books of verse followed across the years. One sad little book tells of his lone childhood. His first play was staged at the Odéon in 1873. Plays then joined poems in his life's work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raunheim-saly-s:
Saly Raunheim was an American mining engineer born on June 7, 1838. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Frankfort on the Main. He died in New York City on September 9, 1904.

The article traces his study at Heidelberg and Freiburg. In 1863 he bought a zinc mine for a French banker. It sold two years later for two million francs. It had cost only thirty thousand francs. In 1879 he moved to the United States. With the Lewisohn brothers he formed a Montana mining company. He later developed copper mines in New Mexico. The entry joins mining skill with a sharp eye for value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-restraints-on-a:
Restraints on alienation limit a person's power to sell land. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Many legal systems know such limits. Jewish law's strongest form was the year of jubilee.

The article draws its rules from Leviticus chapter 25. Sold farmland returned to its owner at jubilee. The key line says the land is God's, not man's. Walled city houses could be redeemed for one year only. After that year the sale became final. Village houses stayed redeemable forever under the law. Levite city houses could never be sold away. The entry shows land held as a trust, not a possession.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodosto-turkish:
Rodosto is a Turkish port on the Sea of Marmora. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lies seventy eight miles west of Constantinople. Turks call it Tekfur-Dag.

The article says a Jewish community existed there by the twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela found four hundred Jews in 1173. Noted rabbis Moses, Abijah, and Jacob lived among them. The community stayed undisturbed for centuries, they say. It never gained great importance, though. A seventeenth century wonder worker wrote on divination there. Cemetery stones mark its chief rabbis across centuries. In 1905 about twenty eight hundred Jews lived in Rodosto. They had a synagogue, a school, and heavy communal debt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rossi-giovanni-:
Giovanni Bernardo de Rossi was an Italian Christian Hebraist born in Castelnuovo on October 25, 1742. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. In 1769 he became professor of Oriental languages at Parma for life.

De Rossi gathered manuscripts and old prints to collect variant Bible readings. Like Kennicott before him, he wanted the Old Testament text compared copy by copy. That work forced him to map the early history of Hebrew printing. His Annales of Hebrew typography, from 1795 and 1799, founded that field. He also compiled a dictionary of Hebrew authors and their works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sa-id-ben-hasan:
Sa'id ben Hasan of Alexandria was a Jewish convert to Islam of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His book argues from Scripture for the mission of Mohammed.

The work, Masalik al-Nazar, tries to prove that mission genuine from the Bible. Like other controversialists, Sa'id accuses the Jews of corrupting the text. He charges that they swapped other names for Mohammed's and Ishmael's there. His preface tells how he converted in May 1298, after a dream. A voice bade him recite the opening sura, and he recovered from illness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-sanwel-b:
Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel, called Sanwel, ben Enoch. He was a Polish rabbi who flourished in the seventeenth century. Samuel was born at Lublin. He served as a dayyan, a judge on a rabbinical court. He held that post first at Jassy and later at Mayence.

Samuel wrote Dibre Shemu'el, a book of sermons on the Pentateuch. Only part of it survives today. The surviving part covers Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus. It was printed at Amsterdam in 1678. A second edition appeared at Venice in 1702. The entry rests on the old Hebrew bibliographies of Benjacob, Fürst, and Steinschneider.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarajevo-turkis:
Isidore Singer and Samuel Wessel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sarajevo. The city is the capital of Bosnia. About 1850 Omar Pasha let its Jews settle anywhere in the city. Until 1878, when Austria-Hungary took Bosnia, all local Jews were Sephardim. They were called Spanioles. After 1878 an Ashkenazic congregation formed from newcomers.

The Ashkenazim built a handsome synagogue in the Moorish style. It was dedicated on September 30, 1902. Many of them worked as lawyers and physicians. The Sephardim were somewhat more numerous and generally Orthodox. In 1895 Sarajevo held 4,060 Jews in a population of 41,543. The two congregations now dealt warmly with each other. Their members even intermarried. Ties between Jews and non-Jews were also unusually cordial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schomberg-isaac:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Isaac Schomberg. He was an English physician. Schomberg was born at Cologne on August 14, 1714. He died in London on May 4, 1780. He was a son of Meyer Löw Schomberg. He studied medicine at Leyden and took his degree there. He then practiced in London.

Schomberg's career turned on a feud with the Royal College of Physicians. In 1746 the censors summoned him to be examined. He sent an excuse they called indecent. The college barred him from practice. After baptism, Cambridge gave him a doctorate by royal mandate in 1749. He passed the college's tests, yet admission was still refused. With Moses Mendez he mocked the fight in a satire, The Battiad. The college relented in 1765, admitting him as a licentiate. He won a fellowship in 1771.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seixas-13396:
Cyrus Adler, L. Hühner, and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Seixas family. The family founder came from Portugal to the United States in 1730. Abraham Seixas, born in New York in 1750, served in the American army. He carried dispatches for General Harry Lee. Benjamin Mendez Seixas helped found the New York Stock Exchange.

The family's star is Gershom Mendez Seixas. Born in New York in 1745, he led Shearith Israel congregation for about fifty years. At the Revolution he backed the Patriot cause at once. When the British fleet appeared in 1776, his flock shut the synagogue and left town. Seixas carried the Torah scrolls to Stratford, Connecticut. In 1780 he helped found Mickvé Israel in Philadelphia. He died in New York in 1816.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shamhazai-or-sh:
Shamhazai, whose name means seizer of the heaven, is a fallen angel in Jewish legend. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. An old Aramaic version links him to the giants of Genesis. He and his fellow angel Azael fell from heaven before the Flood.

A midrash tells how the pair challenged God over mankind. God warned that earthly passion would master them too. They begged leave to live among men and honor His name. Once on earth, desire for human women overcame them at once. The entry retells a tale used to explain evil, angels, and the Flood generation in one sweep.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shklov-13596:
Shklov is a Russian town on the Dnieper, in the government of Moghilef. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Jews settled there early, likely in the sixteenth century. Its spot on the Russia-Poland border brought repeated war.

Cossacks destroyed Shklov in 1655, the entry records. Swedes sacked it in 1708 under General Löwenhaupt. Napoleon's army invaded and pillaged it in 1812. Jews formed most of the town and suffered most each time. By 1905 about 12,000 Jews lived there, near eighty-eight percent. They ran two synagogues, many prayer houses, a hospital, and schools. Their trade in wheat and goods ran wide across the region.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-jose-b:
Simeon ben Jose ben Lekonya was a tanna of the fourth generation of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was a contemporary of Judah ha-Nasi, the Mishnah's editor. He educated the son of his brother-in-law Eleazar.

Only a few legal sentences by Simeon have survived. He explained the thirty-nine kinds of Sabbath work cleverly. The word melakah, work, occurs thirty-nine times in Torah, he said. That count is inexact, the entry admits frankly. Simeon seems to have skipped some passages on purpose. His homilies compare Israel to rock and stones enduring. Nations are potsherds that break either way they fall. If the pot falls on the stone, woe to the pot. The entry keeps a neat parable of survival.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-skuteczky-damia:
Damianus Skuteczky was a Hungarian painter of genre and portrait works. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Kis-Györ on February 9, 1850. He studied at the Kunstakademie under Geiger. A state scholarship then let him travel to Italy, where he settled at Venice.

His scenes of Venetian life first made his name. His Evil Tongues, shown at the Vienna Exposition, drew wide notice. In 1885 he returned to Hungary for good. He lived by turns at Budapest and at Neusohl. His best-known works include Daily Bread and Schadenfreude. He also studied the history and technique of Renaissance art.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tell-el-amarna-:
Tell el-Amarna is the ruin of an Egyptian royal city. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and George A. Barton wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its name comes from local Bedouin tribes. The ruins sit on the Nile's east bank in middle Egypt. Rock-cut tombs ring the dead city's site.

Amenophis the Fourth built the city early in his reign. He broke with all gods except Aten, the sun disk. Thebes resisted his reform with old religious interests. So he founded a fresh capital free of them. A palace and Aten temple rose at the site. Nobles' houses gathered around the new court. After his death the old religion reasserted itself. The court moved back to Thebes soon after. The entry tells of a capital built for one god.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiktiner-judah-:
Judah Löb ben Simhah Tiktiner was a Russian rabbi of the eighteenth century. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as head of the rabbinical court at Zagora. Later he lived at Wilna.

His book Shalme Simhah appeared at Wilna in 1806. It ran to two volumes of legal novellae. The notes treat the halakot of Asher ben Jehiel. An opening section lays out basic principles of the Talmud. Casuistic writings by Tiktiner follow those principles. The work stops short of completion, though. It reaches only as far as the treatise Ta'anit. Steinschneider and Benjacob cataloged the book for later scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trenel-isaac-14:
Isaac Trenel was a French rabbi who directed Paris's central rabbinical school. Isidore Singer and Israel Lévi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Metz in 1822, he died at Paris in 1890. He studied Talmud under his uncle at Marmoutier. Further study followed at Merzig in Prussia.

After Metz's rabbinical school, he served briefly at Besançon. He resigned and moved to Paris as a charity secretary. He then assisted the chief rabbi of Paris. In 1856 he became director of the Ecole Centrale Rabbinique. The school moved to Paris in 1859. He kept the directorship until his death. With N. Sander he compiled a Hebrew-French dictionary. He also wrote a study of Hillel the Elder.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vidal-naquet-sa:
Samuel Emanuel Vidal Naquet was a French financier. He was born at Paris on August 22, 1859. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied law in Paris and joined the bar in 1882. In 1885 he entered his father's bank.

On his father's death, Vidal Naquet became the bank's chief. Since 1888 he and his brother Charles have edited a market paper. The paper is called Cote de la Bourse et de la Banque. He wrote many of its lead articles himself. Readers knew him as a top French expert on financial law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiener-jacques-:
Jacques Wiener was a Belgian engraver of medals. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hoorstgen, in the Rhine Province, in 1815. He died at Brussels on November 3, 1899. At thirteen he went to Aix la Chapelle for training. His uncle Baruch, an artist, taught him there.

Wiener studied further in Paris from 1835. In 1839 he settled in Brussels as a medal engraver. His fame rested on fidelity to minute detail. He designed the first Belgian postage stamps. In 1849 he arranged their making in England. Overwork cost him his eyesight in 1872. Belgium's king sent condolences at his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolflein-of-loc:
Wolflein of Lochamen was a medieval song maker in Bavaria. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is known for one book of songs from about 1450. That book is called the Lochheimer Liederbuch. It holds folk songs of Germany in set order.

One song in the book bears lines in Hebrew letters. The lines speak of love to a woman named Barbara. A phrase in a second song was used by Jews alone. Those clues point to a Jewish hand in the book. Yet one song holds a Christian grace at meals. A female name like Barbara was rare among Jews then. So the entry leaves his faith an open case. It rests on small clues in the songs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-b-eleaza:
Yizhak ben Eleazar of Caesarea was a teacher of law in the 300s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He taught in the old synagogue of that port town. His pupils and friends loved him with rare warmth. One man set him as high there as God in Zion.

His rulings treat a wide range of daily law. One treats trade deals told to a pupil of his. One treats fraud in the sale of goods to men. One treats the writ that frees a wife from her man. One treats the tithe on dates and on date honey. One treats signs found on a corpse in the field. He passed on the words of two older sages as well. He was famed for his skill at the cook's art too.
kadambari-ridding-1896:
C. M. Ridding Englished Banabhatta's Kadambari in 1896, the first complete English rendering of the great Sanskrit prose romance. Bana began the tale in the seventh century and his son finished it after his death. Lovers are born, die, and are reborn across lives, with a parrot narrating much of the tangled story.

The prose piles clause on clause in famous, breathless splendor, a style Indian critics rank supreme. Reincarnation lets the plot fold love and loss into a vast, looping design. Ridding's translation gave the West its fullest taste of a book India calls the crown of prose fiction.
king-babylonian-magic-sorcery-1896:
Leonard W. King published Babylonian Magic and Sorcery in 1896, the first English book on its subject. King edited a series of cuneiform prayers against witchcraft. The leading group is called the Prayers of the Lifting of the Hand.

Babylonians who believed themselves cursed used these rites for relief. The prayers ask gods to break spells, drive off demons, and restore health. King prints transliterations and translations from tablets in the British Museum. Victorian readers could hear ancient Mesopotamia's fears in its own words. The book pioneered the English study of Babylonian ritual texts. Assyriology students still cite its editions.
le-plongeon-queen-moo-egyptian-sphinx-18:
Explorer Augustus Le Plongeon argued that Maya rulers carried their culture to Egypt. His 1896 book Queen Moo and the Egyptian Sphinx tells that bold story. Le Plongeon dug in Yucatan and photographed its ruins for years.

He reads Maya texts as the tale of Queen Moo and her kin. Their line, he claims, crossed the sea and raised the Sphinx. His photos of ruins remain useful to scholars today. His grand links won few believers, then or now. The book is dated but fun, a diffusionist dream in full sail.
leadbeater-devachanic-plane-1896:
C. W. Leadbeater mapped the home of souls past death in The Devachanic Plane, his guide of 1896. Leadbeater was a chief voice of the new creed in its next crop. Devachan is the bright plane where the soul rests and grows ere its next birth on earth. He claims to have seen it by hid sight.

Each rank of soul gets its own zone and bliss in his map. The guide mates his prior map of the plane of dreams. Fans took both as fact for years. The book is a core text of the creed's scheme. Leadbeater claimed his sight was trained by adepts of the East. Doubts dogged those claims, yet his maps of hid planes still shape occult art.
leibniz-new-essays-langley-1896:
Alfred G Langley published his translation of Leibniz's New Essays Concerning Human Understanding in 1896. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz wrote the work in 1704 as a reply to John Locke's Essay, but it appeared only in 1765, after both men were dead. Langley gave English readers the full text.

In dialogue form, Leibniz answered Locke point by point, defending innate ideas against the blank slate. He argued that the mind holds truths as veins in marble hold a statue's shape. The essays range over perception, language, and the nature of substance. They form Leibniz's fullest statement of his rationalism, and a model of how two great philosophers can disagree with courtesy and depth.
levi-magical-ritual-of-the-sanctum-regnu:
A. E. Waite turned Eliphas Levi's hand writ rites into print in The Magical Ritual of the Sanctum Regnum, out in 1896. Levi left the rites in draft at his death. Waite, a young sage of the occult in London, shaped and glossed them for use in English.

The rites show Levi as a hands-on mage, not just a sage of books. Calls, signs, and tools fill the pages. The book links Levi to the Golden Dawn, the group then at work in London. It is a bridge twixt two ages of rite. Waite was young when he did this work, yet his name soon led the field. The care here shows why groups sought his hand.
levi-transcendental-magic-1896:
Eliphas Lévi's Transcendental Magic appeared in English in 1896, in Arthur Edward Waite's translation of Lévi's Dogme et Rituel. Lévi, a French writer and former seminarian, had set out a full system of magic in the 1850s. Waite's version carried that system to English readers.

Lévi taught that one hidden force, pictured as astral light, lay behind magic, myth, and sacred symbols. Ritual, will, and imagination were the tools for working with it. He drew on Kabbalah, tarot, and church teaching to build a single scheme. The book sparked the occult revival of the late nineteenth century and shaped nearly every magic order that followed.
lewis-the-monk-1796:
Matthew Gregory Lewis wrote The Monk while still in his teens. The book came out in 1796 and shocked the town at once. Its hero, Ambrosio, is a famed priest in Madrid. Pride and lust drag him down a path of crime and black rites.

A nun who bleeds and roams, a robber band, and the Inquisition fill the tale. A young nun's fall and a mother's curse add to the grim store. The book pushed the Gothic line to its wild edge for its age. Age has not dulled its power to shock and to hold a reader.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Motley's tenth volume spans the dark winter of 1618 and 1619. Political and religious parties trade growing rancour across the Netherlands. Spanish intrigues exploit the divisions, and King James proves inconsistent. Barneveld, the Republic's guide for a generation, lies hidden from sight.

Amid the crisis, Brewster and Robinson's congregation worships at Leyden. Motley recounts their decision to leave Holland for America. Robinson's farewell sermon and prayer mark their parting. The Pilgrim story thus enters this Dutch history near its tragic close. The winter setting underscores the Republic's internal gloom, Motley writes. His sympathy rests plainly with the fallen Advocate throughout.
marsh-pithecanthropus-erectus-java-1896:
O. C. Marsh, Yale's famous fossil hunter, weighed in on the Java ape-man in 1896. Eugene Dubois had reported skull and thigh bones from Trinil in Java. Marsh's short notice appeared in the American Journal of Science.

Marsh reviews Dubois's evidence and gives a cautious American welcome. He treats the bones as a real form between apes and humans. The piece carried weight because Marsh had named many dinosaurs himself. For English-speaking science, his verdict helped make Pithecanthropus a serious subject rather than a traveling curiosity. His notice ran only a few pages, yet it traveled widely.
maspero-struggle-of-nations-1896:
Gaston Maspero turns to war and realms in The Struggle of the Nations, in English from 1896. It is the mid tome of his three tome past of the old East. Egypt, Syria, and Assyria clash in an age of great kings. Chariots, sieges, and state craft fill the tale as realms rise, strike, and fade in turn.

Maspero had run digs and site guards in Egypt at first hand. That grit grounds his grand sweep. McClure's English prose keeps his grace. Fans of the old East still start with this set. This tome is its war book.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-2-january-18:
McClure's Magazine for January 1896 is volume six, number two. Ida M. Tarbell's life of Lincoln again leads the issue. This part shows his first trials in Illinois as a young man.

Lincoln clerks in Denton Offutt's store and meets the Clary's Grove boys. He studies grammar, runs for the assembly, and serves in the Black Hawk War. Poems by Eugene Field and a tale by Herbert D. Ward add lighter fare. Murat Halstead tells how Blaine lost the race for president in his day. A piece on the sun's light adds science to the month's mix. Elizabeth Stuart Phelps starts Chapters from a Life in this issue too.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-3-february-1:
February 1896 brings volume six, number three of McClure's Magazine. Tarbell's Lincoln leads again, now in New Salem from 1832 to 1836. He seeks work, buys a store, and starts to study law.

Lincoln serves as postmaster, surveys with a grapevine chain, and meets debt. The tale of Ann Rutledge stands in this part of the life. Ian Maclaren and Anthony Hope give fiction, and Will H. Low writes on painting. Murat Halstead treats the sad close of Garfield's term as president. A tale of the fastest railroad run adds speed and risk. Robert Louis Stevenson's Touchstone gives the issue a famed short tale.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-4-march-1896:
McClure's Magazine for March 1896 is volume six, number four. Tarbell's Lincoln enters the bar and moves to Springfield in this part. His first speech and first protest against slavery stand in the heads.

Rudyard Kipling gives the tale The Ship That Found Herself. Eugene Field and John Hay add verse and a tale of a young hero. Cleveland Moffett writes on the science of kite flying for weather work. Robert Barr adds a dramatic tale, and Will H. Low goes on with painting. Notes at the end treat a search for justice and the real Lincoln. Kites that draw down electric force show the age's bold science.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-5-april-1896:
April 1896 brings volume six, number five of McClure's Magazine. Two pieces lead on a new marvel in photography. They treat the Rontgen rays and their first use in America.

Pictures show bones through flesh, a ring on a lady's hand, and a frog. Tarbell's Lincoln reaches the campaign of 1840 and his wedding to Miss Todd. Anthony Hope starts Phroso, and Kipling gives a soldier and sailor poem. Mrs. E. V. Wilson's Rachel and more of a life close the issue. Notes praise the funds raised for short tales that year. New Lincoln pictures and a Grant life are flagged for readers too.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-6-no-6-may-1896:
McClure's Magazine for May 1896 is volume six, number six. Will H. Low's Century of Painting leads this issue. His subject is Jean Francois Millet, the French painter of farm folk.

Low tells of Millet's roots, his early sway, and his life at Barbizon. He shares his own short knowledge of the man and his studio talk. A self drawn portrait and Millet's joke coat of arms face the piece. Low weighs the place time and shared views have given the painter. Millet's own words on his pictures are quoted in the piece. Low lets the painter's talk stand beside his own judgment.
mctaggart-hegelian-dialectic-1896:
Studies in the Hegelian Dialectic, published in 1896, is J. M. E. McTaggart's first book, a critical exposition of Hegel's method. McTaggart, the Cambridge don who became idealism's most rigorous English voice, here tests the dialectic joint by joint.

He follows Hegel's categories as each passes into its opposite and is preserved in a higher unity, asking at each step whether the move is earned. His verdict is mixed: the method survives, much of its application does not. The book is lucid where its subject is not. It began McTaggart's lifelong project of rebuilding metaphysics with an auditor's conscience.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Volume five of the St. Cloud letters opens book two at letter one. The writer dates it from Paris in September 1805. He has come back to court and watched the Sovereign's levees.

Napoleon was warm and mild before he left to be crowned in Italy. He came back from Milan peevish, abrupt, and rude at his first audience. A naval hope helps explain the swing, the writer argues. Nelson's acts crushed the fleet plan that had raised his mood. A female friend of Madame Bonaparte knew part of the cause. Fleets and kingships weigh more than temper in his account.
mooney-ghost-dance-1896:
James Mooney worked for the Smithsonian and lived among Native peoples, recording their beliefs with care. His 1896 report studies the Ghost Dance faith that spread across the West after 1889. It closes with the Sioux outbreak of 1890 and the killing at Wounded Knee.

Mooney traces the faith to the Paiute prophet Wovoka, who preached peace, dance, and the return of the dead. He prints songs, letters, and firsthand accounts from many tribes. He also shows how fear and rumor among settlers turned a peaceful faith into a crisis. Because he listened before he judged, his report remains a founding work of American ethnography.
openalex-w1989230896:

The guide shows each step inside a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. It focuses on descriptive data tasks for beginners. Forest plots, the summary graphs of meta-analysis, are covered. Step-by-step detail lowers the entry barrier for clinicians. No costly specialist software is required for the method. The paper serves researchers with modest tools and budgets.
openalex-w2063294396:
Gianfranco Grompone, Patricia Martorell, Silvia Llopis and colleagues tested a probiotic strain in tiny worms. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Resisting oxidative stress helps healthy ageing. Live food bacteria might offer such protection. Evidence for that idea was scarce.

The team fed many bacterial strains to nematode worms. They then exposed the worms to oxidative stress. One Lactobacillus strain protected the worms clearly. Survival rose, and lifespan rose by about a fifth. Gene tests linked the effect to a known longevity pathway. The strain also calmed inflammation in human gut cells. The results mark it as a probiotic candidate. Human benefits still need direct testing.
openalex-w2105334596:

The boson appeared as a narrow bump in the data. Its measured mass sat near the accepted Higgs value. Its total width was very small, as expected. Production strength matched the standard model prediction closely. Spin and parity tests favoured the standard Higgs pattern. Rival spin options were ruled out strongly. The channel gave the sharpest early Higgs portrait.
openalex-w2142566496:

From over a thousand review titles, twenty-seven reviews were included. In children and teens, the best reviews gave strong evidence linking more sitting time with obesity. Evidence was moderate for blood pressure, cholesterol, self-esteem, social behavior, fitness, and school results. In adults, strong evidence linked sedentary behavior with death from all causes combined.

openalex-w2166063496:
