The aged type alone supplied almost half the organic mass. A small nitrogen-rich local type also appeared, and a filter-based method gave broadly matching source shares.
openalex-w2171391496:

The essay closes by laying out the steps of documentary analysis in order, giving beginners a clear path into the method.
openalex-w2558867396:

A volunteer committee from many professions built the framework through systematic review and wide consultation. Their survey drew over two thousand responses from thirty-three countries. It found dozens of different names for a handful of food texture and liquid thickness levels. Respondents strongly backed international standardization. IDDSI therefore sets one global set of terms and definitions. It is meant for patients of all ages, in all care settings and cultures.
openalex-w2792647196:
Luiz E. O. C. Aragão, Liana O. Anderson, and Marisa Gesteira Fonseca lead a team tracking Amazon fire emissions in Nature Communications in 2018. Brazil cut Amazon deforestation sharply after 2004, through a national action plan. Deforestation rates fell about two-thirds by 2015 compared with the earlier average. Carbon emissions from clearing fell with them.

Drought years tell a different story, the authors show. In the 2010 drought, fire emissions ran far above the following wet year, reaching over half of global land-use emissions that year. Fires in human-modified regions increasingly burn independently of fresh clearing. The paper's title states the result: drought-related fires counteract the decline in deforestation emissions. Protecting the Amazon's carbon gains therefore means fighting fire, not only chainsaws. Climate-driven drought makes that task harder each decade.
openalex-w2964962196:
Alok Sharma, Edwin Vans, Daichi Shigemizu, and colleagues published this methods paper in Scientific Reports in 2019. It presents DeepInsight, a way to turn data that are not images into images. The converted images can then be fed to convolutional neural networks, the models that excel at picture analysis.

The method matters because small, telling differences in genomic and other data are hard to spot directly. Image-based networks pull out features on their own, with no extra extraction step. They can also catch complex patterns and hidden correlations in data. By reshaping raw values into pictures, DeepInsight lets deep networks work on data far beyond photos. The authors offer it as a general tool for data science.
openalex-w3169375696:
Concepción Marcos, David Díaz, Katharina Fietz, and colleagues systematically review what marine protected areas give to nature and society. The authors gather evidence on ecosystem services, the practical gains ecosystems provide to people, from these protected zones. They also weigh wider social goods and benefits, such as food, income, and recreation. Sorting strong claims from weak ones matters, because protection is expanding fast. The review helps managers judge what well-run protected areas can truly deliver.
openalex-w4283381496:

A new edition therefore shifts daily practice in labs and clinics.

The article lays out the thinking behind the fifth edition and its main changes. It explains how new evidence on genes and disease behaviour reshaped several groups. Earlier editions grew from a 1990s expert scheme and were revised as knowledge deepened. An overview of the companion myeloid tumour classification was planned separately.
openalex-w4293212596:
The Astropy Collaboration, led by Adrian Price-Whelan, Pey Lian Lim, N. Earl, and colleagues, reports on the Astropy Project and its latest core release. The article summarises what the core package does and what the wider project has changed. It describes links with observatories and space missions that rely on the tools. It also covers Learn Astropy, the project's teaching arm. The authors close with the challenges of sustaining volunteer-driven software that a whole field now depends on.
openalex-w4308295896:

Such statements define which patients weight-loss surgery is recommended for. Obesity is now recognised as a chronic disease, tied to lasting low-grade inflammation and immune problems.

Worldwide surgical experience has grown greatly since the last indications were written. Long-term studies have proven the surgery an effective and durable treatment for severe obesity. The new statement updates patient selection to match that evidence. It aims to end outdated limits that kept proven treatment from people who could benefit.
openalex-w7204250996: Some people form blood clots again and again, and the cause often goes unnamed. openalex-w7204469096: Brazil's private health plans follow national rules, but care looks very different from state to state. openalex-w7208774396:

For inclusion, quick one-off adaptations are not enough: diversity belongs inside curriculum planning itself, with teachers mediating the tools rather than merely handing them over.

openalex-w7213365596:

That shift demands deep changes in institutional and business postures so dignity is protected in daily working life.

Alagoas stood out on every indicator: its hospital mortality was clearly higher than in the other two states, and it also showed the longest average stay and the highest average admission value. Pernambuco and Sergipe did not differ clearly from each other. openalex-w7220959296:

plos-pbio-0020096:
Hajime Hirase, Lifen Qian, Peter Barthó, and their team imaged living brain support cells for PLOS Biology in 2004. Astrocytes are star-shaped cells that support neurons. They signal with waves of calcium, and the team watched those waves move through networks of astrocytes in living animals.

Seeing the waves in an intact brain, rather than in a dish, shows how they really spread and sync. Calcium waves may help astrocytes coordinate blood flow and neuron support across a wide area. The work pushes imaging methods forward as well. It gives researchers a way to watch non-neuron brain cells at work in real time, a view that was long out of reach.
plos-pbio-0020196:
Michèle Crozatier, Jean-Michel Ubeda, Alain Vincent, and their team studied fly immunity in PLOS Biology in 2004. When a wasp lays an egg inside a fruit fly larva, the larva must surround it with blood cells and kill it. That defense is called encapsulation.

A gene named collier, the fly version of a family of early B-cell factors, proves vital for the response. Without it, the larva cannot mount the cell attack properly. The study links a gene known from vertebrate blood development to an insect defense, hinting at deep shared roots. It also gives immunity research a clean genetic handle on how blood cells are called into action.
plos-pbio-0020296:
Matt Kaeberlein, Kathryn T. Kirkland, Stanley Fields, and their team tested an aging theory in yeast in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cutting food intake extends life in many species, an effect called calorie restriction. In yeast, the gene Sir2 was thought to be the required middleman for that benefit.

The team found yeast can live longer on less food even without Sir2. So the pathway forks: Sir2 helps in some settings but is not the only route. That result kept the field honest about a tidy story. It pushed aging research to map several paths from diet to lifespan, a map that remains central to work on healthy aging.
plos-pone-0000096:
Yuuki Hayashi, Takuyo Aita, Hitoshi Toyota, and their team charted a protein fitness landscape by experiment in PLOS ONE in 2006. A fitness landscape maps how each change in a protein's sequence affects how well it works. Theory draws these maps as hills and valleys, but real ones are hard to measure.

By making many variants of one protein and testing each, the team drew a real section of such a map. It proved rugged: small steps could help, harm, or do nothing, in no simple pattern. Rugged maps explain why protein evolution can get stuck at local peaks. Measured landscapes like this one ground a famous theory in laboratory fact.
plos-pone-0000196:
Evangelos Evangelou, Demetrius M. Maraganore, and John P. A. Ioannidis published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome-wide association studies scan the whole genome for disease links, and meta-analysis pools many such studies for stronger evidence. The authors lay out strategies for doing that pooling well, applying them to Parkinson disease.

Single studies of gene effects are often too small to trust. A sound meta-analysis can separate real signals from chance hits. The paper gives practical guidance on combining genome-wide datasets and shows it at work on Parkinson's, where genetic clues have been hard to pin down.
plos-pone-0000296:
Nick J. B. Isaac, Samuel T. Turvey, Ben Collen, and colleagues published this conservation paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The EDGE approach ranks species by combining how threatened they are with how phylogenetically distinct they are, how much unique evolutionary history they carry. The authors apply it to mammals, setting conservation priorities on both grounds.

A species like the aardvark holds a whole branch of the mammal family tree. Losing it loses more history than losing one of many similar rodents. The paper lists which mammals score highest on threat plus distinctness. It gives conservation a defensible way to spend limited funds.
plos-pone-0000396:
Wei Zhang and colleagues hunted for DNA letter changes tied to where a gene is switched on, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genes make UGT1A enzymes, which help the body process drugs and its own chemicals, and different family members work in different tissues. The team searched for single-letter variants linked to those tissue-specific expression patterns.

A variant that changes where an enzyme is made can change how a person handles a drug. That makes this search part of pharmacogenetics, the study of how inherited differences shape drug response. Cataloging such variants is a step toward dosing medicines by a patient's genes rather than by averages.
plos-pone-0000496:
Antonio Graziano and colleagues improved stem cell bone building with a pitted surface, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. They grew stem cell-derived osteoblasts, bone-forming cells, on scaffold surfaces containing concave pits. The shaped surfaces improved the cells' performance and led to significant bone tissue formation.

Cells read the geometry of what they sit on: pits of the right size can nudge stem cells to become bone and lay down mineral. For regenerative medicine, the scaffold is half the therapy. A surface design that boosts bone formation could serve in implants for fractures and jaw work. Growing real bone there beats filling gaps with inert material.
plos-pone-0000596:
Thomas Karrasch and colleagues reported a warning about a plant compound often assumed to be protective, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Luteolin is a flavonoid found in vegetables and supplements. The team used NF-κB EGFP transgenic mice. These mice glow where the inflammation switch NF-κB is active. In them, the flavonoid luteolin worsened chemical-induced colitis. It did so by blocking NF-κB-dependent protective molecules.

NF-κB drives inflammation but also protects the gut lining; blocking it can backfire. The reporter mice made that double role visible in living tissue. The paper cautions against assuming natural antioxidants are safe in inflamed organs, and it refines where anti-inflammatory drugs should and should not act.
plos-pone-0000696:
Alexander Zumdieck, Karsten Kruse, Henrik Bringmann and colleagues gave a physical analysis of the ring that splits a cell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. During cytokinesis, a contractile ring of actin filaments squeezes the cell into two. The authors analyze how stress builds in that ring and how its filaments turn over, constantly replaced while the ring shrinks.

Their case study is the embryo of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, a classic model. They present a general analysis of force balances and material exchange in the ring. Physics of this kind matters because division errors drive disease. A ring that both contracts and renews itself is an engineering puzzle worth solving exactly.
plos-pone-0000796:
Morten Nielsen, Claus Lundegaard, Thomas Blicher and colleagues presented NetMHCpan, a predictor for a core step in immune recognition, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Binding of peptides to MHC molecules is the single most selective step when the cellular immune system recognizes pathogens. The human MHC class I system, HLA-I, is extremely polymorphic, with a huge and growing registry of variants.

Older predictors handled only specific HLA types. NetMHCpan aims at any HLA-A and HLA-B protein of known sequence, giving quantitative binding predictions. Pan-specific prediction matters for vaccine design across diverse populations. A peptide vaccine must bind the HLA variants real people carry. Binding only the common laboratory ones is not enough.
plos-pone-0000896:
Jon Beadell, Colm Atkins, Erin Cashion and colleagues compared immune traits in four island bird groups, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hawaii's native birds have been hit hard by bird malaria and pox brought in by people. With fewer parasites around and smaller gene pools, island birds might share a changed immune profile.

The team measured immune signals across four island taxa and found they do not all point the same way. That divergence is itself the lesson: a parasite poor home does not reshape every species alike. For conservation, the work warns against treating island birds as one uniform case.
plos-pone-0000996:
Isabel Miranda, Rita Rocha, Maria Santos and colleagues showed that a changed genetic code creates variety in a human pathogen, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The genetic code was once thought frozen and universal. Found exceptions in bacteria and eukaryotes alike ended that idea, showing codon assignments can shift.

Candida albicans, a fungus that infects people, reads one codon in an unusual way. The team argue this alteration acts as a phenotype diversity generator, producing varied cell surfaces and traits from one genome. Variety helps a pathogen dodge immunity and drugs. A code quirk once treated as a curiosity here becomes a survival strategy.
plos-pone-0001096:
Meei Ling Sheu, Shing Hwa Liu and Keng Hsin Lan tested a plant compound against gastric cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Honokiol is a small natural product from magnolia, reported to fight tumors and the blood vessels that feed them. Its molecular mechanisms, and whether it works against gastric cancer, were unknown.

The team report honokiol induces cleavage of a stress protein, GRP94, through calpain enzymes, and triggers apoptosis, ordered cell death, in human gastric cancer cells. It also reduced tumor growth in their model. Natural products often fail for lack of a mechanism; here the mechanism is the headline. Gastric cancer remains hard to treat, so new routes matter.
plos-pone-0001196:
Insulin affects the brain as well as the body, raising activity in the cerebral cortex of lean people. Otto Tschritter and colleagues tested a long-acting insulin, detemir, in overweight people, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. In obese individuals the brain's response to insulin is reduced, a sign of cerebrocortical insulin resistance.

The authors asked whether insulin detemir is a suitable tool to restore the cerebral insulin response in overweight humans. They tracked cerebrocortical beta activity, a rhythm of brain electrical activity that insulin stimulates. Their work bears on how brain insulin resistance might be reversed, with implications for appetite and weight control.
plos-pone-0001296:
Flu seasons differ around the world, but the global pattern had never been fully described for each virus type. Brian Finkelman and colleagues assembled laboratory-confirmed data on influenza activity from 1997 to 2005, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They covered the A/H3N2 and A/H1N1 subtypes and influenza B.

The authors describe global patterns in seasonal activity, including viral coexistence and latitudinal gradients, meaning how timing shifts with distance from the equator. Such maps help time vaccination campaigns and anticipate which strains circulate where. The work turns scattered national reports into one comparative picture.
plos-pone-0001396:
Joost Woltering and Antony Durston wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on body plan genes in zebrafish. Hox genes lay out the head to tail axis in animals. Small RNA genes sit inside the Hox clusters too, and they are kept across many species. The pair studied one such RNA, called miR-10, in fish embryos.

The authors show that miR-10 holds back two Hox genes in the fish. By curbing those genes, the small RNA helps set where body parts form. This adds a layer of fine control to the classic Hox plan. It also shows how tiny RNAs shape growth long before the animal takes its final form.
plos-pone-0001496:
Michael Rosenberg and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how muscle like motors build their bundles. Myosin motors form part of the cell's inner frame. Each motor has a long coiled tail, and tails must pack into bundles for the motor to pull at full force. The team asked what steers that packing.

They show the net charge along the tail rod rules both packing and where bundles sit in the cell. Charge is a simple trait with a large effect here. That rule helps labs predict how tail changes will alter cell pull. It may also guide design of man made motor materials.
plos-pone-0001596:
Andrew Kitchen, Michael Miyamoto, and Connie Mulligan wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the Americas were first peopled. They weigh gene, dig, land, and climate proof in one frame. Past tales had split on route and pace. The team set out a three stage model that fits the full proof set.

In their model, a root group first split in Asia. It then waited out the ice age in the far north, then spread south in a swift wave. Each stage rests on a distinct line of proof. A model that honors all lines beats one that picks a favorite. It gives digs and gene hunts a shared map.
plos-pone-0001696:
Pablo Perel and co-authors checked whether clinical trials in Latin America match the region's health needs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Since 1990, non-communicable diseases and injuries have caused most deaths and disability-adjusted life years in Latin America. Trials, though, may cluster on topics of interest to rich countries or drug makers.

The team compared the global burden of disease with randomized clinical trials run in Latin America and published in the five leading medical journals. The full text gives the disease-by-disease comparison and where the gaps fall. A mismatch means research money flows away from the conditions that most shorten and worsen lives in the region.
plos-pone-0001796:
Tianyi Mao, Daniel H. O'Connor, Volker Scheuss, and their co-authors measured a class of glow-based calcium sensors in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Genetically encoded calcium indicators, or GECIs, promise to track calcium in chosen neuron groups and even in specific cell compartments. To read their glow as activity, though, users need careful quantitative characterization.

The team characterized a promising GCaMP-type indicator and worked out its subcellular targeting, how to send it to exact cell locations. The full text gives the brightness, speed, and calcium response curves. Calcium imaging is now a workhorse of neuroscience, and papers that calibrate the sensors keep thousands of later experiments honest.
plos-pone-0001896:
Dongkook Park and co-authors mapped hormone-making cells in the fruit fly in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. These cells release peptide signals that steer growth, feeding, and other body tasks. A gene switch called DIMMED, or DIMM, had been tied to how such cells mature in the fly Drosophila.

The team checked two things across the whole fly: which peptide cells carry DIMM, and whether all cells with DIMM make peptides. A full map was still missing. Sorting this out helps labs use the fly to study how hormone cells form and fail. The map also gives a base for work on like cells in other species.
plos-pone-0001996:
Magdalena Zychlinska and co-authors studied a common virus in mouse B cells grown from stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Epstein-Barr virus infects more than ninety-five in a hundred adults and stays in their B cells for life. It is also tied to several cancers, yet it infects human cells in ways mice do not copy easily.

The team made mouse B cells from embryonic stem cells and infected them with the virus. They report that the virus's latent genes, the set it uses while lying low, were expressed only in a restricted way. Limits like this show where mouse models can and cannot stand in for human infection.
plos-pone-0002096:
Charles Rudick and co-authors traced bladder pain to a classic allergy chemical, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mast cells trigger inflammation that comes with local pain, but the steps from cell to pain were unclear. Interstitial cystitis is a bladder disease that causes debilitating pelvic pain of unknown origin. It often shows no consistent inflammation, though its symptoms correlate with mast cell signs.

As the title states, histamine derived from mast cells mediates cystitis pain in their model. Histamine is the chemical antihistamines block in allergy. If it drives bladder pain too, drugs that calm mast cells or block histamine may help a hard-to-treat pain.
plos-pone-0002196:
Tabitha Wanja Mwangi and co-authors counted malaria attacks in children and found an uneven pattern, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. If all children of the same age faced the same exposure, their malaria episodes should spread out evenly, following a Poisson pattern with no clumping.

Long-running studies hinted instead that some children suffer far more attacks than chance would allow. The team tested that idea and found over-dispersion: the burden falls heavily on a subset of children. Knowing that malaria clusters in certain children helps health programs aim bed nets, drugs, and follow-up care where they will do the most good.
plos-pone-0002296:
Jérôme Ausseil and co-authors asked what drives early brain damage in a storage disease of children, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIB is a lysosomal storage disease that causes early mental decline. Faulty breakdown leaves abnormal fragments of heparan sulfate, a complex sugar, and the brain shows severe damage with chronic inflammation.

It was unclear whether the inflammation causes the neurodegeneration or follows it. Using mice with the disease, the team addressed that causal question. They report that early degeneration progresses independently of microglial activation by heparan sulfate. The order of events matters, because it decides which process a drug must stop first.
plos-pone-0002396:
Research by Li and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Shufeng Li, Jiahuang Li, Jian Cheng, and others. Its subject is non-Syndromic Tooth Agenesis in Two Chinese Families Associated with Novel Missense Mutations. The rest of the title points to the TNF Domain of EDA (Ectodysplasin A). Here we report two unrelated Chinese families with congenital missing teeth inherited in an X-linked manner.

We mapped the affected locus to chromosome Xp11-Xq21 in one family. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002496:
Greenstein and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Robert J. Greenstein, Liya Su, Ramon A. Juste, and others. Its subject is on the Action of Cyclosporine A, Rapamycin and Tacrolimus on M. avium Including Subspecies paratuberculosis. Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis (MAP) may be zoonotic.

Recently the “immuno-modulators” methotrexate, azathioprine and 6-MP and the “anti-inflammatory” 5-ASA have been shown to inhibit MAP growth in vitro. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002596:
Led by Pennings, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Jeroen L. A. Pennings, Tjeerd G. Kimman, Riny Janssen, and others. Its subject is identification of a Common Gene Expression Response in Different Lung Inflammatory Diseases in Rodents and Macaques. To identify gene expression responses common to multiple pulmonary diseases we collected microarray data for acute lung inflammation models from 12 studies.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002696:
Research from Ausra Milano and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers molecular subsets in the gene expression signatures of scleroderma skin. Authorship is credited in the record to Ausra Milano and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Scleroderma is a clinically heterogeneous disease with a complex phenotype. The authors add a further point. The disease is characterized by vascular dysfunction, tissue fibrosis, internal organ dysfunction, and immune dysfunction resulting in autoantibody production. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002796:
Work by Yanxing Han and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was demonstration of a novel HIV-1 restriction phenotype from a human t cell line. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Yanxing Han, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Although retroviruses may invade host cells. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002896:
Sacha Coesel, Miroslav Obornik, Joao Varela and co-authors traced the pigment pathway of marine diatoms in 2008. Carotenoids are pigments all light-using organisms make for harvesting light and guarding against damage. Diatoms are tiny algae with an unusual past, so their pigment pathway was of special interest and still poorly studied.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team reconstructs where the pathway came from and what its genes do in diatoms. That history helps explain how these algae became such strong photosynthesizers in the oceans. The work also informs efforts to use diatoms for fuels and fine chemicals.
plos-pone-0002996:
Paul Robach, Jose Calbet, Jonas Thomsen and co-authors tested how low oxygen changes the benefit of erythropoietin in 2008. Treatment with recombinant human erythropoietin raises the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity and clearly boosts maximal oxygen uptake in normal air. In severe acute hypoxia, low oxygen, that boost had not appeared.

The PLOS ONE study finds the ergogenic effect on maximal oxygen uptake depends on how severe the hypoxemia is. That nuance matters for altitude physiology and for sport, where the hormone is both a therapy and a banned doping agent. It defines when extra red cells stop helping.
plos-pone-0003096:
Brett Shepard, Davide De Forni, David McNamara and co-authors tested the protein TRAIL against HIV burden in 2008. During uncontrolled HIV disease, TRAIL and its receptor are increased. Sensitivity rises because the viral protein gp120 pushes the receptor up, while successful antiretroviral therapy brings TRAIL back down.

The title reports a beneficial effect of TRAIL on HIV burden without detectable immune consequences. Published in PLOS ONE, a treatment that cuts burden without immune harm would be notable. The study explores borrowing the body's own death signal against infected cells. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003196:
Juan Esteban Kamienkowski and Mariano Sigman study dual-task delays in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When two tasks are presented within a short interval, a delay in carrying out the second task has been systematically observed. Theory has argued that sensory and motor steps can proceed in parallel, while coordination between these modules creates the bottleneck.

The authors examine response time and error distributions, under the title Delays without Mistakes. Readers learn how people can slow down sharply yet keep accuracy. That pattern helps test models of attention limits that simple average times cannot distinguish.
plos-pone-0003296:
Ceres Maciel, Vani Xavier de Oliveira Junior, Marcos Antonio Fázio and colleagues test angiotensin peptides against malaria in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium species cause malaria, the worst insect-borne parasite for people. Finding and developing new drugs for malaria treatment and prevention is the goal of much research. Angiotensins I and II and six lab-made peptides were examined.

The authors report anti-Plasmodium activity of angiotensin II and related synthetic peptides. Readers see a blood pressure hormone family turned to fight a parasite. Peptide leads are valuable in malaria, where drug resistance keeps eroding standard treatments.
plos-pone-0003396:
Alexandre F. DaSilva and colleagues scanned the brains of pain patients in this 2008 study. The patients had trigeminal neuropathic pain, a severe pain of the face. Long-term pain had been linked to shrinkage in some brain areas. The team measured both brain structure and brain activity in the same people.

The two sets of changes lined up in the same parts of the cortex. Where tissue was thinner, activity was also altered. That match suggests chronic pain reshapes the brain itself, not just its signals. The work may help explain why such pain is so hard to treat.
plos-pone-0003496:
Jesús Gonzalo-Asensio and co-authors reviewed a master switch of tuberculosis in this 2008 paper. PhoP is a regulator protein inside Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Removing it weakens the germ sharply, a state called attenuation. Weakened phoP mutants showed promise as live vaccine candidates in early tests.

The study pieces together how PhoP drives virulence. Its network touches many traits the germ needs to cause disease. One switch thus explains a large share of TB behavior. That focus gives vaccine and drug work a clear target. PhoP also drew interest because weakened strains may work as live vaccines.
plos-pone-0003596:
Wilco P. Pulskens and co-authors studied an alarm receptor in injured kidneys in this 2008 paper. Toll-like receptors can detect danger molecules released by damaged tissue. That detection triggers a pro-inflammatory response. One family member, TLR4, is present on kidney epithelium at RNA level.

Its expression rises further after injury. The team showed TLR4 coordinates the kidney's innate immune response to ischemia and reperfusion. Restored blood flow after blockage causes its own damage wave. Blocking that coordination could spare kidneys that friendly fire. Kidney transplants face this same injury when the organ is stored and moved.
plos-pone-0003696:
Francisco R. Pinto, José Melo-Cristino, and Mário Ramirez published this statistics paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Many fields sort items into clusters and then need to judge how well two sortings agree. The Wallace coefficient measures that agreement in one direction. It lacked a formal way to state its uncertainty.

The authors derive a confidence interval for the coefficient, so agreement comes with honest error bars. They apply the tool to microbial typing, where labs sort bacteria by their traits. The method helps researchers tell whether two typing schemes really tell the same story.
plos-pone-0003796:
Sanjay Premi, Jyoti Srivastava, Ganesan Panneer, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Turner syndrome usually means a girl has one X chromosome instead of two. When Y chromosome material is present in such patients, the risk of a tumor called gonadoblastoma rises.

The team analyzed the Y chromosome in fifteen patients diagnosed with Turner syndrome. They found striking mosaicism, with the SRY and DAZ genes duplicated in tandem in the Y material. The findings matter for screening, since hidden Y fragments change a patient's cancer risk.
plos-pone-0003896:
Satoshi Yamanaka, Ihor Zahanich, Robert P. Wersto, and co-authors grew heart muscle cells from stem cells in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article tackles a hard problem in heart cell study. Heart cells taken from newborn animals barely divide in dishes. Animal models with lasting gene changes also adapt in ways that blur results.

The team built flat cultures of heart cells derived from embryonic stem cells. They then removed the retinoblastoma gene for a short time in those cells. After that loss, the heart cells divided at a higher rate. The model gives labs a cleaner way to study heart cell growth.
plos-pone-0003996:
Niv Sabath, Giddy Landan, and Dan Graur presented a method for genes that overlap in 2008. Measuring selection strength in protein-coding genes helps reveal adaptation. Overlapping genes occur in all domains of life. They have seemed to show oddly high degrees of positive selection.

Their PLOS ONE article offers a way to estimate selection in overlapping genes at once. A gene read in two frames faces two sets of pressures. Standard methods can confuse those pressures and misread adaptation. A joint method gives cleaner estimates for the many overlapping genes in genomes. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004096:
Anitha Moorthy, Amita Gupta, Ramesh Bhosale, and co-authors studied drug resistance in HIV-exposed infants in 2009. Daily nevirapine given to infants cuts HIV spread through breast milk. The SWEN trial in India compared single-dose with six-week extended dosing. Babies in the trial carried subtype C HIV when infected.

Their PLOS ONE article assessed nevirapine resistance in those infants. Protection that breeds resistant virus could limit later treatment options. Balancing transmission prevention against resistance is a central program question. The Indian data inform dosing policy for breastfeeding mothers with HIV. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004196:
Serge Mostowy and colleagues published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Septins are conserved proteins that build filaments inside cells and are needed for tasks such as cell division. The team had earlier found one septin, SEPT9, on phagosomes, the compartments that swallow particles into the cell.

They asked how septins act when bacteria enter host cells. Using Listeria, a food-borne bacterium with a well-studied entry route, they show that septins regulate bacterial entry. The finding adds a new player to the cell's border control, with consequences for how infections begin.
plos-pone-0004296:
Giorgio Colombo, Massimiliano Meli, and Giulia Morra published this prion study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The conversion of the normal prion protein into its infectious form is the key event in prion diseases. The process is believed to involve a multi-step change of shape, from a helix-rich form to a sheet-rich form.

The authors modelled what happens when methionine sulfoxides form on helix-3 of the protein, a change caused by oxidation. They report that these sulfoxides switch on the destabilisation of the normal fold needed for conversion. A small chemical burn may thus be the first domino in prion disease.
plos-pone-0004396:
Animal species differ hugely in how many individuals they have. Yet their mitochondrial DNA shows oddly similar levels of variety. That sameness led some to think mitochondrial effective population size stays near constant. Gwenael Piganeau and Adam Eyre-Walker challenged that idea in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks for signs that the size really does vary.

Effective population size is the breeding pool that shapes genetic variety. If it varies, mitochondrial variety should carry traces of that variation. The authors present evidence that it does. Their result cracks a tidy claim built on the sameness puzzle. It reopens debate about what sets mitochondrial diversity across animals.
plos-pone-0004496:
Gene variants near a gut defense switch are linked to Crohn's disease of the small intestine, report Maureen Koslowski, Irmgard Kubler, Mathias Chamaillard, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Crohn's disease in the ileum, the last part of the small bowel, shows reduced levels of natural antibiotics called defensins, made by Paneth cells. The switch, TCF-4, also named TCF7L2, guides how Paneth cells develop.

TCF-4 directly controls the genes for those defensins. The team looked at variants in the gene's promoter region, the stretch that sets how much of it is made. They found variants associated with small intestinal Crohn's disease, as the title reports. The result ties a gut defense failure to inherited variation in one control switch.
plos-pone-0004596:
Which virus a very young baby carries decides how severe its bronchiolitis becomes, report Christophe Marguet, Marc Lubrano, Marie Gueudin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bronchiolitis is a chest infection of infancy that fills small airways with mucus. Modern tests revealed that various single viruses, or co-infections with several, can cause it. One virus, RV, seemed to play a growing role in early respiratory disease.

Whether the carried virus shapes severity remained controversial. The team set out to determine, prospectively, how the specific virus relates to how sick very young infants get. The answer helps doctors predict which babies will need hospital support. It also sharpens the search for which infant chest viruses deserve vaccines.
plos-pone-0004696:
Marie-Anne Debily and colleagues mapped the gene network tied to a breast protein called PIP, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The PIP gene is switched on in many breast cancers. Past reports clashed on whether it helps or harms, so its real role stayed unclear.

The team joined gene scans with other data to find genes that rise and fall with PIP. They also sought the paths those genes act in. A network view can show if PIP is a driver, a marker, or both. That helps guide which breast tumors to treat and how to track them.
plos-pone-0004796:
Michael Singer, Kevi Mace, and Elizabeth Bernays showed that parasitized caterpillars eat more plant toxins as self medication, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Self medication is a healing behavior change in response to disease or parasites. Past literature focused entirely on finding cases where particular behaviors link to healing outcomes in wild and captive animals under observation.

The team framed increased toxin eating as adaptive plasticity in caterpillars. Parasitized larvae ate more toxin rich food and benefited. The work broadens self medication beyond primates. It also shows diet choice can be a form of immunity. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004896:
David Burns, Weihai Ying, and Tiina Kauppinen studied selective down control of nuclear poly ADP ribose glycohydrolase, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Formation of ADP ribose polymers by polymerases serves cell signaling functions. Extensive activation of PARP-1 is a dominant cause of cell death in ischemia reperfusion, trauma, and swelling. Making enzymes that remove polymers key regulators of survival after severe cellular stress and DNA damage.

Selectively lowering the nuclear removal enzyme alters polymer persistence. Balance between synthesis and removal decides fate. Stroke and trauma therapies target this axis. Nuclear specificity matters for safety. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here.
plos-pone-0004996:
Saving nature is not only about buying parks. Conservation easements pay landowners to keep land wild. Isla Fishburn and colleagues tracked this tool's growth in PLOS ONE in 2009. They noted an imbalance in conservation research. Many studies ask where to protect biodiversity. Few ask how investments should be structured.

The study examines the rise of easements as a conservation approach. It asks where easement money works best. It also weighs easements against buying land outright. The analysis guides smarter spending for biodiversity. As easements grow, such guidance matters more. Landowners, funders and agencies all need to know what this tool can and cannot do.
plos-pone-0005096:
Proteins touch each other through matching modules called domains. Knowing which domains interact explains protein networks. Chittibabu Guda and colleagues built a top-down method to infer them. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They worked across eight model organisms. Protein interaction data are plentiful. Domain-level data are scarce.

The method infers domain-domain interactions from the protein data. Comparing species reveals which interactions are ancient. It also reveals which are new inventions. The work builds a shared wiring diagram for life's machinery. Such diagrams help predict unknown interactions. They also show how evolution reuses old parts. Model organisms from yeast to human share more wiring than expected.
plos-pone-0005196:
Bipolar disorder runs in families, but the genes behind it are still being found. One candidate is SP4, which codes for a transcription factor that shapes gene activity. Zhou and colleagues examined the human SP4 gene in PLOS ONE in 2009, building on work in mice.

In mice, lower Sp4 activity harms the hippocampus and leads to behavior changes tied to mental illness. The human study found SP4 acts as a susceptibility gene for bipolar disorder, as the title states. That link adds a concrete gene to the biology of a hard-to-treat mood disorder.
plos-pone-0005296:
Kidney transplantation is the most common solid organ transplant in the world, and donor kidneys are scarce. Catching rejection early protects each precious graft. Reuter and colleagues tested a scan-based method in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The method uses PET imaging with a sugar tracer, FDG, in small animals. Scan signals revealed acute rejection of transplanted kidneys without invasive biopsies. A non-invasive warning system could let doctors adjust treatment sooner and help each graft last longer. Rats are small and heal fast, so a scan that works in them can be tried in many drug tests before it is shaped for use in a large hospital.
plos-pone-0005396:
Helicobacter species form a small but notable part of the normal gut flora in animals. Some intestinal species trigger colitis in mouse models, by unclear routes. Chaouche-Drider and colleagues studied a commensal rodent Helicobacter in gut epithelial cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The normally harmless species activated two innate immune sensors, TLR2 and NOD1, in epithelial cells. Sensing without disease is how the gut keeps watch over its residents. The work shows the fine line between a commensal that is monitored and a relative that provokes inflammation. The gut lives at peace with most of its germs, yet the line to colitis is thin. And this work shows one way the gut wall tells a friend it can live with from a foe it must fight.
plos-pone-0005496:
Bhavin Sheth, Ngan Nguyen, and Davit Janvelyan asked whether sleep helps people remember faces, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Sleep is known to firm up many kinds of memory after learning. Remembering faces is a basic social skill that people use every day.

Volunteers learned faces, then either slept or stayed awake before being tested. The team compared how well each group later picked out the faces they had seen. The study tests whether face memory gains the same boost from sleep that other memory types do, a question with few clear answers before.
plos-pone-0005596:
Sonia Boria and co-authors studied how children with autism read intentions in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When we watch someone grasp a cup, we grasp both the goal and the reason behind it, such as drinking. Context and the way the act is done give those clues.

The team tested whether children with autism pick up both kinds of information from watched actions. Any gap in reading intention, as opposed to goal, would shape how support and teaching should be designed. The study adds detail to what is known about social understanding in autism.
plos-pone-0005696:
Luqman Tariq and co-authors assessed in 2009 whether quick screening and advice for heavy drinking in Dutch primary care is worth its cost. Heavy alcohol use adds a large burden of disease that early help could cut. Doctors can screen patients during normal visits and give brief advice on the spot.

The study weighed the program's costs against the health gains it buys. Such value checks help health systems choose among many good ideas with limited funds. If brief advice pays off, it can be spread widely at low cost per person. The Dutch results give other countries a model to test at home.
plos-pone-0005796:
Christiane Segarra, Sylvain Lehmann, and Joliette Coste examined in 2009 how a common gene variant affects the prion protein in human white blood cells. All known cases of variant CJD, the human form of mad cow disease, shared one genotype at codon 129 of the prion gene. That narrow pattern raised questions about everyone else.

The team studied how the protein is made and processed in mononuclear cells across genotypes. Processing differences could explain why only some genotypes sicken. Blood cells are also a possible route of spread, so their handling of prions matters for transfusion safety. The work refines risk where data were thin.
plos-pone-0005896:
Gloria Salazar and co-authors described in 2009 how a brain zinc transporter ties itself into clusters that change its job. ZnT3 loads zinc into synaptic vesicles; that zinc is released with signals between neurons. Proteins often work in pairs or groups, held by weak or strong bonds.

Here, dityrosine bonds lock ZnT3 into oligomers, covalent clusters that set where the protein sits and how much metal it moves. A permanent bond is an unusual way to control a transporter. Faults in brain zinc handling appear in several disorders, so the mechanism is a candidate factor. The chemistry is spelled out for follow-up.
plos-pone-0005996:
Hot fields draw crowds, money and speed, but perhaps at a cost to truth. Thomas Pfeiffer and Robert Hoffmann tested that worry at large scale in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper checks published claims about protein interactions and asks whether findings from popular fields hold up less well than those from quieter ones.

Theory had predicted that reliability falls as a field grows more popular. The team's check of real claims backs that prediction, they report. A result of this kind matters far beyond one dataset: it speaks to how science rewards speed, and why slow fields and repeat studies deserve more credit than they usually get.
plos-pone-0006096:
A protein first found in mammal mitochondria turns up in bacteria too. Annelise Chapalain, Sylvie Chevalier, Nicole Orange and colleagues studied that bacterial cousin in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper characterizes a bacterial ortholog of the translocator protein TSPO, a protein of the outer mitochondrial membrane tied to many core jobs in our own cells.

The bacterial version regulates virulence, the germ's power to cause disease. An ancient protein doing infection work in bacteria hints at deep roots for a molecule doctors know from brain scans and drug binding. It also offers a fresh target: blocking the bacterial version might disarm a germ without killing it outright.
plos-pone-0006196:
Plasminogen is a blood protein that can be switched on to dissolve clots, and it is built from seven linked domains. Jack Kornblatt studied the dog form of the protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Inside each domain, sulfur bonds between cysteine units hold the shape firm.

Breaking just a few of those bonds made the molecule open out and then clump and fall out of solution. The energy held by the broken bonds was measured as part of the work. The result shows how a small chemical change can undo a large protein. It offers a clean lesson in what keeps folded proteins stable.
plos-pone-0006296:
Starfish eggs pause early in their division cycle until a hormone restarts them. Keiichiro Kyozuka and colleagues studied that restart in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The hormone 1-methyladenine triggers two fast responses: a release of calcium inside the cell, and rapid reshaping of the actin skeleton.

The team examined how guanine nucleotides regulate both responses during maturation. Calcium signals and skeleton changes must be timed together for healthy egg development. Starfish oocytes are a classic, clear model for meiosis, the special division that makes eggs. The findings refine the sequence of switches that wake the egg.
plos-pone-0006396:
Plotting a DNA sequence as a walk across a page can expose hidden order. Maria Poptsova and colleagues analysed 2D DNA walks of hundreds of chromosomes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Across bacteria, archaea, fungi, and humans, the walks range from symmetric half-turns to pseudo-random wanderings.

An in silico transformation of gene order and strand position returns most chromosomes to symmetry, they report. A hidden chromosome symmetry thus lurks under apparent disorder. The transformation reveals rules of genome organisation. Such order may reflect how chromosomes evolved and fold.
plos-pone-0006496:
Yuka Hara, Rahmah Mohamed, and Sheila Nathan searched a disease bacterium's surface for vaccine targets in PLOS ONE in 2009. Burkholderia pseudomallei causes melioidosis, a disease with high illness and death rates in endemic areas. It affects both humans and animals. No vaccine exists against it.

The team focused on outer membrane proteins that the immune system can see. They identified immunogenic ones, proteins that provoke an immune response. Surface proteins are natural vaccine candidates because antibodies can reach them. Their list gives vaccine developers concrete targets to test. Melioidosis is common in parts of Asia and northern Australia.
plos-pone-0006596:
Xiaojing Sun, Tiffany Hoage, Ping Bai, and colleagues studied heart enlargement in zebrafish in PLOS ONE in 2009. An adult zebrafish heart possesses a high capacity of regeneration. However, it was unclear whether and how myocyte hyperplasia contributes to cardiac remodeling in response to stress. Hyperplasia means making more cells; hypertrophy means cells growing larger.

Studying anemic zebrafish, their title reports cardiac hypertrophy involves both myocyte hypertrophy and hyperplasia. The fish heart grows by both routes. That dual ability may underlie its famous regeneration. Mammal hearts rely mostly on enlargement, which may be why they scar instead.
plos-pone-0006696:
Sofia I. I. Kring and co-authors tested gene variants tied to body weight and diabetes in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on three candidate genes from brain chemistry pathways. Two are serotonin receptors, called 5HT2A and 5HT2C. The third is COMT, which acts on dopamine and noradrenaline signals. The same pathways also help regulate energy balance.

The researchers looked at single-letter DNA differences in these genes. They checked whether the variants track with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Results like these test whether mood-related genes also shape metabolism. Any confirmed link could refine risk prediction for both conditions. The study adds to the search for shared roots of mental and metabolic health.
plos-pone-0006796:
Maryam Rakhshandehroo and colleagues compared a metabolic regulator between mice and humans in PLOS ONE in 2009. The regulator is the transcription factor PPARα. Mouse studies showed it controls liver fat metabolism. It also shapes the acute phase response to illness. Far less was known about its role in human liver.

The team compared gene regulation by PPARα in mouse and human liver cells. Similarities would validate mouse studies for human medicine. Differences would warn against direct translation. Many drugs aim at this pathway for blood fat problems. Knowing where species diverge helps judge those drugs honestly.
plos-pone-0006896:
Lauren K. Dunn and colleagues studied why breast cancer spreads to bone in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most patients with advanced breast cancer develop bone metastases. Metastases cause pain, fractures, high calcium, and nerve damage. Chemotherapy adds further bone loss. Bone-specific treatments can only relieve symptoms, not cure.

Low oxygen in tumors and a signal called TGF-beta drive the spread. They act through parallel pathways in tumor cells and bone. Tumor-secreted factors attack the bone microenvironment from several sides. Parallel routes explain why single blockers often disappoint. Targeting both pathways together is the study's implied strategy for better control.
plos-pone-0006996:
Julien Herrou, Anne-Sophie Debrie, Eve Willery, and colleagues traced the evolution of a bacterial control system in PLOS ONE in 2009. The system, BvgAS, regulates virulence in Bordetella bacteria. One species, B. pertussis, causes whooping cough in humans. Its close relative B. bronchiseptica infects many mammals with chronic respiratory disease.

The team compared how this two-component system evolved across the group. A third relative, B. parapertussis, causes a milder whooping cough. Small changes in a shared regulator may explain their different hosts and diseases. That makes BvgAS a case study in how pathogens adapt.
plos-pone-0007096:
Mark McCormick studied fish on a disturbed coral reef in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reefs face growing stress from human activity and climate change. Disturbances are expected to grow stronger and more frequent. Coral reefs rank among the most at-risk ecosystems on Earth. McCormick asked how such change filters fish by their behavior.

He examined selection acting through behavior in the disturbed habitat. Bold or shy fish may fare very differently when cover and conditions shift. If behavior decides who survives, reef communities can change in hidden ways. His work links personality-level traits to the fate of reef populations.
plos-pone-0007196: Michael Rosenblum, Steven G. Deeks, Mark van der Laan, and colleagues addressed HIV treatment in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their title states the central finding directly. Risk of virologic failure falls as the time a patient keeps HIV suppressed grows longer. That pattern holds once adherence to antiretroviral therapy passes about half of prescribed doses. It gives doctors and patients a clearer picture of how sustained suppression protects treatment.
plos-pone-0007296:
Marina de Leeuw, Shlomi Reuveni, Joseph Klafter, and colleagues tested a physical rule for folded proteins in 2009. A recently suggested equation of state described natively folded proteins. The equation rests on a fractal view of proteins, on a classic instability idea, and on marginal stability in physical systems.

The authors verify the equation against a set of thousands of proteins. Their question is how proteins can be both flexible and stable at once. Those two traits seem opposed, yet working proteins need both. Their PLOS ONE test supports a shared physical principle across many protein shapes.
plos-pone-0007396:
Elsa van der Loo, Steffen Gais, Marco Congedo, and colleagues measured brain rhythms in tinnitus patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Non-pulsatile tinnitus is a subjective ringing heard by a large share of the population. As a phantom sound, it is related to hyperactivity and reorganization of the auditory cortex, the brain's hearing center.

Magnetoencephalography studies had shown correlations with brain oscillations. The authors examine gamma oscillations in the contralateral auditory cortex. They relate oscillation strength to tinnitus intensity. Their work supports brain rhythm measures as objective markers for a condition usually judged only by patient report.
plos-pone-0007496:
Franck Chatelain and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on potassium channels carried by viruses. These tiny channels let potassium ions pass through membranes. Blockers such as barium and the drug amantadine can plug them. Understanding exactly where blockers act remains a goal for drug design. The team used genetic selection to breed channel versions that resist the blockers.

The resistant channels pointed to one key site in the channel's selectivity filter. That spot decides how strongly barium and amantadine can block the pore. Pinpointing it clarifies the basic mechanics of how these channels work. It also shows where future channel-blocking drugs might grip. The study turns resistant mutants into a map of the channel's most important real estate.
plos-pone-0007596:
Takashi Miyamoto and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how nitric oxide causes pain. Nitric oxide is a gas the body makes, and it can trigger acute pain in people. It also deepens pain after inflammation and injury in animals. Evidence pointed to actions both in the spinal cord and in peripheral nerves. The team tested which sensors carry the peripheral signal in mice.

Two channels on sensory neurons, TRPV1 and TRPA1, mediate the pain nitric oxide causes in the periphery. Those channels are already known as detectors of heat, irritants, and inflammation. Placing them downstream of nitric oxide completes a chain from gas to pain. Blocking them could yield painkillers aimed at the gas's local effects. The study gives pain research defined targets in the body's outer wiring.
plos-pone-0007696:
Valentina Dal Secco and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how immune cells talk in mouse lymph nodes. Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, calm immune responses and shape how new responses begin. Dendritic cells are the messengers that present targets to T cells.

The authors found that dendritic cells adjust their output of chemokines, the signals that call other immune cells in. The adjustment depends on how many Tregs are present. In effect, Tregs can tune the traffic of cells through a lymph node, not just switch responses off.
plos-pone-0007796:
Esther-Maria Antao and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It hunts genes that a poultry pathogen needs to start infection. Avian pathogenic E. coli causes whole-body infections in chickens. The losses to the poultry industry worldwide are large.

The team used signature-tagged mutagenesis in a chicken infection model. Each mutant bacterium carries a tag, so failures can be traced to single genes. The screen found a new fimbrial adhesin, a hair-like grip protein. Adhesins let bacteria latch onto host tissue, the first step of disease. A new grip protein is a candidate target for vaccines or drugs.
plos-pone-0007896:
Cedric Pennetier and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a new mix of chemicals for malaria bed nets. Bed nets are treated to repel or kill the mosquitoes that spread malaria. Resistance to pyrethroid insecticides had become widespread in the main vector, Anopheles gambiae.

The mix pairs a repellent with an organophosphate insecticide. The authors tested it against natural, free-flying mosquitoes. They measured both killing power and the mosquitoes' behavior. A repellent plus a different poison can work in synergy. Such combinations may rescue bed nets where pyrethroids now fail.
plos-pone-0007996:
Michael Stauber and colleagues watched two clock genes at work in mouse embryos for PLOS ONE in 2009. Vertebrate bodies are built in segments, laid down by a ticking system called the segmentation clock. Two of its gears are Lunatic fringe and Hes7, which pulse on and off in growing tissue.

The pair did not need the same support along the body. What keeps one gene pulsing near the head end differs from what keeps the other going near the tail. That split shows the clock adapts as the body lengthens, a detail that helps explain how segments form evenly from neck to tail.
plos-pone-0008096:
Vernon Lee and colleagues counted half a century of flu deaths in Singapore for PLOS ONE in 2009. Tropical lands do not see flu in neat winter waves, and their long-term burden was poorly counted. The team used excess deaths, deaths above the normal rate, from 1950 to 2000.

Even without winters, flu claimed a steady toll in the tropic city. Deaths spiked in known pandemic years and rose in lesser waves between them. The half-century record gives tropical health teams the hard base they lacked for vaccine planning and hospital readiness.
plos-pone-0008196:
Jennifer MacKellar, Samuel W. Cushman, and Vipul Periwal studied fat tissue growth in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Fat tissue grows in two ways: more cells, or larger cells. A class of diabetes drugs called thiazolidinediones affects fat tissue shape. These drugs make the body more sensitive to insulin. The team tested their effects in Zucker fatty rats.

The rats are a standard model of obesity. The authors compared how the drugs influenced cell growth and the recruitment of new fat cells. The difference between growth modes matters for metabolic health. Their findings help explain how these drugs reshape fat tissue.
plos-pone-0008296:
Donald C. Franklin and Peter I. Whelan tracked tropical mosquitoes in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Annual biological rhythms are often drawn as predictable cycles. Quantitative proof that cycles repeat steadily across years is rare. In the monsoon tropics, intense seasonal rainfall drives population swings. Short-lived animals such as mosquitoes respond strongly to that rhythm.

The authors measured mosquito assemblages across the year. The communities demonstrated textbook annual cycles in their data. Confirming such cycles helps predict when mosquitoes peak. That timing matters for controlling the diseases mosquitoes carry in tropical regions.
plos-pone-0008396:
Diederik van de Wetering and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about the fight with Salmonella germs. These germs live inside our own cells, where drugs and guards reach them with more work. A chain of signals, named the type-1 path, is key to win such fights. Germ sensors on white blood cells start the chain when they spot a germ. The team traced the steps that lead to a key signal, IL-12.

Two early signals from the germs let white cells make IL-12. They did so by first waking a third signal in a set of killer-like cells. Three cell types thus work in a row to raise the alarm. The chain is a base for shots aimed at germs that hide in cells.
plos-pone-0008496:
James Krycer and co-authors compare cholesterol control in prostate cancer cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Interest has grown in links between cholesterol and prostate cancer. Two cell lines, LNCaP and PC-3, are widely used models. Past reports said prostate cancer cells may lack normal feedback control of cholesterol. That control runs through a factor that senses sterol levels. The team test both lines under the same conditions.

They measure how each line keeps cholesterol in balance. Differences between lines matter for drawing general conclusions. A line that lacks feedback will respond unlike one that retains it. The study helps labs choose models and read results with care.
plos-pone-0008596:
Kohei Yamada and co-authors link a protein to abnormal brain wiring in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A peptide called PACAP is involved in multiple brain functions. Mice lacking PACAP show abnormal behavior. To find the cause, the team sought genes altered in a brain region of those mice. That region is the dentate gyrus, part of the hippocampus. One altered gene was Stathmin1, which regulates cell skeleton dynamics. They increase Stathmin1 expression in the dentate gyrus of normal mice.

Increased Stathmin1 causes abnormal axonal arborizations there. Axons branch in excessive or misdirected patterns. Such wiring flaws may underlie the abnormal behavior of PACAP-deficient mice. The work connects a peptide, a gene, and brain circuit formation.
plos-pone-0008696:
Vincenzo Penteriani, María del Mar Delgado, and Letizia Campioni listened to owls under different moons. Their short study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Moonlight changes how well animals can see each other at night. Many creatures adjust their calls and displays to the light available. Owls rely on both voice and visible signals when they interact.

The team tracked owl calling across the lunar cycle. Brighter nights brought more calling, making the birds chattier. Good light may help an owl judge a rival it can also see. The result ties a basic sky rhythm to nightly animal talk.
plos-pone-0008796:
María Sánchez, James Lloyd-Smith, and Wayne Getz reviewed how the world watches two linked epidemics. Their article appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis and HIV feed each other in many regions. HIV weakens defenses that normally hold TB in check. Tracking either disease alone misses the coupled dynamics. The WHO and partner agencies run joint surveillance efforts.

The authors assessed those efforts and the models behind them. Mathematical models can flag where the pair will surge next. Better joint monitoring means resources reach co-epidemic hotspots sooner. The review argues surveillance should treat TB and HIV as one problem.
plos-pone-0008896:
Antoine Bénard, Patrick Mercié, Ahmadou Alioum, and colleagues measured the payoff when HIV patients quit smoking. Their cohort study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bacterial pneumonia remains a major threat to people with HIV. Modern combination therapy has not removed that risk. Many patients also smoke, adding lung damage. The benefit of quitting, in this group, had never been quantified. The Aquitaine cohort in France followed patients from 2000 to 2007.

Patients who stopped smoking showed a clear drop in pneumonia risk. The size of the benefit gives clinics a hard number to cite. Cessation programs earn a stronger place in HIV care. Quitting becomes a medical treatment, not just advice.
plos-pone-0008996:
Wyatt Potter and co-authors connected the cell's fuel gauge to how brain circuits strengthen, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gauge is AMPK, an enzyme that senses low energy in cells. Long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of nerve connections, underpins learning and memory. The same process may also help seizures harden into epilepsy.

The team tested how AMPK activity affects this strengthening in neurons. Keeping potentiation going requires new RNA and protein, which cost energy. The fuel sensor helps decide whether the cell can afford that cost. The link ties memory research to metabolism, with epilepsy as a shared concern.
plos-pone-0009096:
Nino Künzli and co-authors followed adults' neck arteries to see whether dirty air thickens them, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Atherosclerosis is the slow clogging of arteries behind heart attacks and strokes. Earlier snapshot studies tied air pollution to thicker artery walls. A snapshot cannot show the disease actually progressing, though.

The team measured the carotid artery wall over time in adults. Wall thickness is a standard marker of subclinical atherosclerosis. People breathing worse outdoor air showed faster thickening. Following progression, not just presence, strengthens the case against polluted air.
plos-pone-0009196:
Chakrit Sawasdidoln and colleagues published this study of a dangerous bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. The germ, Burkholderia pseudomallei, causes a disease called melioidosis. That illness is known for coming back after treatment seems to work. The germ can also grow as a biofilm, a slimy layer of cells stuck together.

The team suspected that germs hiding in biofilms survive drugs that kill loose cells. They grew the germ under conditions that push it to form biofilms. Growth in those conditions greatly raised its resistance to drugs. That result supports the biofilm explanation for why this disease so often returns.
plos-pone-0009296:
Leandro Vendruscolo and co-authors published this rat behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sugar intake has climbed sharply in recent decades, most steeply among teenagers. The known harms include obesity and diabetes. What heavy sugar use does to the young brain was far less clear.

The team fed adolescent rats excess sugar, then tested them as adults. The early diet selectively changed motivation and reward function later in life. Other behaviors were left largely alone. The result suggests the teenage years are a sensitive window when diet can retune how the brain values rewards.
plos-pone-0009396:
Manisha Kulkarni, Rachelle Desrochers, and Jeremy Kerr published this malaria mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In Africa, malaria risk can change sharply within a few kilometers. The difference tracks where vector mosquitoes find their habitat. Control teams with limited supplies need to know exactly where risk concentrates.

The authors built high resolution niche models of malaria vectors in northern Tanzania. The models predict mosquito habitat from environmental data. Sharper maps could let managers send nets and spraying to the true hotspots. The study asks whether such models add a real new capacity to predict malaria risk.
plos-pone-0009496:
Claudia Filippone and co-authors grew red blood cell precursors from plain blood samples in PLOS ONE in 2010. These early cells are normally drawn from bone marrow after a drug pushes them into the blood. That step is hard on donors. The team asked whether the cells could be grown from a normal blood draw, with no push and no pre sorting.

The grown cells matched the traits and function of cells won the usual way. So a simple draw can supply material for blood research. It also helps work on parvovirus B19, a virus that infects just these cells. Easier access should speed both kinds of study.
plos-pone-0009596:
Timothy Joyner and co-authors modeled anthrax risk in Kazakhstan in PLOS ONE in 2010. Anthrax spores can persist in soil for decades. Livestock, wildlife, and people can all catch the disease. Central Asia's steppe holds many old outbreak sites. The team modeled where the germ could thrive now. They then ran the model under several climate change scenarios.

Maps from the model show how suitable ground may shift as the climate warms. Some areas could grow more favorable to the germ, and others less. Health and farm officials can use such maps to focus watching and vaccination. Planning ahead beats reacting after spores wake.
plos-pone-0009696:
Saving newborns in rural Bangladesh depends heavily on care that reaches mothers at home. Gary Darmstadt and colleagues tested whether a package of community-based care could change that. Their trial covered villages in Mirzapur and was evaluated in PLOS ONE in 2010. Community workers delivered care and guidance to mothers before and after birth.

Villages were assigned by cluster, so whole areas got the package or standard care. The evaluation checked whether the program actually reached mothers and babies as planned. Twelve unions took part in the trial. Results from trials like this guide how poor regions scale up newborn care.
plos-pone-0009896:
Lung germs force the immune system to balance attack and restraint. Urvashi Bhan and colleagues studied two bacterial sensors that cooperate during lung infection in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The sensors are TLR4 and TLR9, proteins that detect bacterial parts. Working together, they controlled levels of two signal proteins, interleukin 23 and interleukin 17. Gram negative names a major class of bacteria based on their cell walls. Those signals help recruit infection-fighting cells in Gram negative bacterial pneumonia. Two sensors working as a team beat lone alarms.
plos-pone-0009996:
Cancer cells can be pushed to die in more than one way at once. Chew Hooi Wong and colleagues triggered two death programs together in cancer cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The two programs were non-canonical autophagy and apoptosis, self-eating and orderly suicide. Non-canonical means the self-eating ran off the usual route. Both were switched on by ROS-dependent activation of ERK and JNK pathways. ROS are reactive oxygen species, damaging molecules cells must control. Hitting two programs at once could corner cells that dodge either alone.
plos-pone-0010096:
The authors were Martin Paulus, Alan Simmons, Summer Fitzpatrick, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study scanned brains of elite warfighters viewing angry faces. Little was known about how top performers process threat in extreme settings. Angry faces are a basic social threat signal, well suited to brain imaging tests.

Elite fighters showed different brain activation from comparison subjects in emotion-related areas. The authors read that pattern as evidence of sharper threat detection. Understanding such differences may inform training and support for people working under extreme danger. The comparison used brain imaging during a simple face task.
plos-pone-0010196:
The authors were Jian Fu, Fang Jin, Jirong Zhang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a possible tumor suppressor in mouse skin. The protein, VILIP-1, senses calcium inside cells and belongs to a neuronal sensor family. In carcinoma cells it had slowed growth and movement, suggesting it acts against tumors in cultured cancer cells.

The team made mice that produce extra VILIP-1 in skin tissue. In those mice, skin keratinocyte growth slowed and tumor development fell. Confirming a lab effect in living animals strengthens the case for VILIP-1 in skin cancer prevention research.
plos-pone-0010296:
The authors were Ki Kang, Pan Wang, Noriko Yamabe, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested a fish oil fat against breast cancer cells. The fat, docosahexaenoic acid or DHA, is a well known omega-3 fatty acid. The team focused on how DHA kills cancer cells in the MCF-7 line. It works through oxidative stress and programmed cell death, called apoptosis.

DHA induced apoptosis in dishes and in living tumor models. It acted through reactive oxygen species and activation of an enzyme, caspase 8. The work supports omega-3 fats as candidate aids in cancer treatment research.
plos-pone-0010396:
Ilana Witten, Phyllis Knudsen and Eric Knudsen studied how barn owls rank sound cues in PLOS ONE in 2010. Owls pinpoint prey in darkness by hearing alone. They blend sound details across many pitches to judge where a sound comes from. The team played owls sounds whose parts seemed to come from different places. High and low pitch bands were split between locations.

Faced with conflicting cues, the owls trusted some bands over others. That pecking order among frequencies is the study's main point. It shows the owl brain weighs evidence rather than averaging blindly. Such weighting rules help engineers build better sound-locating machines. They also explain how owls stay accurate when noises mix. Hearing, for an owl, is a ranked vote among cues.
plos-pone-0010496:
Adam Bachstetter and co-workers reported that spirulina, a blue-green algae supplement, supports brain stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adult brains keep small stem cell zones that make new neurons. Inflammation strongly suppresses those cells' growth. The team had earlier shown spirulina's promise in this setting. Here they tested it against inflammation caused by a bacterial toxin, LPS, in rats.

Spirulina promoted stem cell formation and blunted the toxin's suppressive effect. A food-derived product with such effects invites interest in brain repair diets. Rat results are early and need much checking before human claims. Still, the link between a common supplement and neurogenesis is striking. The study opens a nutritional angle on brain stem cell support.
plos-pone-0010596:
Ning Li and colleagues studied how brain cells grow their branching arms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pyramidal neurons in the cortex collect signals through tree-like branches called dendrites. A gene switch called Cux1 marks many of these neurons in the upper cortex layers.

The team altered Cux1 in mouse brains and watched the branches change. Without normal Cux1 function, dendrites grew in simpler, stunted shapes. Extra Cux1 produced richer branching. Branch shape decides which signals a neuron can receive, so a single switch that sculpts branches helps explain how cortical circuits get wired.
plos-pone-0010696:
Han Tun and colleagues profiled the most common kidney cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma grows from the kidney's filtering tubes. Early tumors look alike under the microscope, yet patients fare very differently.

The team compared gene activity in early tumors with matched healthy kidney tissue. A pathway signature separated tumor from normal with high accuracy. Tumors also carried marks of how mature their cells were. Signatures like this could sort patients by risk at diagnosis. Better sorting means closer watching for some and lighter treatment for others.
plos-pone-0010796:
David Gross, Erik Snapp, and David Silver studied how cells build fat droplets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells store energy as triglyceride fat inside droplets that bud from an inner membrane system. Proteins called FIT, for fat storage-inducing transmembrane, are needed for those droplets to form. FIT2 is the form found across most animals.

The team mapped which parts of FIT2 sit where in the membrane. Its shape and placement showed how it might bend the membrane to start a droplet. Faulty fat storage underlies metabolic diseases and fatty liver. A structural map of the droplet-making machinery gives drug and basic research a firmer footing.
plos-pone-0010896:
Patrick Gérardin, Rachid El Amrani, Béatrice Cyrille and co-authors published this pregnancy and flu study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pregnant women were flagged as a high-risk group during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, with reports of severe breathing problems and intensive care stays. The team measured how the pandemic virus actually behaved in pregnancy on the island of La Réunion.

Over the twelve-week pandemic wave, about three hundred pregnant women came to maternity departments with flu-like illness, and lab tests sorted true pandemic flu from other causes. Women with the pandemic strain ran slightly higher fevers, but the overall clinical burden stayed low. Gérardin and colleagues offer a calming counterpoint to alarming reports from elsewhere, while showing why local data matter when judging risk in pregnancy.
plos-pone-0010996:
Robert Hoehndorf, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo, Michael Dannemann and co-authors published this computational biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Biology increasingly stores knowledge as directed acyclic graphs, tree-like structures such as gene function and anatomy vocabularies. Valuable links hide between separate graphs, but finding them by hand is impractical, so the authors built statistical tests for the job.

Their tests weigh the shape of both graphs and how specific and relevant each proposed link is, rather than just counting matches. Applied to a large biomedical case linking several ontologies, the tests recovered relations that experts judged biologically meaningful, confirmed by both manual and automatic checks. Hoehndorf and colleagues give data curators a principled way to stitch knowledge graphs together, making existing annotation data far more useful.
