plos-pone-0011096:
Parker, Melathopoulos, White and colleagues wrote about honey bees in PLOS ONE in 2010. They compared bee groups living in different places. Bees face local weather, food plants and seasons that vary a lot, and the team asked how groups adjust to those local terms.

The study mapped ways bee groups fit their home conditions. Such local fitting helps explain why bees from one place may do poorly when moved elsewhere. The results matter for beekeepers who move hives and for people protecting wild bees. Knowing local strengths could help bees cope as climates shift.
plos-pone-0011196:
Drewe, Tomlinson, Walker and colleagues compared badger TB tests in PLOS ONE in 2010. Badgers can carry tuberculosis that also affects cattle, but testing live badgers is tricky. The team measured how accurate three available tests are and how they are best combined in practice.

Their guidance helps field teams choose tests for different aims, such as screening or confirming cases. Better testing sharpens control of cattle TB, a costly farm problem in Britain. It also reduces needless culling by sorting infected from healthy animals more fairly. The work links lab accuracy to real wildlife management choices.
plos-pone-0011296:
Cree, Rioux, McCauley and colleagues searched MS risk genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Multiple sclerosis risk was already tied to one famous immune gene variant. The team asked whether another locus in the same immune gene complex adds risk on its own, separate from that known variant.

They found a class I locus that contributes to susceptibility independently. Added genetic risk refines prediction of who is most likely to develop the disease. It also hints that more than one immune pathway feeds into MS. Neurogenetics gains a firmer map for tracing how the immune system turns against the brain's insulation.
plos-pone-0011396:
Chenguang Wang and co-authors built a math model in 2010 for a subtle form of inheritance called imprinting. An imprinted gene behaves differently depending on whether it came from the mother or the father. That parent-of-origin effect can shape traits and disease risk, and it can vary across generations in ways simple models ignore.

Their model allows the imprinting effect itself to change as genes pass down a family, instead of treating it as fixed. That flexibility fits real pedigrees better, where a trait may strengthen or fade across generations for reasons older models cannot capture. Geneticists studying complex traits gain a tool that matches the biology more closely. Better models mean fairer tests when researchers ask whether imprinting helps explain conditions that run unevenly through families.
plos-pone-0011496:
Parveen Sharma and co-authors asked in 2010 what address label keeps a heart protein parked in the right compartment. Phospholamban controls the heart's calcium pump and must stay in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's inner membrane network, to do its job. At one end of the protein sits a pair of arginines, a motif known to act as a stay-here tag for other proteins.

The team tested whether that double-arginine tag is the anchor holding phospholamban in place. Precise questions of this kind matter because a protein in the wrong compartment is as useless as a missing one, and heart calcium control depends on placement. If the tag is a general retention signal, the same logic may keep many membrane proteins home. The study adds a small but firm brick to the map of how cells sort their own machinery.
plos-pone-0011596:
Ciro Cattuto and colleagues recorded face-to-face contacts with wearable sensors, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Knowing who meets whom, and for how long, is key to predicting how infections and ideas spread. Until recently, such data came mostly from surveys and memory, which miss much of daily contact.

The team gave people small RFID tags that log close encounters with fine time detail. The records reveal bursty, uneven contact patterns that simple averages hide. Modellers can now build spread forecasts on measured behaviour rather than guesses, which should improve plans for outbreaks and other social processes.
plos-pone-0011696:
Hongmei Zhang and co-authors compared motor neurons from a mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this disease, motor neurons sicken and die, weakening muscles. The team recorded the electrical behaviour of motor neurons two ways: grown in dishes from embryos, and in slices of spinal cord closer to real life.

Comparing the two preparations showed how development in a dish differs from development in the body. Dish-grown neurons told only part of the story. The gap warns researchers that findings from cultured neurons need checking in intact tissue before guiding treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0011796:
Stefan Wuchty, Geoffrey Siwo and Michael Ferdig mapped how viruses hijack human proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Maps of links inside cells are now quite full, but large maps of host and germ protein links lagged behind. Such maps can show how disease works and give a base for new drugs.

The authors gathered virus-targeted human proteins into one big network and studied its layout. The map exposes the cell machinery that many viruses home in on. Shared targets draw drug hunters, since a drug that blocks one shared part might slow several viruses at once.
plos-pone-0011896:
Jiong Li and colleagues used a large population cohort in 2010 to ask whether severe stress during pregnancy leaves a mark on the child. The stress they studied was bereavement, the death of a close family member while a mother was pregnant. Earlier work had suggested prenatal stress might raise the risk of obesity later in life.

Following the children into their school years, the team compared rates of overweight between those exposed to bereavement before birth and those who were not. A link between a mother's grief and her child's weight would show how early the roots of weight problems can reach. It would also argue for supporting pregnant women through loss as a health measure, not only a kindness.
plos-pone-0011996:
Barny Cox, James Briscoe, and Fausto Ulloa showed in 2010 that a small protein tag fine-tunes the Hedgehog signaling pathway. Hedgehog signals guide development and keep adult tissues in order, acting through the Gli family of transcription factors. The pathway raises Gli activity in part by controlling the proteins' state.

The team found that SUMOylation, the attachment of a small SUMO tag by the enzyme Pias1, regulates Gli activity. Tagging systems like this act as dimmers rather than switches, adjusting output up or down. Dimmer controls are attractive drug targets because they promise partial correction of a pathway that, fully blocked or fully open, causes severe problems.
plos-pone-0012096:
Svetlana Zykova, Anders Tveita, and Ole Petter Rekvig wrote for PLOS ONE in 2010 about kidney damage in lupus. In this form of the disease, clumps of cell material and immune proteins settle in the kidney's filters and harm them. The team's earlier work had linked worsening damage to the loss of an enzyme in the kidney that normally breaks down stray cell material.

Here they show that enzyme's activity and levels are shut down as the kidney disease turns severe, in both mice and human cases. When the cleanup enzyme fades, harmful clumps can build up unchecked. The finding points to a clear step in how mild lupus kidney disease becomes dangerous, and to a possible target for future treatment.
plos-pone-0012196:
Zhong-Dong Shi, Giya Abraham, and John Tarbell studied how fluid flow reshapes blood vessel wall cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When a vessel is injured, its muscle cells and repair cells suddenly face changed flow, from blood inside or fluid leaking through the wall. Flow can switch the genes these cells use, changing whether they stay calm or turn into scar-like builders.

The team compared flat and three-dimensional cell cultures and traced the sensing route from a sugar-coated surface sensor to a growth signal inside. Knowing which sensor carries flow's message helps explain how vessels heal badly, thickening after surgery or stenting. It also gives tissue engineers rules for growing vessels that behave like real ones.
plos-pone-0012296:
Christine Cox, Kristin Gotimer, Amy Roy, and co-authors asked whether the resting brain predicts risky behavior, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Studies of risky decision-making usually scan people while they gamble in the laboratory, and they point to a broad network of regions involved. This team instead looked at brain activity at rest, with no task at all, and related it to how risk-prone each person is.

If the idle brain's wiring already carries a signature of risk taking, then dangerous tendencies might be read without staging risky choices. That would help research on addiction and reckless behavior find its subjects and its mechanisms faster. It also hints that personality lives in the brain's default organization, not only in its responses.
plos-pone-0012396:
Sara Hardell, Hanna Tilander, Gretchen Welfinger-Smith and colleagues measured long-lived pollutants in fish from Alaska's Aleutian Islands in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. PCBs and certain pesticides persist for decades, travel far on wind and water, and build up in food webs. Remote island fish show how far these chemicals reach, and local people eat those fish.

The team tested fish for PCBs and three organochlorine pesticides and reported the levels they found. Even in this remote chain, the pollutants were present. Data like these set a baseline for tracking cleanup progress and guide health advice for communities that depend on local seafood for food and culture.
plos-pone-0012496:
Adam Handel, Alexander Williamson, Giulio Disanto and colleagues updated the combined evidence linking mono to multiple sclerosis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE meta-analysis. MS seems to arise when genes and environment combine, and infection with Epstein-Barr virus is a near-universal step in patients' histories. Having infectious mononucleosis, the illness EBV often causes, may mark especially risky infection.

Pooling past studies, the authors estimated how much mono raises later MS risk. Their updated figure strengthens the case that EBV is a real part of the causal chain, not a bystander. That strengthens efforts toward an EBV vaccine as a possible MS prevention strategy.
plos-pone-0012596:
Blaveri and co-authors turned to a bred strain of rat that shows signs much like human depression. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper uses the Flinders rat line, an animal model known for matching many traits of the human illness. The team measured gene activity across the brain of these rats on a genome-wide scale.

By comparing the pattern with normal rats, they picked out molecular pathways linked to the sad, withdrawn behaviour. Pathways found this way give drug researchers new places to look for causes and treatments. The work treats depression as a whole-brain gene problem, not just a chemical shortage.
plos-pone-0012696:
Hagopian, Weber, Hwee and co-authors examined energy machinery in mice bred to make their own omega-3 fats. These fat-1 mice carry extra unsaturated fats, which can be damaged by oxygen yet may also protect health. Their 2010 study measured complex I, a key engine of the cell's energy chain, in the altered mice.

Hydrogen peroxide output from complex I was lower, and several energy chain enzymes changed activity. The pattern suggests omega-3 fats reshape, rather than simply harm, cell energy systems. That nuance matters for judging fish oil style diets.
plos-pone-0012796:
Song, Dean and Knothe Tate mapped the flow of fluid around seeded stem cells at a tiny scale. Stem cells answer mechanical cues from their surroundings, yet tools to deliver exact cues while watching single cells were missing. Their 2010 study built a way to seed cells and chart flow fields around them in place and time.

The maps cover features smaller than one cell, where the cell actually feels force. Precise force maps let engineers design scaffolds that push stem cells toward bone, cartilage or other fates. That control is central to tissue engineering.
plos-pone-0331996:
Lauren Shingler, Edward D Siew, and co-authors asked whether urine tests taken years before heart bypass surgery could warn of later kidney injury. About one in five bypass patients develops sudden kidney damage after the operation. Their 2026 study used a large national cohort of older American adults and focused on those who later had bypass surgery.

Four urine markers of kidney tubule health had been measured about five years before surgery. Higher levels of one marker tied to tubule strain meant higher odds of kidney injury, while higher levels of two protective markers meant lower odds. A fourth marker showed no link. The results hint that quiet kidney weakness, visible years ahead, shapes risk after major surgery.
plos-pone-0335296:
Andrew M. Kittle and Anjali C. Watson published a study in PLOS ONE on leopards living alongside dense human settlement in Sri Lanka's tea-growing Central Highlands, outside any protected park. The island's apex predator shares this farmed landscape with many people and dogs, and coexistence must be negotiated daily. Camera traps measured density and space use, and activity curves revealed when the cats move.

Leopard density was a little lower than in the famous national parks but not significantly, a sign the farmed landscape suits them well. Leopards did not simply avoid people: areas with middling human and dog presence were used most, Males settled at middling distances from settlements. Females favored places rich in natural prey for raising cubs. The clearest adaptation was timing: these leopards were less active by day and more at dusk than park leopards, partitioning the day from diurnal humans. Same fields, different hours.
plos-pone-0337296:
Xinze Cui led a team of ten authors on this 2026 study of balance in elite freestyle aerial skiers, whose landings demand superb postural control. Force plates record the body's sway point, but standard measures miss subtle differences among top athletes. The team combined time-frequency images of sway with statistical features in a two-stream deep learning model, tested on twenty-five skiers standing quietly.

The model sorted athletes into high, medium, and low stability groups with roughly ninety-five percent accuracy. Cui offers the tool for pinpointing balance weaknesses that targeted training could fix.
plos-pone-0341096:
Sufyan and colleagues built a two-stage AI system for lung spots on chest scans in a 2026 study. Finding small lung growths early saves lives, but hospitals cannot always share scans freely for training. Their system first outlines a spot using shape-aware attention, then judges whether it looks dangerous, all while data stays split across sites.

Privacy-preserving training lets hospitals cooperate without pooling patient scans. A built-in uncertainty check flags doubtful calls for human review. Tests spanned three public scan collections. The authors present the design as a fit for connected hospital devices, where computing power is limited and privacy rules are strict.
plos-pone-0343196:
Lu Chen led a team of six authors on this 2026 power engineering paper about restoring electricity after faults in local distribution networks. Solar panels, batteries, and other small energy sources add flexibility but also unpredictability. Their framework pairs an expert-guided learning system with virtual power plants, which coordinate those small sources, and maps the grid as a graph so switching choices respect real connections.

On a real-world network simulation, the method restored service faster, recovered more load, and caused fewer voltage violations than standard learning approaches, especially when small energy sources were plentiful.
plos-pone-0343896:
Meg Walker and seven colleagues examine animal bones from two flooded caves near Mount Gambier in South Australia to learn how such deposits form, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Underwater caves preserve remarkable fossils, but scientists understand poorly how bones change down there. The team dated forty-one bones from domestic animals and compared specimens buried underwater with those in dry cave passages.

Wet-buried bones were generally better preserved and more complete, though some carried black staining, algae attack, and distinctive round etch marks. Microscopic tunnels inside the bone differed too: light-loving microbes tunnelled the submerged bones, land microbes the dry ones. The signatures give archaeologists a way to read a bone's burial history from the bone itself.
plos-pone-0346096:
Yanran Chen and colleagues track how sentence structure changed in English and German over one hundred sixty years of parliamentary debates, in this 2026 PLOS ONE linguistics paper. Earlier studies leaned on a single automated parser and a single measure, word distance, leaving room for the tool itself to fake a trend.

The team built fifteen syntax measures capturing tree shape as well as word order, and ran six different parsers, old and new, to cross-check. Parsers often disagreed about trends, confirming the risk, while the richer measures caught subtler shared patterns of change in both languages. The lesson for digital humanities is methodological: language history written by one algorithm needs a second opinion.
plos-pone-0346396:
Mengjiao Yin and Yingying Xia analyse in 2026 how Chinese workers talk about burnout on social media, and which posts draw a crowd. Texts came from five major platforms and were cleaned to a set of just over a thousand posts. Hand coding in stages found the main themes, while two language tools plus human checks scored the feeling in each post.

Coding produced a layered set of themes about work pressure, fairness, and blame shifting from the person to the system. Feeling in a post predicted likes in their models, showing some emotional styles win far more engagement. The authors argue burnout talk online now forms a shared, critical public conversation.
plos-pone-0346496:
Alessandro Miani and colleagues ask whether conspiracy-minded people write like conspiracists. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Three hundred eighty-five people took part across two studies. Each watched the thriller Leave the World Behind. Each then wrote an essay on what the film meant. A language model scored the essays for conspiratorial plots.

The team's registered guess failed. A person's conspiracy mindset did not predict the essay's story line. The link showed up in word choice instead. Strong believers used more conspiracy-flavored words. They also used fancier words and longer, more tangled sentences. The authors think the mindset leaks into language first. Full plots may come later, or mainly online.
plos-pone-0346696:
Yixuan Zeng, Jing Kang, and Chua Yan Piaw survey two hundred seven Chinese university students about learning with generative AI, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Chatbots and text generators are reshaping study habits, and the team modeled how students explore with these tools, exploit them for known tasks, and adapt their roles around them.

Two inner qualities drove the behavior most: how well students adjusted their own role in the partnership, and their confidence in their abilities. Support from the university and a good fit between tool and task also mattered. The findings suggest institutions teach students to direct AI deliberately, rather than simply granting access and hoping for gains.
plos-pone-0346796:
Margaret N. Mwangi and co-workers study why smallholder farmers in Kenya rarely plant quality potato seed. Good seed lifts yields and diets, yet most farmers save their own tubers. Their 2026 study surveys more than five hundred households and sorts what drives seed buying, how much farmers use, and whether food security improves for those who adopt.

Fewer than half the farmers used quality seed. Scarcity, distance, and price were the main blocks, while schooling, income, credit, and farmer groups pushed adoption up. Households using quality seed ate more varied diets, with more animal foods, fruits, and vegetables. The authors recommend growing certified seed locally so it reaches villages cheaper.
plos-pone-0346996:
Xiaobo Zhang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 plant disease report from southern China. A medicinal begonia grown in Guizhou and Hunan provinces suffered heavy leaf spot outbreaks in 2024, with most plants hit and a fifth of the leaf harvest lost. The team isolated the fungus from sick leaves, identified it by shape and several genes, and proved it caused the disease by infecting healthy seedlings.

The culprit was Corynespora cassiicola, never before reported on this host in China. Zhang's identification gives growers a firm diagnosis to build control measures around.
plos-pone-0347096:
David Sabin-Miller, Mary C. McGrath, and Marisa C. Eisenberg put the familiar left-to-right political spectrum under a microscope. They compared several fine-grained ways of measuring Americans' ideology: how people label themselves, how their policy views add up, and how observers place individual political statements on the spectrum. The 2026 study asks whether this one-dimensional picture deserves its central place.

Self-labels and policy-based scores agreed strongly, though policy scores painted people as somewhat more centrist and liberal. Outside judges, remarkably, placed statements in much the same spots as each other, even for clashing ideas and whatever the speaker's identity. The authors argue the shared one-dimensional map is a real feature of public thinking.
plos-pone-0347296:
Maham Shahzadi and colleagues examine how future quantum computers could break the featherweight security protocols that let tiny RFID tags authenticate themselves. These protocols guard supply chains and access cards on minimal hardware, and quantum search algorithms can, in principle, slash the effort needed to crack them. Their 2026 analysis works through attacks on three published ultra-lightweight schemes.

The team demonstrates full-disclosure attacks, extracting the secrets that should stay hidden, on all three protocols, assuming a powerful quantum machine that does not yet exist. They close with design principles for minimalist ciphers that could resist such attacks. The paper is an early warning for post-quantum security in the smallest devices.
plos-pone-0347996:
Mingming Han and Yiwei Yang build explainable computer models of where landslides strike in China's Shaanxi province. The loess hills of the north and the mountains of the south fail in different ways. Their 2026 study trains four learning models on fifteen factors covering land shape, rock, plants, and human activity, then uses an explanation method to show which factors drive each forecast.

One model won in both regions. In the north, risk formed scattered patches driven by people and water together. In the south, risk ran in bands ruled by height and rock type. Clear thresholds for slope, height, and crowding emerged. Prevention can now be tuned by region instead of using one rule for the whole province.
plos-pone-0348096:
Xin Chen and colleagues mined a month of Weibo posts to see how China's public felt about parcel delivery services right after pandemic controls were lifted. Delivery is a daily lifeline in China, and the December twenty twenty-two reopening strained it with sick couriers and shopping festivals. The team weighted post popularity, traced topics over time, and scored the mood of posts by ordinary and official accounts.

Public feeling leaned negative, and it swung with pressure events like the mid-December shopping festival, infection peaks, and the New Year holiday. Six themes recurred: package safety and after-sales service stayed constant concerns, while courier rights and government response rose as newer ones. For delivery firms and regulators, the timeline shows service failures quickly become public mood, and worker welfare is now part of that story.
plos-pone-0348196:
Izabela Olszak and Aleksandra Borowicz look for teaching methods that help deaf and hard-of-hearing children speak a foreign language. These learners face distinct hurdles in hearing, language, and communication, so standard lessons often fit poorly. Their 2026 study works with fifty-five primary school pupils and draws on classroom watching, pupil surveys, and talks with teachers and specialists.

Lessons rich in pictures and other visual support worked best for building speech. Teaching tuned to each child's pace and needs also helped, as did learning together in groups. Because views came from pupils, teachers, and experts alike, the advice rests on more than one angle. Schools gain practical guidance for language classes that include every learner.
plos-pone-0348496:
Nathan Phillips, Robert Ackley, and Andee Krasner measured methane gas inside nearly two hundred homes in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, comparing houses with natural gas service to the twenty without. Methane, the main ingredient of natural gas, leaks at every stage of the supply chain, but indoor levels had never been surveyed this way. Sensitive instruments read air in basements and on each floor, plus outdoor air for comparison.

Homes with gas service consistently held more methane indoors than outdoors, in ninety-three percent of cases exceeding the typical gas-free home, and follow-up checks found equipment leaks in most of a subset. Gas-free homes matched outdoor air. The findings add an indoor chapter to the methane story, with implications for both climate accounting and household air quality.
plos-pone-0348596:
Xiaobo Yang tackles a bottleneck in medical artificial intelligence: expert labelling of scans is scarce and expensive. His semi-supervised system, ADGNET, learns Alzheimer's diagnosis from brain MRI images using few labels, by training two tasks at once. One branch rebuilds images to learn their structure without supervision; the other classifies disease, sharing what the first discovers.

Tested on two public datasets, one of thousands of flat images and one of hundreds of three-dimensional scans, the system beat leading rivals by several points across six measures. Heat maps showed it attending to the hippocampus and temporal lobes, regions Alzheimer's hits early. Yang presents it as a route to capable models on small labelled collections.
plos-pone-0348696:
Kganetso Sekome and co-workers test whether a lifestyle program for high blood pressure can work in rural South Africa. The program mixes group lessons with personal coaching on movement and diet. Their 2026 study checks how well the program was delivered, whether adults over forty with hypertension stuck with it, and how they felt about taking part.

Recruitment hit its target and nearly everyone stayed to the end. Participants said the program met their hopes, kept them motivated, and posed few barriers. Delivery followed the plan closely, with only small dose tweaks, and satisfaction rated high. A larger trial now has solid ground to stand on, since the approach proved workable where clinics are far apart.
plos-pone-0348796:
Birtukan Kebede Moti, Gudina Egata, and Desalegn Wirtu Tesso measured how common malnutrition is among adults admitted to large specialised hospitals in western Ethiopia, a problem often missed during busy admissions. More than eleven hundred patients chosen at random were assessed at intake with a standard bedside scoring method that grades nourishment from a short interview and examination.

Well over half the patients were malnourished to some degree, and about a quarter were severely so. Risk rose steeply with age and was higher for men, for patients with other illnesses, and for those eating a narrow range of foods. Having no formal schooling multiplied the odds several times over, while city living lowered them. The authors urge routine nutrition checks at admission so treatment can start before weakness slows recovery.
plos-pone-0348896:
Carolyn Hill and colleagues screened nearly three hundred female trail runners for eating disorders and for low energy availability, the state where training burns more than eating replaces. Two validated questionnaires did the screening, and answers were set against training history, body measures, and medical signs. The runners averaged seven to eight training hours a week and several years in the sport.

More than half screened positive on each questionnaire, a striking share. Eating disorder risk tracked with higher body mass index, certain education levels, and a positive depression screen. Low energy risk tracked with reduced libido, depression again, and, protectively, longer time in the sport. The authors urge coaches and clinicians in endurance sport to watch for under-fuelling as a routine health risk, not a rarity.
plos-pone-0349096:
Aziz and colleagues examined germs in spring drinking water and plant-based cleaning in a 2026 study. Shared springs in poorer regions often carry bacteria that cause illness. The team catalogued bacteria in spring water, judged health risk for adults and children, and tested leaf and root extracts from two common greens.

Several spore-forming bacteria were found, and all tested strains resisted some drugs and heavy metals. Root extracts killed spring bacteria best in dish tests. When used to treat water outside the body, both plants lowered germ counts without harming sprouting seedlings. Cheap local plants might offer villages a first line of water cleanup, though safety testing must continue.
plos-pone-0349196:
Anindya Mukherjee and colleagues reviewed hospital records for Indian patients with advanced breast cancer treated with two modern hormone-blocking partner drugs, palbociclib and ribociclib, between twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-three. These drugs, used with hormone therapy, are standard in wealthy countries, but published experience from Indian clinics is scarce. The team measured how long the cancer stayed controlled and which patient traits predicted doing better.

Patients who were fitter at the start kept their disease controlled longer. So did those whose cancer was found already spread. The same held for patients who received the drugs with their first hormone treatment, and for those who had never had chemotherapy. Control often lasted beyond twenty months. Formal analysis confirmed fitness, treatment order, and past chemotherapy as the strongest predictors. The authors say everyday Indian outcomes match trial expectations when the right patients get the drugs early.
plos-pone-0349396:
Yulong Liu and colleagues introduce a statistical model for measuring how finely people can tell sensations apart, using sorting tasks instead of the usual forced comparisons. A volunteer sorts a set of stimuli, such as tiles at slightly different angles, by feel, and a maximum likelihood method converts the sorting into a precise measure of discrimination. The team validated the model in simulations and in a touch experiment.

Sorting five stimuli across three trials gave the best balance of speed and reliability in their tests. Traditional perception tests trade accuracy against time so sharply that they stay confined to laboratories. A cheap, efficient method matters for screening touch problems clinically and for product design, where fingertip sensitivity decides quality.
plos-pone-0349596:
Yi Zhang and colleagues set out a plan for reviewing what is known about a newer class of opioid painkillers. They asked about the drugs' effects on the body's automatic controls, such as heart rhythm and blood pressure balance. The drugs, including oliceridine and tegileridine, were designed to relieve pain with fewer breathing and stomach side effects. Approval studies focused on those benefits and largely skipped the nervous system's quiet background regulation.

Following standard scoping review rules, the team will search four major databases plus drug regulator files for cell, animal, and human studies reporting heart or autonomic outcomes. Findings will be arranged in an evidence matrix by drug and study type. No results exist yet. The protocol also steps into a live debate over whether these drugs truly signal differently in cells or simply act more weakly.
plos-pone-0349696:
Bin Li, Xianhong Zeng, and Shuyu Ji used a large national social survey to test whether playing sports improves mental well-being in China, and whether the answer depends on local sports resources. Data came from the China General Social Survey, and the team guarded the result with a statistical technique that strips out hidden two-way causation, such as happier people simply exercising more.

Participation lifted psychological well-being broadly, and the effect survived the strict checks. Crucially, the benefit shifted with the resources around the person: facilities, environment, and safety conditions changed how much good participation did. The finding steers policy beyond telling people to exercise, toward building the places and conditions that let exercise deliver its mental health return.
plos-pone-0349796:
Sabina Panth and colleagues tested bark extracts of the rudraksha tree for blood sugar and antioxidant effects. Diabetes drugs work but carry side effects, so plant options draw study. Chemical screening found rich plant phenols and flavonoids. One fraction beat a standard antioxidant in lab tests, and extracts blocked two starch breaking enzymes more strongly than a standard diabetes drug in dishes.

In diabetic animals dosed for twenty eight days, the bark extract lowered fasting blood sugar clearly, trimmed blood fats slightly, raised good cholesterol slightly, and rebuilt liver sugar stores. Computer modelling added plausible target fits. Traditional use gains early lab support, though dose and safety in people remain untested.
plos-pone-0350096:
Zhiyuan Gao, Jiaolei Zhang, and Lei Cao questioned the yardstick engineers use to judge how prefabricated buildings would fare in an earthquake. Factory-built frames joined by steel hoops and bolts can slip at their connections, and the usual measure, sideways drift between floors, misses accumulating damage. Their 2026 study built computer models of the joints, checked them against lab tests, and compared a six-story prefabricated frame with a conventional poured-concrete twin.

A two-part damage measure that counts both deformation and absorbed energy told a different story from drift alone. Drift flattered the building early, understating damage mechanisms, yet overstated its collapse resistance later. Weighting damage floor by floor by energy use sharpened the picture further. The authors argue fragility ratings for prefabricated frames should retire the single drift yardstick.
plos-pone-0350196:
Huibo Yan analyzed three decades of global burden data to chart HIV and AIDS among Chinese adults of reproductive age, and to project the epidemic to 2035. Treatment has turned HIV into a chronic condition, yet trends in this key age group were poorly characterized. The 2026 analysis drew on the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study, tracking incidence, prevalence, deaths, and healthy years lost from 1990 onward.

Standardized rates climbed steeply across the period, with prevalence up roughly eightfold and mortality up far more, and men consistently worsened faster than women. Unsafe sex accounted for about seventy percent of HIV deaths in 2023. Forecasts suggest male incidence levels off by 2035 while female rates keep rising, widening the gap. The author calls for prevention designed separately for men and women.
plos-pone-0350296:
Fuerkaiti Abulimiti and co-authors tracked heart disease burden tied to salty diets and kidney dysfunction across the twenty largest economies. Ischaemic heart disease remains a leading killer, and both salt and failing kidneys raise blood pressure and damage vessels. Their 2026 study mined a global disease database from 1990 to 2021 and projected trends forward.

The team compared deaths and disability across sexes, ages, and countries using standardised rates. Breakdowns separated the roles of population growth, ageing, and true risk change. Patterns differed sharply among the twenty economies. Abulimiti and colleagues aim the results at policymakers weighing salt reduction and kidney screening as heart protection, with attention to the places carrying the heaviest load.
plos-pone-0350396:
Jennifer McCracken, Sally Wheelwright, and Clare Shaw interviewed people with advanced cancer, and their carers, about feeding by vein in 2026. When the gut fails, such nutrition is a major choice, and what information families need to decide well was poorly understood.

Five patients and six carers from hospitals and support groups shared their experiences. Themes covered feeling they had little real choice, the weight of hope, patchy communication, and the daily reality of home feeding. Talks about stopping were often missing. Participants asked for clear facts on risks, benefits, and recognising complications, delivered by a named, reachable team.
plos-pone-0350496:
Alaattin Ozen and colleagues in Turkey reviewed why some cancer patients stop radiation treatment early, in work published in 2026. Finishing the full course matters for control of the disease, yet records from ten thousand patients showed a small share quit.

About three in a hundred stopped. The leading reason was a decline in general condition. More than half of those who stopped had been treated for comfort rather than cure, lung cancer was the most common diagnosis, and the brain was the most treated site. The pattern argues for stronger support of frail patients during treatment, before decline forces a stop.
plos-pone-0350996:
Huixiang Ouyang and colleagues mapped psychology research about threat. Papers spanned more than six decades of publishing. The count passed fifty thousand papers. Three large databases supplied the records. Topic models read titles and short summaries. Twenty five topics emerged from the maths. Network tools then grouped topics into four lands.

Four lands covered brain processing and clinical threats. Social threats and collective threats completed the map. Lands linked weakly to each other. No land formed a central hub. Interest grew more varied over time. Event driven work rose as theory work faded. The field reacts to headlines, the authors warn. Shared theory across lands is still missing.
plos-pone-0351296:
Marta Luciani and seven colleagues trace the rise of a distinctive Bronze Age pottery from northwestern Arabia in this 2026 archaeology study. The pottery, known today as Qurayyah Painted Ware, carries bold two-color designs and appears across a wide region. Working from dozens of samples taken from a kiln site at Qurayyah itself, the team combined technology studies, mineral analysis, and chemistry to reconstruct how the ware was made and spread.

Their analyses show the ware was invented locally in the late Middle Bronze Age and kept a consistent recipe and look for centuries. Later versions became a sought-after export found as far away as sites in Jordan. Because the ware combined a stable identity with wide distribution, the authors argue it worked like an early brand, linking distant buyers to a known place of origin.
plos-pone-0351396:
Rana Rizk and colleagues checked whether a short diet questionnaire still works when shortened further for pregnant women in Lebanon. The standard screener scores how closely someone eats a Mediterranean-style diet, but one of its items covers alcohol, which pregnancy rules out. Five hundred pregnant women completed the twelve-point version alongside detailed food records and repeated day recalls for comparison.

The shortened screener held together acceptably as a scale, and its answers grouped into four sensible food patterns. Against the fuller records, though, its accuracy was weaker than hoped. The authors blame items that miss pregnancy-specific and local foods, plus plain reporting error. Clinics can still use it as a fast first look at diet in pregnancy, but anyone needing precise intake for Lebanese mothers should reach for fuller methods.
plos-pone-0351496:
After knee ligament surgery, athletes must relearn steady landings. Wasim Labban and colleagues compared how quickly people settle after a jump, in this 2026 PLOS One study of twenty-one patients nine to twenty-four months after ligament reconstruction and twenty healthy volunteers.

Everyone jumped with both legs onto force plates and held the landing for ten seconds while the plates tracked wobble. The surgery group took significantly longer to stabilize than the healthy group, showing balance control still lagging well into recovery. The team also split results by sex to see whether recovery differs for women and men. Such tests could help decide when a return to sport is truly safe.
plos-pone-0352096:
Frédéric Tovissodé, Florian Justwan, and Bert Baumgaertner tackle a measurement problem in the study of reasoning. Their 2026 study asks how people's evidence-gathering styles connect to their decisions. The number of styles explodes as information piles up. Researchers normally tame it by forcing evidence into preset categories. That throws away the fine detail that might matter. Their setting instead hides evidence content behind queries. Participants reveal by their choices what they judge relevant.

The analysis pairs those choices with supervised clustering. An explanation method from machine learning shows which gathered pieces actually drove each decision. Theoretical boxes around evidence types can then relax. The pathway from seeking, to processing, to deciding becomes traceable in one frame. The authors demonstrate the approach's fruitfulness on reasoning data. For misinformation research, the payoff is real: knowing which evidence a person bothered to fetch may predict their conclusions better than demographics.
plos-pone-0352696:
Neslihan Aydemir, Ali Oral, and Tuğçe Yıldırım measure the social sting of inflammatory bowel disease. Their 2026 study surveyed one hundred forty-six patients under regular follow-up. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis cause symptoms that are hard to hide. Urgency, pain, and bathroom dependence invite awkward public moments. The team asked patients about ten concrete stigma experiences. Self-esteem was measured alongside, with a standard scale.

Nearly two-thirds of patients reported at least one stigma experience. Social avoidance was the commonest form. Discomfort in public settings ranked high as well. Overt discrimination, by contrast, was rarer. Crohn's and colitis patients reported broadly similar patterns. Stigma is therefore not a side note to bowel disease. It is a majority experience that can shrink social life and complicate disease management. Clinicians who ask only about gut symptoms miss a burden patients clearly carry.
plos-pone-0353196:
Lo and colleagues measured metals and other elements in killer whales from the eastern North Pacific in a 2026 study. Samples of liver and kidney came from stranded whales found from California to Alaska and Hawaii. The group included fish-eating whales, mammal-eating whales, and a rarer group that hunts sharks.

Calves carried lower levels of some harmful elements than adults, while adult males and females showed higher mercury in several tissues. Fish-eating whales differed from mammal-eating whales on a few helpful minerals as well. Age and life stage shaped the body burden more than most other factors, which helps track ocean pollution through top hunters.
plos-pone-0353396:
Martin, Martin, and Lyimo tested young children with diarrhea for a toxin-making gut germ in northern Tanzania in a 2026 study. The germ, passed from animals, can cause severe illness in small children, yet pastoral areas had little data. Stool samples from one hundred fifty children at four facilities were tested for toxin genes and drug sensitivity.

About one child in eight carried the germ by the study's gene test. All toxin findings of one type also carried helper genes tied to stronger disease. Knowing which antibiotics still work locally guides treatment when children arrive dehydrated. The results fill a data gap for herding regions where children and livestock live closely together.
plos-pone-0353696:
Qiang Zeng and seven colleagues search for genes that drive Wilms tumour, a childhood kidney cancer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Comparing tumour tissue with healthy kidney in public gene datasets, they found close to a thousand genes behaving differently. Six hub genes stood out, and one, named CDCA8, was more active in tumours and linked to worse survival for patients.

Cell experiments then showed that switching CDCA8 down slowed the tumour cells' aggressive behaviour. The gene appears to protect a second protein that powers cell energy production, keeping it from being broken down. That pairing is a possible future drug target, though the authors stress the evidence is still preliminary.
plos-pone-0353796:
Giorgio Allegri and co-authors present in 2026 a deep learning tool that automatically outlines bone support cells in fluorescence microscope images. Hand analysis of such images is slow, uneven between people, and hard to standardise, yet bone biology needs precise counts of bone building cells, bone eating cells, vessels, and mineral. Tens of thousands of prepared images trained and checked the network.

The tool matched experienced biologists closely on the measures tested and cut analysis from days to seconds across varied conditions. The authors offer it freely to the bone research community as a reliable way to speed preclinical work and make results easier to compare.
plos-pone-0353996:
Yibiao Li and three colleagues mine five million location-tagged social media posts to map happiness across fifty Chinese cities, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sentiment software scored the emotional tone of Weibo posts, and machine-learning models then weighed seventeen possible explanations, from greenery and income to air pollution and temperature.

Posts ran happier on weekends and holidays. Greenery was the single strongest predictor of a city's expressed happiness, ahead of income per person, fine-particle pollution, and temperature. Warmer future climate scenarios shifted the projected pattern in the models. The authors offer the map as planning evidence: planting and protecting urban green space may be a measurable public-mood policy, not just an environmental one.
plos-pone-0354096:
Mohan Ram and coauthors published a 2026 wildlife study in PLOS ONE on Asiatic lions returning to Barda Wildlife Sanctuary in Gujarat. The species survives in this one region, and lions recolonized Barda after an absence of over a century, a male arriving alone and managers adding five females. The team radio-collared six lions and analyzed droppings to learn how newcomers use space, choose habitat, organize socially, and eat.

Each lion ranged widely but defended a much smaller core, and cores overlapped less than home ranges, signaling emerging social structure. Lions favored mixed forest broadly and grassland inside their cores. Wild pigs dominated the diet, with cattle a notable second, a recipe for friction with herders. Deer reintroductions aim to widen the prey base. Barda is promising, they say, but the sample is small, and habitat and conflict work will decide if it becomes a true second stronghold.
plos-pone-0354596:
Jara-Rizzo and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare thinking styles across five groups: problem gamblers, problem buyers, video gamers, pornography users, and a control group. Addiction research knows that substance users often show poor mental flexibility, quick impulsive choices, and compulsive habits. Whether the same marks appear in everyday behaviors that can turn addictive was less clear.

On a standard questionnaire, the buyers stood out with higher impulsivity and compulsivity than the other groups. On a card-like learning task, buyers also adapted worst when the rules of reward quietly changed, lagging behind gamers and pornography users overall. Yet when the team modeled the exact moment of rule change, every group paid a similar cost; no group was uniquely stuck. The authors conclude these traits show up unevenly across behaviors, so treatment should be tailored to the person and the habit, not copied from substance addiction wholesale.
plos-pone-0354696:
Erick J Martínez Rodríguez led a team of eight authors testing hemp against yellow fever mosquitoes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Aedes aegypti spreads yellow fever, dengue, and Zika, and it shrugs off many repellents. The team tested hemp leaf extracts and cannabidiol, a hemp compound, on adult females of the species.

Martínez Rodríguez's group measured both toxic and repellent effects. Plant-based options could give communities a greener weapon against a deadly vector, especially where synthetic products are costly or resisted. Mosquito control needs many tools, since the insects adapt quickly. Careful lab results like these are the first filter: only extracts that pass here earn field trials.
plos-pone-0354796:
Kathryn C. Kemp and colleagues published a 2026 psychology study in PLOS ONE on sex differences in social cognition, the ability to read other people's minds and signals. Earlier research often found women scoring higher, but results replicated inconsistently. This team recruited adolescents and young adults spanning minimal to clinical levels of social difficulty, then tested gaze perception, reading mental states from limited cues, and social inference.

Women and girls outperformed men and boys on most tasks, including judging gaze direction and inferring mental states from subtle information. Those gaps mostly survived adjustments for general thinking ability, age, and psychiatric symptoms. One exception appeared on a complex, shifting social inference task, where the difference vanished once symptoms were accounted for. The authors suggest females may be especially sensitive to eye-related social signals. They argue services for social difficulties should expect different presentations by sex when designing assessments and treatments.
plos-pone-0354896:
Galib Muhammad Shahriar Himel and four colleagues review how deep learning has been applied to MRI scans of osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone cancer of adolescence, in this 2026 review. Following standard reporting guidelines, they assessed thirty-eight studies from the past five years covering tumor outlining, sorting, and outlook. The methods sorted into seven families, from classic radiomics to convolutional networks, vision transformers, and multimodal systems.

Multimodal models achieved the best average overlap with expert tumor outlines, with standard convolutional networks close behind and lightweight networks performing well. Radiomics-based tools also predicted tumor death after chemotherapy with good accuracy. But the reviewers stress a stark gap: every model was tested only on past data at a single center. None has faced testing across many centers, as needed before use in care.
plos-pone-0355196:
Xuexue Kong and colleagues breed a mosquito strain in the lab that resists a growth-regulating insecticide, then check whether common spray insecticides also fail against it. The mosquito spreads several viruses, and control programs rotate chemicals to slow resistance. After many generations of exposure, the selected strain survived the growth regulator at about ten times the normal killing level. It also shrugged off three widely used spray chemicals. The strength of that shrug was similar.

No changes appeared in the usual target genes. Instead, the mosquitoes ran detox enzymes harder, and blocking those enzymes largely restored the chemicals' bite. Resistance carried costs: slower growth, shorter female life, and fewer viable eggs. Kong and colleagues warn that rotating between these chemical families alone will not outsmart this shared defense.
plos-pone-0355296:
Chandler Tyrrell, Sinéad Keogh, and Brídín Carroll publish a protocol in 2026 for the first scoping review, to their knowledge, on whether digital health technologies make older adults lonelier or less lonely. Video visits, patient portals, and remote monitoring are replacing in-person care, and loneliness, the felt lack of connection, and social isolation, its objective counterpart, both damage health in later life. Whether the technology helps or harms remains unmapped.

Following the preregistered plan, the reviewers will chart which technologies have been studied, how loneliness and isolation were defined and measured in each study, and where the evidence is missing. The distinction between feeling lonely and being alone runs through the design. The authors aim to give researchers, policymakers, and service designers a map solid enough to build on, rather than another round of assumptions about older adults and screens.
plos-pone-0355396:
Kendra Wyant, Jiachen Yu, and John Curtin followed people in early recovery from alcohol use disorder for up to three months in this 2026 study. Relapse risk is highest in that early window, and the team wondered whether patterns in phone calls and texts could warn of a coming lapse. Participants also reported their drinking several times a day.

The researchers built prediction models combining the phone data with background information gathered at the start, such as past drinking and mental health. Phone communication patterns did carry some signal about next-day drinking, but on their own they predicted poorly. More importantly, adding them did not improve on what the starting information already predicted. The authors conclude that this kind of passive phone sensing may add little to lapse prediction.
plos-pone-0355496:
Sameer Padhye and colleagues introduce in 2026 a software package for the R language that makes DNA barcode records easier to pull and use. Barcodes let scientists name species from short gene pieces, and a global system stores the records with specimen, place, and naming data. Its website suits hands on work, but many teams need coded access to both public and private records.

The new package logs users in, returns records in a shared core format, and reshapes them into common R tables. Custom workflows can then produce outputs ready for publication. The aim is repeatable curation and analysis before data are released openly.
plos-pone-0355596:
Wenxiang Zhou and co-authors reviewed how researchers pair body sensors with artificial intelligence inside immersive virtual reality lessons. Headsets can now track eyes, brain signals, skin, and heart while a learner works. Their 2026 scoping review gathered nineteen empirical studies from a decade of work and compared their sensing and analysis choices.

Eye tracking was the most common signal, followed closely by brain measures. Pairing those two was the favourite combination. Skin conductance studies were rare in the set. Most work targeted thinking states, feelings, or performance. Zhou and colleagues map a young field still standardising how signals are cleaned, merged, and checked before classroom use.
plos-pone-0355696:
Xuan Lu and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on hard-to-treat illness. It concerns people treated at once for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and HIV, two infections that complicate each other. The authors study adherence, taking medicines as prescribed, for bedaquiline, a key TB drug, and for antiretroviral therapy.

As the title reports, how close in time a dose falls to a counseling session is tied to adherence: doses were taken more reliably nearer to counseling. That timing link suggests support fades and needs renewal during long treatment. TB and HIV programs can use it to schedule counseling when it does the most good.
plos-pone-0355996:
Md Al Amin Islam Utshob and fellow engineers design, on paper and in simulation, a layered light sensor that reads the fat content of milk. Fat level sets milk's grade and price, yet lab testing is slow. Their sensor watches how light bends off a stack of thin films; the bend shifts with the liquid's optical density, which tracks fat. Computer methods checked the design three ways, and a hybrid search tuned each layer's thickness.

At the richest setting tested, the sensor's response was sharp and its reflected signal clean, beating many published designs on headline measures. Utshob and colleagues stress the work is numerical, so a built device must still prove itself on real milk. If it holds up, dairies could grade milk in seconds at the tank.
plos-pone-0356296:
Derartu Ahmed and seven colleagues ask whether how fast a smoker's body clears nicotine relates to heart attack risk among people living with HIV, in this 2026 study. Smoking is two to three times more common in this population and already multiplies cardiac danger; faster nicotine metabolism is known to deepen dependence. Within a large American HIV clinical cohort, the team compared just over one hundred thirty smokers who suffered a heart attack with matched smokers who did not, using stored blood samples.

Cases did clear nicotine slightly faster on average, and the odds of being a fast metabolizer were modestly higher among cases. But the difference was not statistically significant, and adjusting for blood pressure treatment, hypertension, and diabetes did not change it. The authors conclude the metabolism rate remains a possible risk marker worth a more precise test in larger samples, not an established one.
plos-pone-0356496:
Seyed Sahab Aarabi and fellow researchers mine a national insurance claims database in Iran to study heart artery imaging costs and access. Their 2026 paper covers a very large set of hospital stays in which doctors threaded a camera into the heart's arteries to look for blockages. They model what drives bills, further treatment, and length of stay at patient, hospital, and province levels.

Hands-on treatment services formed the biggest cost share, and harder cases cost far more than simple ones. Men and older patients more often received follow-up procedures and stayed longer. Richer provinces with more beds and imaging machines used the test more, and dirty air also tracked with higher use. The results point funders toward clear gaps in fairness.
plos-pone-0356596:
Min Seok Kim, Seonghee Nam, Jeongwoo Lee, and Se Joon Woo compared three injected eye drugs for a common blinding disease of older adults. Which carries the highest risk of serious internal bleeding? Their 2026 nationwide study used South Korean insurance records from 2014 to 2023. It followed patients newly treated for the wet form of age-related macular degeneration. The drugs were ranibizumab, aflibercept, and brolucizumab.

Bleeding severe enough to require surgical clearing was rare with all three drugs. But it occurred more often after brolucizumab and aflibercept than after ranibizumab. The authors caution that bleeding risk alone should not pick a patient's drug. The medicines differ in other ways. Still, the ranking gives doctors concrete numbers for counseling and for watching higher-risk patients closely.
plos-pone-0356696:
Aysenur Nazik interviewed nine adults in Türkiye who grew up with an autistic brother or sister, exploring how autism shapes the lives of the siblings who do not have it. Her 2026 qualitative study used in-depth interviews and careful thematic analysis, a perspective she notes is rarely heard in Turkish research, which tends to count siblings rather than listen to them.

Four themes emerged. Sibling bonds swung between closeness and distance, strained by communication barriers and sometimes aggressive behavior. Participants carried caregiving and protective duties well beyond the usual sibling share, and faced stigma and misunderstanding socially. Yet many also credited the experience with building their empathy, patience, and resilience. The study asks services to treat siblings as people with needs of their own.
plos-pone-0356796:
Yongai Ling and coauthors published a 2026 clinical study in PLOS ONE on breathing changes in carbon monoxide poisoning. Patients often breathe fast and blow off carbon dioxide, called hypocapnia, usually read as simple compensation for acid building up in the blood. The team re-examined nearly a thousand emergency patients, split by blood acidity, and modeled what actually drives their carbon dioxide levels.

The acidotic group had more poison bound to their blood, more lactate, and lower carbon dioxide. Acidity, as base excess, was the strongest predictor of carbon dioxide, each step down tracking a clear fall. But the overall fit was modest, and the relationship ran stronger in acidotic patients and in men. Compensation, they conclude, explains only part of the story: other factors also push breathing, and clinicians should not assume low carbon dioxide is purely the body's tidy response.
plos-pone-0356996:
Yuhong Lv, Rumi Hisakata, and Hirohiko Kaneko use pupil size to guess which of two overlapping images a person is silently attending to. Their display fuses two icons, one rendered in fine detail and one in coarse blobs, and the two swap rendering styles rhythmically while viewers hold attention on one chosen icon. Pupils were tracked throughout, under still and moving versions of the display.

Pupils shrank when the attended image carried fine detail and widened when it carried the coarse version, with the clearest swings when at least one image moved. Turning that pattern into a guessing rule beat seventy percent accuracy in favorable conditions. Lv and colleagues propose pupil reading as a hands-free input channel for people with very limited movement.
plos-pone-0357096:
Md Naziur Rahman and co-authors screen compounds from the desert rose plant in simulation as possible blockers of a growth receptor that drives the most common lung cancer. Existing blocker drugs work, but cancers learn to resist them and side effects bite. The team scored the plant's chemicals for predicted anticancer activity, docked the best against the receptor's engine region, checked drug-like traits and safety, and ran a long motion simulation on the winner.

Several compounds docked strongly, and one plant steroid-like compound bound tightest, holding its grip through the full simulation. Rahman and colleagues stress that all evidence here is computational. The shortlist now needs bench tests to learn whether any compound truly slows cancer cells.
plos-pone-0357296:
Ashley Cardenas led a team of eight authors studying cell-to-cell energy gifts in the spine, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Mesenchymal stromal cells can donate their mitochondria, the cell's power plants, to struggling neighbor cells. The team characterized that transfer to healthy and diseased cells of the intervertebral disc, the cushions between spine bones.

Cardenas's work details how and how much transfer occurs in disc cells. Degenerative disc disease causes much back pain and has few repairs, so a natural rescue mechanism is of real interest. If donor cells reliably recharge failing disc cells, new cell therapies could be designed around that transfer. Careful characterization comes first, and this study supplies it for an important target tissue.
plos-pone-0357496:
Jaroslaw Grobelny and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE adapting a sustainable career scale for Poland. A sustainable career balances health, happiness, good output, and social contribution over a working life, but questionnaires built in one culture do not travel on their own. The team ran focus groups to check cultural fit, piloted the items. They confirmed the structure in testing and checked that the scale measures the same thing across gender and age. Respondents were followed over time for stability and links to well-being.

The Polish version kept the four dimensions: happiness, health, productivity, and social empowerment. Scores were consistent and stable over time, and dimensions behaved distinctly, as theory predicts, with some weakness around health. Later scores connected to well-being outcomes in the expected directions. The adaptation looks sound so far, giving Polish career researchers a tested tool and global research a transfer test.
plos-pone-0357796:
Bharati Pandey and Chetna Tyagi studied udder infection in Sahiwal cattle at the gene level, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Mastitis, infection of the udder, costs dairy farmers heavily in lost milk and treatment. The Sahiwal is a hardy Indian breed. The pair tracked long non-coding RNAs, gene regulators, across stages of the disease.

Pandey and Tyagi identified which of these RNAs change at each mastitis stage, and sketched the regulatory networks they may form. Those networks show how the udder's defenses shift as infection worsens. Breeders and vets could use such markers to spot susceptible animals or stage disease more precisely. For smallholder farmers, earlier and cheaper detection of mastitis protects both income and animal welfare.
plos-pone-0357896:
Dan He, Zixuan Chen, Jing Zhou, Yiman Hou, Qimeng Li, and Zihang Qin published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies Chinese cities and how high-speed railway access shapes urban expansion, the outward growth of built-up land. Their analysis works through a mediating effect model.

A mediating model asks not just whether rail access and growth move together, but through which middle steps the influence passes. New stations often trigger development far beyond the tracks themselves. Urban planners deciding where to place stations and how to zone land around them can use mechanism evidence like this instead of simple before-and-after claims.
plos-pone-0358196: Zhang and another author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on heat and gun violence. They examined how temperature relates to firearm violence, and they compared ways of measuring that link. Different metrics can tell different stories, so the comparison itself is part of the work. If hot days raise risk, cities could time outreach and patrols with the weather in mind.
plos-pone-0358596:
Qiusu Wang studied university teachers and generative AI in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Many teachers tried AI tools under pressure or out of curiosity, but lasting use is another matter. Wang asked whether teachers who feel skilled with these tools are the ones who plan to keep using them.

Working from a well-known model of how people adopt technology, Wang linked perceived skill with intent to continue. The results tell universities that training which builds real confidence matters more than hype or mandates. Support that raises skill can turn a brief trial into steady, thoughtful use in teaching. That distinction affects how schools should spend their AI budgets.
plos-pone-0358796: Bartoszewicz and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on urine infections tied to catheters in intensive care. They described the traits of ICU patients who caught a bacterial infection from a urinary catheter. They also tracked how those patients fared. Catheters are common in intensive care, so knowing who is at risk helps units prevent infections that lengthen stays.
plos-pone-0358996: Nyende and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE interview study set in the Busoga region of eastern Uganda. They asked local stakeholders how teens use sexual and reproductive health services there. Views came from the people who run, fund, or rely on those services. Hearing these views can show why teens do or do not seek care, and where clinics and outreach could do better.
plos-pone-0359096:
Xianyu Li leads a team of seven comparing three calcium silicate sealers used in root canal treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Dentists pack these materials into a cleaned tooth root to seal it, and the chemistry can irritate or help the tissues around the root tip. The study set three commercial products side by side, with a long used repair material as a reference point.

In the lab the team measured acidity, how much each sealer dissolves, and which elements leak out, then exposed human ligament cells to the materials. All were strongly alkaline, and the products released different amounts of calcium and triggered different cell responses, including changes tied to inflammation and mineral building. Two sealers reduced cell survival at stronger doses. The comparison gives dentists a clearer picture of trade offs between brands.
plos-pone-0359196:
Ratidzo Chirimo and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article set in Zimbabwe. It studies adults living with HIV who take first-line antiretroviral therapy built on dolutegravir. The authors measure the burden of two metabolic problems, high blood sugar and abnormal blood fats, and hunt for their determinants.

The study is cross-sectional, taking a snapshot of patients on this widely used HIV treatment. As HIV care succeeds and patients live longer, heart and metabolic risks become the next threat. Clinic teams in Zimbabwe and similar programs can use burden figures like these to add screening for diabetes and cholesterol to routine HIV visits.
plos-pone-0359396: Rosle and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a trial on older adults and digital health skills. The program, called ODDHeaL, teaches older people to find and judge health information online. The plan sets out how the team will judge whether the program works. Digital skills matter more as booking, results, and advice move online for older patients.
plos-pone-0359596:
John Telesphory Mhagama and Kanwal Garg wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on farming technology. It presents a recommender system, software that suggests choices, built for smart farming. Their system is multimodal and context-aware, meaning it draws on several kinds of data and on the situation at hand.

An AI recommender for farmers could weigh soil, weather, crop stage, and images before suggesting actions like watering or fertilizing. Using multiple data types at once should make suggestions fit the actual field better than a single sensor could. Agricultural technology developers are the readers most likely to build on this design.
plos-pone-0359796:
Nsulwa John Mlazi and Baraka Kichonge published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a solver, a piece of mathematical software, for modeling solar photovoltaic modules, the panels that turn sunlight into electricity. The solver adapts its current-voltage step size as it works.

Adaptive steps aim for both accuracy and efficiency: fine steps where the curve bends sharply, coarse steps where it is smooth. Accurate panel models underpin solar system design and fault checking. Electrical engineers who simulate solar arrays before building them are the readers who gain from a faster, truer solver.
pmc-13237496:
Li and colleagues build a strain-tuned metal sponge that splits peroxide cleanly for sensing. Their aerogel blends palladium with bismuth, and stretching the metal's atomic spacing changes how its electrons behave. Tuned this way, the material activates hydrogen peroxide into hydroxyl radicals with unusual selectivity, the first step in many chemical tests.

The team uses that controlled activation to tell pesticides apart, a task where sloppy chemistry blurs one compound into another. Orbital tuning, the meeting of electron clouds between metal and target, is their lever for precision. Such designer catalysts could make field tests for farm chemicals sharper and cheaper.
pmc-13240796:
Barbonus and co-authors at Leipzig University graded how well four AI chatbots adjust drug doses for older patients with weak kidneys. Wrong doses in renal impairment cause preventable harm in geriatric care. The team devised a quality score, AQUOS, for chatbot answers. One hundred discharge cases with many medications supplied the test prompts.

Sixteen hundred answers were scored, in English and German, at two separate times. Answer quality fell as kidney function worsened and medication lists grew more complex. English prompts scored slightly higher, and repeat answers were highly consistent. Even the best chatbot fell short of what the authors judge safe for clinical use.
pmc-13241396:

pmc-13252796:

pmc-13253596:

pmc-13254196:
