Vandenbroucke, von Elm, Altman, and co-authors explain and expand the STROBE guidance for observational studies. Medical research often relies on watching groups over time rather than running trials. Reports of such studies were frequently too thin to judge quality or to apply elsewhere.

Alongside the checklist itself, this companion paper gives the reasoning and evidence behind each item. Examples show what good reporting looks like in practice. The pair of papers gave epidemiology a common standard, helping authors write clearer studies and helping readers spot weak ones before acting on them.
pmc-2690996:
Langmead, Trapnell, Pop, and co-authors introduce Bowtie, a tool for aligning short DNA reads to large genomes. New sequencing machines produced millions of short reads that each had to be placed on a reference genome. Older aligners were too slow or used too much memory for that flood.

Bowtie aligns reads to the human genome with great speed while using little memory. Its design trades a small amount of flexibility for a large gain in throughput. Bowtie quickly became basic infrastructure for genomics, letting ordinary computers handle datasets that once needed clusters.
pmc-3991396:
Xue, Schmidt, Sander, and their team studied human macrophages in 2014 using gene activity data. Macrophages are immune cells that can switch into many states to fight germs or heal tissue. That switching involves deep changes in which genes are turned on, yet the programs behind it were poorly mapped.

By linking genes into networks, the team found that macrophage states form a broad spectrum, not just two poles. Many triggers blend shared and unique gene programs in fine gradations. That spectrum model helps explain why these cells behave in such varied ways, and it gives immune research a richer map for disease studies.
pmc-5335496:
Weiss, Xu, Peddada, and their colleagues wrote in 2017 on normalization for microbial abundance data. Data from 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing, a standard census of bacteria, present challenges to ecological and statistical interpretation. Library sizes often vary over several orders of magnitude, and the data contain many zeros.

Researchers usually want to compare relative abundances of microbes between samples. The authors show that the right normalization and testing strategy depends on the characteristics of the data at hand. A poor choice can invent differences or hide real ones. Their guidance helps microbiome teams avoid false claims about which bacteria rise or fall with disease or diet.
pmc-5584396:
Karger, Conrad, Böhner, and their co-authors presented CHELSA in 2017, high-resolution climate data for the Earth's land surface. Many fields in environmental and ecological science need climate data at fine detail. Coarse global grids miss the sharp variation found in mountains and coasts.

CHELSA provides climatologies built from downscaled model output of temperature and precipitation. Downscaling sharpens broad climate model results to fine local grids using terrain effects. Ecologists use such data to model where species can live now and under future climates. The dataset gave land researchers a free, consistent climate layer at a scale that matches real landscapes.
pmc-6323896:
Yasset Perez-Riverol and colleagues reported the 2019 state of the PRIDE database. PRIDE stores mass spectrometry proteomics data from labs worldwide. It is the largest public store of its kind and a founding member of the ProteomeXchange group.

The update describes better support for measuring protein amounts, not just naming proteins present. New tools help submitters check files before upload and help users reuse data. Shared raw data let others repeat analyses and build larger combined sets. The paper is the reference for citing the archive and its companion resources.
pmc-6912996:
Ben Van Calster, David McLernon, Maarten van Smeden, and coauthors warned about calibration in prediction models in 2019. A risk model can rank patients well yet give badly wrong risk numbers. That second flaw, poor calibration, gets little attention.

Poorly calibrated models mislead doctors and patients who act on the stated risk. The authors show how calibration should be checked and reported, for classic and machine learning models alike. They argue journals and reviewers must demand it. Anyone building a clinical score will find here the standards their work will be judged by.
pmc-7100496:
Daniel Ahorsu, Chung-Ying Lin, Vida Imani, and coauthors built the Fear of COVID-19 Scale in 2020. The pandemic brought fear, worry, and anxiety to people worldwide. Clinicians had no short, tested tool for measuring that specific fear.

The authors wrote a brief set of items and tested them in a general population sample. The scale held together as one factor and matched other anxiety measures as expected. Its brevity suits busy clinics and large surveys. Researchers in many countries soon translated it to track fear as the pandemic evolved. The authors report the scale in English and Persian versions tested in parallel samples.
pmc-7252096:
Carly Ziegler and colleagues examined in 2020 how the virus that causes COVID-19 gets its first foothold in the human body. The virus uses a protein called ACE2 as its doorway into cells, helped by host enzymes that prime its spike protein. The team asked where in the body this doorway sits, and whether the body's own alarm signals change how much of it is made.

Using gene activity data from airway cells and tissues, they report that the gene for this doorway switches on more strongly after interferon, one of the body's virus alarm signals. They also pinpoint the exact cell types that carry it in the nose and elsewhere. That finding raised an important caution about how alarm signals might, in some settings, widen the virus's entry points.
pmc-8233496:
Koichiro Tamura, Glen Stecher, and Sudhir Kumar announced MEGA11 in 2021, the eleventh version of a long running software package for evolutionary genetics. The package, whose name stands for Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis, gathers many methods for comparing DNA and protein sequences. It is used worldwide to reconstruct how species and pathogens are related.

The update describes additions that strengthen the building of timetrees, diagrams that place evolutionary splits on a dated scale. It also covers other new tools added since the previous version. MEGA is known for making sophisticated evolutionary analysis usable by biologists without deep computing training, and this release extends that reach.
pmc-8748196:
Malte Luecken and co-authors benchmarked in 2021 the methods used to merge single-cell data from many samples into one atlas. Atlases combine samples gathered in different places, labs, and conditions, which leaves tangled batch effects, technical differences that masquerade as biology. Reliable integration, removing those effects while keeping real differences, is required before joint analysis can be trusted.

The team compared dozens of method variations across many datasets and tasks, scoring how well each removed batch effects and preserved true cell differences. Their results give atlas builders a practical guide to choosing a method for their data. The benchmark itself became a reference point for a fast moving corner of genomics.
pollock-first-book-jurisprudence-1896:
Frederick Pollock, an Oxford professor, wrote A First Book of Jurisprudence in 1896 for students of the common law. Pollock aimed to give beginners a map of legal theory without Austin's dryness. The book became the standard English introduction of its generation.

He treats the nature of law, the state, sovereignty, rights, and duties in plain chapters. Custom, precedent, and statute are weighed as sources of law. Pollock writes with wit and learning, drawing examples from English courts. His book trained generations of lawyers to ask what law is before asking what it says. It still reads freshly today.
raleigh-discoverie-of-guiana-1596:
Walter Raleigh sailed to South America in 1595 hunting the golden city of El Dorado, and The Discoverie of Guiana, printed in 1596, is his report. Raleigh, courtier, poet, and soldier, led the voyage up the Orinoco river country himself. His book became the founding English text on South America.

Raleigh describes rivers, peoples, and gold reports with a salesman's sparkle and a scout's eye. He found no golden city, yet his glowing account launched a century of Guiana fever in England. Later adventurers chased his promises at great cost, Raleigh among them. The Discoverie remains a brilliant, dangerous piece of persuasion, and a key early English voice on the continent.
rig-veda-griffith-1896: The complete Rig Veda in Ralph Griffith's 1896 translation. These 1,028 Sanskrit hymns are Hinduism's oldest scriptures, praising gods of sky and fire. This edition preserves that ancient collection. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
sanguis-naturae-or-a-manifest-declaratio: Sanguis naturae, 1696. The blood of nature. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
santayana-sense-beauty-1896:
George Santayana published The Sense of Beauty in 1896, his first book, drawn from lectures at Harvard. Santayana defines beauty as pleasure objectified: pleasure seen as a quality of the thing itself. He studies why forms, colors, and sounds please us. The senses, association, and expression each play a part.

The book founded a serious American aesthetics on natural grounds. Santayana treats beauty as part of nature, not a mystery above it. His prose is already the polished style he became known for. Later work on art and taste often starts here. It remains a graceful entry into the philosophy of beauty.
scott-elliot-story-of-atlantis-1896:
W. Scott-Elliot told the theosophical story of Atlantis in his sketch of 1896. Theosophy taught that a great continent sank beneath the Atlantic in deep time. Scott-Elliot gives its geography, history, and peoples in earnest detail. Root races and sub races march across his chapters, each with its rise and fall.

Four maps show the continent shrinking through its cataclysms. The book drew on clairvoyant research honored inside the Theosophical Society. Its companion, The Lost Lemuria, treats the sister continent. Together they defined the society's lost continent doctrine. The Gutenberg text keeps the maps and the scheme. It is a scripture of the movement, in effect.
sienkiewicz-quo-vadis-1896:
Henryk Sienkiewicz published Quo Vadis in 1896, his epic of love and persecution in Nero's Rome. The Nobel-winning epic of the early Church became, in its day, the best-selling novel in the world. Its title comes from Peter's vision on the Appian Way: Quo vadis, Domine, whither goest thou, Lord.

Vinicius, a Roman officer, loves Lygia, a Christian hostage, and pursues her through Petronius's polished, rotting court of Nero. The fire of Rome, the arena's beasts, and Ursus's bare-handed rescue of Lygia from a bull fill the spectacle. Petronius, the arbiter of elegance, steals the book's wit, while Peter and Paul give its faith a face in Rome. Conversions, martyrdoms, and Nero's fall close a tale that taught millions their image of the early Church under persecution. Sienkiewicz's Nobel of 1905 rested largely on this book's world fame.
sinnett-the-growth-of-the-soul-1896:
A. P. Sinnett traced the long road of the soul in The Growth of the Soul, his book of 1896. It builds on his prior hit, a sketch of the creed of the East. Here he tells how a soul grows through birth, death, and birth once more, age by age.

Each life adds skill, sight, and strength to the soul. At last it nears the rank of the Masters. Sinnett writes in calm, clear prose for lay fans. The book is the creed told as the tale of one soul's rise. Years of notes from his Masters feed the claims in this book. Sinnett asks fans to judge the fruit, not just the strange source.
smith-lectures-justice-police-revenue-ar:
Adam Smith lectured on jurisprudence at Glasgow in 1762 and 1763, and students' notes preserved the course. Edwin Cannan edited those notes as Lectures on Justice, Police, Revenue and Arms in 1896. Smith treats justice first, then police, meaning public order and plenty. Revenue and arms close the scheme of government he lays out.

Long lost, the lectures reveal the foundation under his Wealth of Nations. Ideas on markets, law, and the state's duties appear here in early form. Cannan recovered the text from a manuscript copy of the notes. The book lets readers watch Smith teach before he became famous. It fills a famous gap in his works.
south-african-constitution-1996:
South Africa adopted its final post-apartheid constitution in 1996, signed by President Nelson Mandela at Sharpeville. The text grew from hard bargaining between the old ruling party and the liberation movements, under an interim charter of 1993. A new Constitutional Court checked the draft against agreed principles before it could stand.

The constitution writes the end of apartheid into supreme law: human dignity, equality, and freedom are its founding values. Its bill of rights runs deeper than most, covering housing, health care, food, and water alongside speech and fair trial. Eleven official languages receive recognition. Born of negotiation between old foes, the charter became the most admired founding law of its time. It is, in Mandela's phrase at its signing, the birth certificate of the new South African nation.
spenser-faerie-queene-vol2-1596:
Edmund Spenser published the second installment of The Faerie Queene in 1596, adding three more books to his great allegorical poem. He never finished the planned twelve books. This volume holds Books Four through Six, together with the surviving fragment of Book Seven.

Book Four treats Friendship, Book Five Justice, and Book Six Courtesy, each through its own knight's adventures. Sir Artegall, the justice knight, carries a sword that levels all excuses. The fragment called the Mutabilitie Cantos stages a trial of Change herself before Nature. Spenser's invention never flags, and his stanza keeps its music. The unfinished poem still stands as the longest major work of the English Renaissance.
the-folly-of-eustace-1896: Hichens wrote of Eustace's folly in this 1896 novel. The young man's mistakes drive the plot. A Victorian moral tale. Writers of history may cite it later. The book preserves that story. The paper lived through the years.
the-jargon-file-version-4-0-0-24-jul-199: Eric Raymond's Jargon File, the hacker's dictionary: the slang, humor, and folklore of computer culture. From "foo" to "wizard," it documents a tribe's language. The Rosetta Stone of geek culture, and very funny. Reading it is like eavesdropping on the tribe that built the internet.
the-little-lame-prince-pg496: Dinah Craik's Little Lame Prince (1875) follows a disabled prince finding strength. His crutch becomes a surprising gift. The Tower library holds the full text. It champions kind hearts over strong legs. Adversity builds character deeply. Victorian children loved the tale dearly. The prince's courage inspires still.
the-phrenological-magazine-volume-12-new: The Phrenological Magazine, volume 12, new series, 1896. Another volume. This book preserves that periodical. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
the-return-of-the-soul-1896: The Return of the Soul, 1896, Robert Hichens's novel. The soul's return. This book preserves that story. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
tob-0096:
Johann Weyer, a Dutch physician of the sixteenth century, risked his name to argue that accused witches were mostly sick, deluded old women. His collected works, the Opera Omnia, include De Lamiis, his writing on witches. Where judges saw pacts with the devil, Weyer saw melancholy and fraud.

He urged courts to use doctors, not torturers, and to punish real crimes rather than imagined flights and sabbaths. Few listened in his lifetime, and witch trials rolled on. Later ages honored him as an early founder of psychiatry. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10096:
Richard Rolle of Hampole was a fourteenth-century English hermit who wrote short prose guides for people seeking a holy life. The Form of Perfect Living and companion treatises gathered here rank among the earliest devotional prose in English. Rolle addressed beginners as well as advanced souls, often in a direct personal voice.

Readers get practical counsel on prayer, resisting temptation, and ordering daily life around love of God. Rolle wrote from experience, not theory, and described tasting the sweetness of that love in urgent terms that can still startle. His guides show medieval English devotion before print, written by a solitary for individual readers.
tob-10496:
Julian of Norwich, an anchoress walled into a cell beside a Norwich church, received sixteen showings, or visions, of Christ's love during a serious illness. She spent about twenty years pondering their meaning before her Revelations of Divine Love reached its fuller form. Her assurance that all shall be well anchors the text.

Julian writes tender, daring theology: God's love is homely and courteous, Christ is also our mother, and sin shall somehow not have the last word. Remarkably, hers is the first book in English known to be written by a woman. Readers from the 1300s onward have treasured its calm confidence.
tob-10796:
Arthur Lloyd, a scholar and missionary who lived in Japan, wrote Hinduism and Buddhism as a study of the two faiths side by side. He knew Asia from long residence, not just from books. His tone is respectful for a writer of his time and church.

Lloyd traces each faith's history, core doctrines, and holy books, then marks where they meet and part. Buddhism grew from Hindu soil, and he shows how karma, rebirth, and release changed as they passed between them. The survey gives general readers of its era a fair, clear bridge between Eastern faiths and Western questions.
tob-4096:
H. Kern, the Dutch scholar, translated the Saddharma Pundarika, known in English as the Lotus Sutra. East Asia's most beloved Mahayana scripture teaches that the Buddha used many skillful means, stories and promises suited to each hearer, to lead all beings toward one final awakening.

Parables carry the teaching: a burning house, a rain cloud that waters all plants alike, a father's hidden jewel. The sutra promises Buddhahood for everyone, without exception. Kern's rendering became the classic Western version. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The Lotus's place in Buddhist devotion needs no proof beyond its reach.
un-sc-res-1296:
Protection of civilians in war was taken up as a theme by the Security Council on 19 April 2000. The Secretary-General had reported on the subject in September 1999, and a working group set up by resolution 1265 (1999) had studied it. The Council voiced regret that civilians form the vast majority of casualties in today's conflicts. Combatants increasingly target them on purpose, above all women, children, refugees, and the displaced.

The Council restated its strong condemnation of the deliberate targeting of civilians. It said protection work must proceed case by case, on the facts of each conflict. It stressed safe and free access for humanitarian workers to people in need. States and parties were reminded of their duties under humanitarian, human rights, and refugee law. The Secretary-General was invited to keep bringing situations to the Council's notice. The text fixed civilian protection as a standing item in peacekeeping mandates.
un-sc-res-1396: Catalogued with a 2002 date, Resolution 1396 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-1496: Resolution 1496 is one of the Security Council's numbered formal acts, kept here as a transcription of the UN's official record from English Wikisource. Inside the text, the members state their findings in opening clauses before turning to decisions. Historians and lawyers use such texts directly, because a single verb in an operative paragraph can change what a government must do.
un-sc-res-1596:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo moved through the Council as Resolution 1596, adopted on 18 April 2005. The arms embargo set in 2003 covered only the restive east. Guns still flowed freely to armed groups in the Kivus and Ituri. Some militias had begun listing their weapons for disarmament, but many had not.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council widens the embargo to cover every recipient in the whole country. It adds travel bans and asset freezes for people the sanctions committee names as violators. Regional states must ground aircraft with false papers and tighten customs checks. Authorized arms shipments may go only to sites named in advance. A review follows by 31 July 2005.
un-sc-res-1696:
Resolution 1696 was the Security Council's first binding vote on Iran's nuclear program, passed in July 2006. Iran had restarted work on enriching uranium, a process that can fuel reactors or bombs. The Council demanded that Tehran stop that work and prove its peaceful intent.

The text gives Iran a deadline and warns that more steps, possibly sanctions, would follow if it refused. It backs the inspectors of the International Atomic Energy Agency as the judges of Iran's conduct. Readers see the opening move in a long standoff that shaped Middle East politics for years afterward.
un-sc-res-1796:
Nepal's mission was renewed one year after its creation, on 23 January 2008. The Council recalled resolution 1740 (2007), which had set up UNMIN. The seven-party alliance had reached a 23-point agreement on 23 December 2007. It fixed constituent assembly elections for 10 April 2008. Nepal's government wrote on 18 December asking for six more months of the mission.

Following that request and the Secretary-General's advice, the Council renewed UNMIN's mandate as set out in resolution 1740 until 23 July 2008. It voiced full support for the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and called on all parties to apply their deals without delay. The parties were urged to use UNMIN's expertise and help as the election neared. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed of progress. Nepal's parties were also asked to protect mission staff and speed the unfinished peace work.
un-sc-res-1896:
On the Council's agenda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo drew Resolution 1896, adopted on 30 November 2009. Armed groups still held ground in the Kivus, Ituri, and Orientale. Outside networks kept supplying them. Civilians faced killings, flight, child recruitment, and widespread sexual violence.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms, transport, travel, and money measures until 30 November 2010. The Group of Experts keeps working to that date, with reports due in May and October 2010. The experts must also draft due care rules for firms that buy Congolese minerals. Buyers should check where minerals come from, so trade stops feeding armed groups. States should publish trade figures for gold and key ores.
un-sc-res-1996:
South Sudan became the world's newest country in July 2011, and Resolution 1996 created its UN peace mission days before independence. The new state split from Sudan after a referendum and decades of war. The mission, UNMISS, was set up to help the government keep peace.

The text gives UNMISS troops and police to protect civilians, support the new state's institutions, and watch the border with Sudan. When civil war broke out inside South Sudan in 2013, that protection duty became the mission's whole story. The founding text shows what the world hoped for the new country at its birth.
un-sc-res-396:
The Sinai emergency force came up for renewal in the autumn of 1976. On 22 October 1976 the Security Council extended the United Nations Emergency Force for six months. The new term ran until 24 October 1977. The Secretary-General had reported on the force and on events in the Middle East. He warned that letting the search for a full settlement relax could prove dangerous. The Council shared that worry.

The parties again had to carry out resolution 338 at once. The Council voiced confidence the force would run with care and economy. China and Libya did not take part in the vote. The force by then was a settled part of the post-1973 landscape.
un-sc-res-96:
A United Nations envoy's Kashmir plan won the Council's support in 1951. Frank Graham had proposed a path to demilitarize the disputed state. India and Pakistan both accepted parts of his plan. They restated their wish for a peaceful settlement. They also accepted that the state's future would follow the will of its people. On 10 November 1951 the Council noted those agreements with pleasure.

Graham had to keep working for a full demilitarization deal. Both parties had to cooperate with him to the fullest degree. He owed the Council a report within six weeks. It would carry his view of the problems before him. His mission lasted years without closing the gap. The demilitarization deadlock froze the Kashmir question in place.
un-sc-res-996:
The Golan Heights observer force gained another six months in May 1995. On 30 May 1995 the Security Council renewed UNDOF until 30 November 1995. The Secretary-General had reported on the force that month. The Council followed its long-standing pattern for the mission. UNDOF watches the separation zone between Israel and Syria. It has done so since 1974.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. The Secretary-General owed a report at the end of the term. It would cover events and steps taken toward carrying out 338. Renewals like this one kept a quiet border under steady watch. The text is short, in the mission's standard form.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1296, adopted on 19 April 2000, is the Council's second major statement on protecting civilians in war. A report from the Secretary-General and work by an informal group set it up. The text regrets plainly that civilians form the vast majority of casualties in armed conflict and are increasingly targeted on purpose, with women, children, refugees, and displaced people hit hardest.

Building on the first civilians resolution of 1999, this one turns concern into a working agenda for peace operations and humanitarian access. It treats attacks on civilians not as side effects but as matters the Council itself must answer, linking their protection to durable peace, reconciliation, and development. Later protection mandates in peacekeeping grew out of this framework.

A change at the top of the peace effort in Bosnia and Herzegovina is welcomed on 5 March 2002. The Peace Implementation Council's Steering Board had named a new High Representative, the international official overseeing the 1995 peace agreement, to succeed the outgoing holder. The Council thanked the outgoing official for his work.

Beyond the appointment, the text looks ahead to the end of the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which included the International Police Task Force. Appreciation is expressed for the mission's work on carrying out the peace agreement. Planning for an efficient handover to whatever presence would take over its tasks is also noted.

At Lebanon's request, UNIFIL is renewed until 31 January 2004 in this text of 31 July 2003. The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's July report and its advice to renew. The renewal follows the same pattern as earlier ones since Israel's 2000 withdrawal.

All violence is condemned, and grave concern is voiced at serious breaches of the withdrawal line by air, sea, and land. The parties are urged to end those violations and to respect the safety of United Nations personnel. UNIFIL is to keep full freedom of movement in its area. Lebanon is again pressed to extend its authority in the south, and mine clearance work is supported.

Congo's arms embargo is widened to the whole country and given financial teeth in Resolution 1596, adopted on 18 April 2005. The Group of Experts had reported on the weapons flow feeding armed groups in North and South Kivu and Ituri. The embargo imposed by Resolution 1493 (2003) was due for strengthening as the transitional government integrated its forces.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides the embargo now applies to any recipient in Congolese territory. Exemptions cover integrated army and police units, MONUC, and notified non-lethal equipment. It orders regional governments to police aviation under the Chicago Convention, ground non-compliant aircraft, keep flight registries, and strengthen customs controls on the Ituri and Kivu borders. It also adds a travel ban and asset freeze on persons the Committee designates as embargo violators, with humanitarian exemptions. It focuses MONUC and Group of Experts monitoring on the Kivus and Ituri.

Iran's nuclear programme draws the first binding Council action on 31 July 2006. The atomic energy agency had reported many open questions about Iran's work, including topics that could have a military side, and could not confirm that no hidden nuclear material or activity existed. Six powers had offered Iran a long-term deal, which it had not accepted.

Acting under Chapter VII, Iran is demanded to suspend all enrichment-related and reprocessing work, including research, in a form the agency can verify. Iran is called on to take the steps the agency's board required to build confidence that its programme is purely peaceful. The six powers' offer of a negotiated long-term arrangement is endorsed. Fourteen members voted in favour and one, Qatar, voted against.

Resolution 1796, adopted on 23 January 2008, extends the UN political mission in Nepal for six months. Nepal's government and the Maoists had signed their peace agreement in November 2006, and the UN mission, UNMIN, was monitoring arms and fighters while helping prepare elections. A seven-party deal reached on 23 December 2007 pointed to a constituent assembly vote on 10 April 2008.

The Council renewed UNMIN's mandate to July 2008. It reaffirmed Nepal's sovereignty and its ownership of the peace process, promising continued support for carrying out the agreements. Civil society's role in preventing conflict was noted, and the tight election timetable, requiring effort from every party, was frankly acknowledged.

Congo's sanctions are renewed with a new focus on minerals in Resolution 1896, adopted on 30 November 2009. The Group of Experts' 2009 reports documented how armed groups in the Kivus, Ituri, and Orientale lived off illegal resource exploitation and outside support networks. The groups included the FDLR and the Lord's Resistance Army. All this came amid killings, mass displacement, and widespread sexual violence.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo, transport controls, and the financial and travel measures until 30 November 2010. It extends the Group of Experts to the same date. The Group gains a new task: drafting due-diligence guidelines for importers, processors, and consumers of Congolese minerals, covering how to check a supply chain's origin. States are called on to make their mineral buyers exercise that diligence and to publish full import and export statistics for gold, cassiterite, coltan, and wolframite.

Malta applied to join the United Nations within weeks of becoming independent, and Resolution 196 answered on 30 October 1964. The Security Council examined the Mediterranean island nation's application and voted unanimously in its favor. Malta had ended British rule in September of that year.

All the resolution does is recommend that the Assembly seat Malta as a member. Brief as it is, that recommendation carried legal weight, since the Assembly cannot seat a new member without it. The text preserves the formal instant when Malta, a small island state between Sicily and North Africa, entered the international community as a sovereign equal.

South Sudan became an independent country on 9 July 2011, and the Council acted the day before to help it start well. Resolution 1996, adopted on 8 July 2011, created a United Nations mission for the new republic. The new state faced weak institutions and continuing violence. Building a state while keeping the peace was a hard task.

The mission, called UNMISS, began work on 9 July 2011 for an initial period of one year. It could have up to 7,000 military personnel and 900 civilian police. Its job was to strengthen peace and security in the new country. It also had to help create conditions for development. The Council authorized the mission to use all necessary means, within its abilities, to protect civilians who were under threat.

Bahrain's admission to the United Nations is recommended in Resolution 296, adopted unanimously on 18 August 1971. The Council welcomed the island state's application rather than merely noting it, a small warmth in an otherwise formula-bound text. Bahrain had just ended its long treaty relationship with Britain and declared independence that same month.

The operative sentence asks the General Assembly to admit Bahrain to membership. Under the Charter that request is the gate every new member must pass through, since the Assembly acts only on the Council's recommendation. Read today, the short resolution marks the start of Bahrain's life as a UN member, as the small Gulf archipelago took its seat beside far larger states.

Odd dates haunt this file. Some lists place it in 1973. The text's own chain of past votes runs to October 1975. Its term reaches to 24 October 1977. The vote, thirteen to none at the 1964th meeting, fits the fall of 1976. China and Libya sat the vote out. The topic was the Sinai peace force, UNEF.

The force stayed on past its old term. The new end date was 24 October 1977. The chief UN official had urged a full year's stay. The text pairs the move with a call to act on the 1973 ceasefire text. It also voices trust that the force would run with thrift. A report was due at the close. Such Sinai renewals kept a buffer in place while peace talks crawled.

Kashmir's fate still turned on a vote that would not come. Frank Graham, the UN's man for India and Pakistan, had a plan. He set it out on 7 September 1951. Troops of both states would thin out in step. Then a free poll could fix the land's path. Resolution 96 passed on 10 November 1951 by nine votes to none. India and the Soviet team held back.

The Council cheered the parts both sides had sworn to. Peace, a firm truce, and a fair poll won praise. Graham was told to push on for the full plan. Both states had to work with him to the hilt. His word on the quest was due in six weeks. The text is warm in tone. Yet the poll at its heart stayed a pledge, not a date.

At its meeting on 30 May 1995, the Council renewed a peacekeeping mandate in the Golan Heights. The mission was the UN Disengagement Observer Force. Its soldiers watch the buffer zone between Israel and Syria. The decision rested on the Secretary-General's report of 17 May 1995.

The renewal ran for six more months, ending on 30 November 1995. Members also called on Israel and Syria to carry out Resolution 338 from 1973. That older text demanded a ceasefire in the October war. It also called for talks toward a lasting peace. The Secretary-General was asked to report again when the new period ended.
uncle-sam-s-letters-on-phrenology-to-his: Uncle Sam's Letters on Phrenology, 1896. The American letters. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
vanthoff-studies-chemical-dynamics-cohen:
Jacobus Henricus van't Hoff made reaction rates a science in Studies in Chemical Dynamics. Thomas Ewan translated the work into English in 1896, in a version revised by Ernst Cohen. Chemical kinetics, the study of how fast reactions run, is its field. Van't Hoff asked what heat, pressure, and mix do to that speed.

He measures reactions, sorts them by order, and states the rules they follow. Temperature receives close care, since small rises can double a rate. The book founded much of physical chemistry's kinetic side. Its methods still echo in modern lab practice. Readers meet a young field learning to measure itself. The clarity of the experiments stands out.
verses-1889-1896: This volume gathers verses from 1889 to 1896. Years versed. The Tower library holds the full text. It versed years. Poets sang. Decades turned. Lines kept. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
waite-turba-philosophorum-1896:
Old sages meet to swap lore in The Turba Philosophorum, a famed text set in English by A. E. Waite in 1896. The name means the crowd of wise men. Each sage speaks in turn on the great art: how base stuff turns to gold, and what signs rule the work.

The speech is dark, rich in beast and star signs. Waite adds notes to help the fan through the fog. The text had drawn adepts for a host of years in tongue past tongue. His take gave it to English fans in full. The Latin name Turba means a crowd in a stir and rout. That rout fits the clash of proud sages in the text quite well.
warren-buddhism-in-translations-1896:
Henry Clarke Warren, a Harvard scholar who worked from a wheelchair after a spinal injury, published Buddhism in Translations in 1896. The anthology appeared in the Harvard Oriental Series, which Warren himself helped to fund. It was the pioneering English source-book of Pali Buddhist texts.

Warren translates passages on the Buddha's life, his sermons, monastic rule, and the path to nirvana from the Pali canon. He orders the extracts so a beginner can follow the teaching as a connected whole. Generations of students first met Buddhism through Warren's careful, sympathetic selections. Warren hoped the book would let Buddhism speak in its own words.
washington-farewell-address-1796:
George Washington published his Farewell Address in 1796, as he left office. The retiring president offers counsel to the nation he helped create. No state paper in American history has been quoted more often.

Shun fixed alliances with foreign powers, Washington warns his countrymen. Beware the spirit of party, and cherish the Union above all. He defends his record while refusing a third term in power. The address reads as the founding father's last political testament. Its warnings on factions and foreign ties still frame debate today in Washington. Schoolchildren once learned its closing lines by heart across the young republic.
wells-island-doctor-moreau-1896:
H. G. Wells wrote The Island of Doctor Moreau in 1896. A castaway named Prendick washes up on a lone isle in the Pacific. A man named Moreau runs the isle, with a grim mate and strange staff. Shrieks from a locked lab tell Prendick that dark work goes on there.

Moreau cuts beasts into man shapes by pain and craft. His Beast Folk learn a Law that bids them not act as beasts. The law frays, the beasts turn, and the isle falls to fire and blood. The tale still stings as a probe of man's place in nature.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-7-189:
Thomas Vaughan's Euphrates, or the Waters of the East, fills volume seven of Westcott's series. Vaughan wrote the mystical treatise in 1655 under the name Eugenius Philalethes. Westcott's 1896 reissue adds Florence Farr's full commentary.

Vaughan pours fiery prose on God, nature, and magic into his pages. He attacks dry scholars and defends a living, enchanted philosophy of nature. Farr, the Golden Dawn's leading adept, explains his symbols for modern readers. Her commentary reads seventeenth-century theosophy through nineteenth-century occult eyes. The pairing shows two eras of English mysticism in conversation. Vaughan's twin brother was the poet Henry Vaughan, which adds literary interest.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-8-189:
Florence Farr wrote Egyptian Magic as volume eight of Westcott's Collectanea Hermetica in 1896. Farr was an actress, a Golden Dawn leader, and a serious student of Egypt. She wrote under her order motto, S.S.D.D., in the original edition.

Her handbook treats Egyptian ritual magic from temple texts and museum study. She explains gods, symbols, and invocations in a practical spirit. Farr approached the material as a working magician, not only a scholar. The result is part scholarship and part grimoire in one slim volume. It shows how the Victorian occult revival imagined ancient Egypt. Farr's authority inside the Golden Dawn gave her reading wide influence.
westcott-collectanea-hermetica-vol-9-189:
W. Wynn Westcott wrote Numbers: Their Occult Power and Mystic Virtues, first published in 1890. Westcott's Collectanea Hermetica reissued it as volume nine in 1896. The handbook catalogues number symbolism from one upward.

Why is seven lucky and thirteen feared in popular lore? Westcott collects answers from Pythagoras, Kabbalah, astrology, and scripture. Each number receives its virtues, gods, and traditional associations in turn. The Golden Dawn used the book as a pocket reference for symbolism. Compact and endlessly quotable, it served students building rituals and talismans. Westcott's medical day job contrasts oddly with this lore. The handbook still introduces readers to Western numerology.
whiston-new-theory-of-the-earth-1696:
William Whiston published A New Theory of the Earth in 1696, fresh from Cambridge. Whiston succeeded Isaac Newton in the Lucasian chair of mathematics. His theory explains the Earth by comets and the biblical Deluge. A comet's watery tail and mantle, he argues, flooded the young world.

He runs the planet's story from creation to its final conflagration by fire. Scripture and the new astronomy must agree, in his scheme, when both are read rightly. The book made comet impact diluvialism a learned position. Its boldness drew fame and trouble in equal share. Whiston's later heresy troubles began in this vein. The theory stands as a landmark of its kind.
white-warfare-science-vol-1-1896:
Andrew Dickson White published Volume 1 of A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom in 1896. White was a founder and first president of Cornell University. He documents, field by field, how theology resisted new science. Astronomy, geology, and geography open the case.

White insists his quarrel is with dogma, not with religion itself. He piles up cases: flat earth claims, comet fears, and bans on anatomy. Critics charged him with bias, and later historians revised many stories. Yet the two volumes became the conflict thesis's main arsenal. They shaped popular views of science and faith for a century. Volume 1 lays the foundation.
white-warfare-science-vol-2-1896:
Andrew Dickson White completed his Warfare of Science with Volume 2 in 1896. This volume moves from medicine and insanity to economics and language. White shows church authority resisting hospitals, vaccination, and new views of disease. He also treats the study of society and the age of the earth.

His method stays the same: case after case, drawn from documents. The tone is earnest and reforming rather than mocking. White wanted science free and religion purified of dogma. Historians now qualify his sharp warfare metaphor. The book remains a vast, readable storehouse of the debate. Together the volumes mark a peak of Victorian liberal history.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-1-1896:
William Angus Knight, a Scottish scholar and Wordsworth devotee, edited the standard eight-volume Poetical Works of Wordsworth in the 1890s. This first volume appeared in 1896. Knight arranged the poems by date and supplied notes from his long study of the poet's life and places.

The volume holds Wordsworth's earliest poems, written from 1787 to 1797, before fame arrived. Readers find schoolboy verse, his first published sonnets, and the young radical's descriptive sketches of France and the Lakes. The long poem An Evening Walk and Descriptive Sketches show his gift still forming. For students, this volume is the entry point to the complete Wordsworth in Knight's careful edition.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-2-1896:
William Wordsworth stands with Coleridge at the head of the Romantic school in England. William Angus Knight put out his Poetical Works in eight books in 1896. Book two holds poems from the year 1803 in Knight's plan of the set. Knight was a Scots sage who gave his life to the poet.

Wordsworth's verse turns on nature, youth, and the mind's growth through calm recall. Short lyrics and sonnets fill much of his work of these years. His plain tongue was a revolt in its day against stiff verse. The set is a stock full dress of the poet's work for its age.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-3-1896:
William Angus Knight's edition of Wordsworth's Poetical Works ran to eight volumes and was the standard text for years. This third volume appeared in 1896. Knight ordered the poems by their dates of writing and added his own notes throughout.

The poems here date from 1803 to 1808, Wordsworth's greatest period. Readers find the Intimations Ode, the daffodils lyric, and many of his finest sonnets in these years. Poems of national feeling, written under the threat of French invasion, stand beside quiet lyrics of memory and loss. The volume captures Wordsworth at his peak, when nearly everything he wrote turned lasting.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-4-1896:
William Angus Knight's dress of Wordsworth's Poetical Works ran to eight books in 1896. Book four stands at the mid point of that set. Wordsworth was the great voice of the Romantic turn in English verse. His poems span more than fifty years of work.

His verse dwells on hills, lakes, and the folk of the north country. It holds that a calm mind, fed by nature's forms, grows wise and kind. Knight sorts the poems with notes on their dates and first prints. The set served schools and homes as the full Wordsworth of its day.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-5-1896:
Book five of Knight's 1896 Poetical Works of Wordsworth takes the set past its mid point. The full set runs to eight books in all. William Wordsworth wrote verse from his youth to his old age as Poet Laureate. Knight was the great Wordsworth man of his age in Scotland.

The poems range from brief songs to long tales in verse of dales folk. Wordsworth's themes hold firm: nature, memory, loss, and the quiet mind. His Ode on the hints of a life past death is one of his famed works. The set gives the whole arc of a long life in verse.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-6-1896:
Book six of the Knight dress of Wordsworth's poems came out in 1896. William Angus Knight built the set in eight books in all. William Wordsworth's long life in verse fills the set from first to last. By book six the work moves deep into his full store.

Wordsworth's art joins high thought to the speech of plain folk. He made the Lakes his ground and the mind's growth his great theme. The Prelude, his long tale of his own mind, crowns his work as a whole. Knight's notes guide the reader through dates, drafts, and prints of each piece.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-7-1896:
Book seven of Knight's Poetical Works of Wordsworth came out in 1896. The set runs to eight books in all and nears its end here. William Wordsworth was Poet Laureate in his last years. William Angus Knight, his editor, was a Scots sage and a keen fan.

Late verse holds its place with the bright work of his youth in this set. Wordsworth kept his themes to the end: nature's calm, the past, and faith. His sonnets on church, state, and old tales fill long runs of his work. The set is the full shelf of the poet for the age that made it.
wordsworth-poetical-works-vol-8-1896:
Book eight ends Knight's dress of the Poetical Works of Wordsworth. The set came out in 1896 in eight books in all. William Wordsworth died in 1850 as the grand old man of English verse. Knight's work gave the age its full Wordsworth in one run.

Wordsworth's fame rests on lyrics, sonnets, and long poems of the mind and the Lakes. He and Coleridge had set verse on a new path with Lyrical Ballads in 1798. Knight's last book rounds out the poems with the aid of his notes. The set still serves as a full text of the poet.
